entries.meaning: From Qatar, or relating to Qatar and its people. ---
examples: A Qatari airline sponsors the tournament.
The stadium was built with Qatari money.
My lab partner is Qatari.
entries.contrast: Always capitalized. A Qatari for a person is a noun, not an adjective.

entries.meaning: Falsely claiming to have medical knowledge or to cure people. ---
examples: He spent thousands on quack remedies.
A quack doctor sold them fake vitamins.
The clinic pushes quack cures for cancer.
entries.contrast: Also a noun (a quack is a fake doctor) and a verb (ducks quack). As an adjective it goes only before a noun: say The remedy is a fraud, not The remedy is quack.

entries.meaning: In math: involving a quantity multiplied by itself, that is, squared. ---
examples: We solved the quadratic equation in class.
She still remembers the quadratic formula from tenth grade.
The growth is quadratic, not linear.

entries.meaning: Having four straight sides. ---
examples: A trapezoid is a quadrilateral shape.
Draw any quadrilateral figure on the board.
The old fort is roughly quadrilateral.
entries.contrast: Also a noun: a square is a quadrilateral.

entries.meaning: Made up of four parts, or four times as big or as many. ---
examples: He had a quadruple bypass last spring.
Police are investigating a quadruple homicide.
She landed a quadruple jump in competition.
entries.contrast: Also a verb (Sales quadrupled last year). For the surgery and the crime the noun after it stays singular: a quadruple bypass, a quadruple homicide.

entries.meaning: Quaint has 2 distinct senses.
examples: They stayed in a quaint little inn on the coast.
It's the quaintest town in New England.
He has a quaint habit of writing thank-you letters.
The idea of a landline seems quaint now.

senses.head: Attractive in an old-fashioned way
examples: They stayed in a quaint little inn on the coast.
It's the quaintest town in New England.

senses.head: Odd or out of date in a way that amuses you
examples: He has a quaint habit of writing thank-you letters.
The idea of a landline seems quaint now.

entries.comparison: -er/-est or more/most — quainter, quaintest or more quaint, most quaint
entries.contrast: It can sound condescending: calling someone's beliefs quaint says they are charmingly out of date.

entries.meaning: Relating to the nature or kind of something rather than to amounts. ---
examples: The study used qualitative interviews instead of surveys.
There is a qualitative difference between the two recordings.
Her research is mostly qualitative.
entries.contrast: A false friend. Russian качественный usually means of good quality — that is quality or high-quality in English. Qualitative only contrasts with quantitative: about kind, not about amount.

entries.meaning: Of a high standard. ---
examples: They sell quality furniture at a fair price.
We try to spend quality time together on weekends.
Quality childcare is hard to find here.
entries.contrast: Mostly a noun (the quality of the work). As an adjective it goes only before a noun; after a verb say high-quality: The tools are high-quality, not The tools are quality.

entries.meaning: Able to be measured or expressed in numbers. ---
examples: The benefits are real but not easily quantifiable.
Give me quantifiable goals for the quarter.
Air quality is more quantifiable than customer mood.

entries.meaning: Relating to amounts and numbers. ---
examples: The report includes quantitative data from 3,000 users.
He works on the quantitative side of the fund.
Their evidence is quantitative rather than anecdotal.

entries.meaning: Kept away from other people or animals so that a disease cannot spread. ---
examples: The quarantined passengers stayed on the ship for a week.
Our whole class was quarantined after the outbreak.
New birds are kept quarantined for thirty days.

entries.meaning: Arguing often, and looking for a fight. ---
examples: Two quarrelsome neighbors dragged the whole street into court.
He gets quarrelsome after a couple of drinks.
The committee is more quarrelsome than it used to be.

entries.meaning: Happening or produced four times a year. ---
examples: The quarterly report comes out in April.
Freelancers pay quarterly taxes.
She writes for a quarterly literary magazine.
entries.form: -ly from quarter — an -ly adjective, not an adverb here
entries.contrast: Quarterly is also an adverb (The board meets quarterly) and a noun (a literary quarterly). As an adjective it stays before the noun: the quarterly report.

entries.meaning: Queasy has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Boats make me queasy.
I felt queasier with every curve in the road.
Investors are queasy about the merger.
The whole plan gives me a queasy feeling.

senses.head: Feeling as if you might vomit
examples: Boats make me queasy.
I felt queasier with every curve in the road.

senses.head: Uneasy and worried about something
examples: Investors are queasy about the merger.
The whole plan gives me a queasy feeling.

entries.meaning: Of a bed or bedding: fairly large — bigger than a full, smaller than a king. ---
examples: The room has a queen-size bed.
We need queen-size sheets, not king.
A queen-size mattress won't fit up those stairs.
entries.form: compound — queen + size; queen-sized is just as common
entries.contrast: A US bed-size word. From small to large: twin, full, queen-size, king-size. A queen-size bed is about 60 by 80 inches.

entries.meaning: Queer has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She writes about queer history in the Midwest.
The festival celebrates queer artists.
He came out as queer in college.
There was something queer about the whole story.
He felt a bit queer after the shot.

senses.head: Relating to people who are not heterosexual or not cisgender
examples: She writes about queer history in the Midwest.
The festival celebrates queer artists.
He came out as queer in college.

senses.head: Old-fashioned: strange or odd
examples: There was something queer about the whole story.
He felt a bit queer after the shot.

entries.comparison: not gradable — in the identity sense; the old strange sense took queerer, queerest
entries.contrast: Once a slur, now reclaimed and used neutrally by many LGBTQ people, in academic writing and in queer studies. Still, do not apply it to an individual who has not used it of themselves. The strange sense is old-fashioned and now sounds odd in American English.

entries.meaning: Complaining in a weak, irritated way. ---
examples: A querulous voice came from the back row.
He grew querulous in his last years.
Her emails get more querulous every week.
entries.contrast: Not related to query. It describes a whiny, complaining tone, not a questioning one.

entries.meaning: Probably not true, honest or good — worth doubting. ---
examples: The numbers came from a questionable source.
Several of the expenses look questionable.
His taste in movies is even more questionable than mine.

entries.meaning: Showing that you have doubts or want an answer. ---
examples: She gave me a questioning look.
He raised a questioning eyebrow.
Students today take a more questioning attitude toward authority.

entries.meaning: Quick has 3 distinct senses.
examples: She's a quick walker — I can never keep up.
Is there a quicker way downtown?
He's always quick to blame someone else.
I took a quick shower and left.
Can we have a quick word before the meeting?
She's quick — she picked up the software in a day.
He has a quick mind and a sharp tongue.

senses.head: Moving or happening fast
examples: She's a quick walker — I can never keep up.
Is there a quicker way downtown?
He's always quick to blame someone else.

senses.head: Taking only a short time
examples: I took a quick shower and left.
Can we have a quick word before the meeting?

senses.head: Able to understand and learn fast
examples: She's quick — she picked up the software in a day.
He has a quick mind and a sharp tongue.

entries.contrast: The adverb is quickly. Come quick! is informal speech; in writing use quickly. Fast is about speed of movement, quick often about a short time: a fast car, a quick trip.

entries.meaning: Getting angry very easily. ---
examples: His father was quick-tempered and everyone in town knew it.
She's less quick-tempered than she was at twenty.
A quick-tempered coach can lose a locker room fast.

entries.meaning: Able to think and answer fast, often in a funny way. ---
examples: The host is quick-witted and never loses the room.
A quick-witted clerk stopped the scam.
You have to be more quick-witted than that to do stand-up.

entries.meaning: Made of two layers of cloth sewn together with padding in between. ---
examples: She wore a quilted jacket over her sweater.
The bedspread is quilted by hand.
Quilted oven mitts protect your hands better.

entries.meaning: Being the most perfect example of a type. ---
examples: He's the quintessential New Yorker — loud, kind, always late.
Diners are the quintessential American restaurant.
That album is quintessential seventies rock.
entries.comparison: not gradable — it already means the most typical
entries.form: from quintessence — the purest form of something

entries.meaning: Unusual in a likable, slightly odd way. ---
examples: It's a quirky little bookstore with a cat in the window.
Her second novel is even quirkier than the first.
He has a quirky sense of humor.

entries.meaning: Having generous, idealistic plans that have almost no chance of working. ---
examples: He launched a quixotic run for governor.
The plan is noble but more quixotic than practical.
Her quixotic campaign to save the old theater lasted two years.
entries.contrast: The pronunciation does not follow the name: kwik-SAH-tik, not kee-HOH-tik.

entries.meaning: Showing that you are puzzled, often with some amusement. ---
examples: He gave her a quizzical look.
She raised one eyebrow in a quizzical expression.
The second question got an even more quizzical look than the first.

entries.meaning: Worth quoting, or saying things that people like to repeat. ---
examples: The coach is endlessly quotable.
It's the most quotable movie of the decade.
He wrote a short, quotable line for the poster.

entries.meaning: Stirring up the anger of a crowd, usually for political ends. ---
examples: He gave a rabble-rousing speech outside the capitol.
The paper called her a rabble-rousing populist.
His second speech was even more rabble-rousing than the first.
entries.form: compound — noun + -ing participle; a rabble is a disorderly crowd

entries.meaning: Rabid has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He's a rabid Yankees fan.
The bill faces rabid opposition in the Senate.
Her most rabid supporters lined up at five in the morning.
A rabid raccoon bit the neighbor's dog.
Animal control caught a rabid fox behind the school.

senses.head: Extreme and fanatical in your opinions or support
examples: He's a rabid Yankees fan.
The bill faces rabid opposition in the Senate.
Her most rabid supporters lined up at five in the morning.

senses.head: Of an animal: having rabies
examples: A rabid raccoon bit the neighbor's dog.
Animal control caught a rabid fox behind the school.

entries.position: both — the rabies sense mostly before a noun
entries.comparison: more/most — more rabid, most rabid (the fanatical sense only)

entries.meaning: Relating to race, or to relations between races. ---
examples: The city studied racial disparities in housing.
Racial profiling is against department policy.
They talked about racial justice in the classroom.
entries.contrast: Racial is neutral and simply names the category (racial demographics). Racist is a judgment: it means based on prejudice. A racial comment is not the same as a racist comment.

entries.meaning: Showing or based on prejudice against people of another race. ---
examples: He was fired for a racist joke.
The policy had a racist effect, whatever its intent.
His later columns were even more openly racist.
entries.contrast: Also a noun (He's a racist). Keep it apart from the neutral racial.

entries.meaning: Slightly shocking, usually because of sexual content. ---
examples: The novel was considered racy in 1955.
She posted a racier photo than usual.
It's a racy comedy — don't watch it with your parents.
entries.contrast: Nothing to do with race the contest or race the group of people — it means mildly sexual.

entries.meaning: Radiant has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The bride looked radiant.
She gave us the most radiant smile.
He was radiant with pride at the ceremony.
Radiant heat from the floor warms the whole room.
The radiant glow of the fire filled the cabin.

senses.head: Looking very happy, in a way that shows on your face
examples: The bride looked radiant.
She gave us the most radiant smile.
He was radiant with pride at the ceremony.

senses.head: Sending out light or heat
examples: Radiant heat from the floor warms the whole room.
The radiant glow of the fire filled the cabin.

entries.meaning: Radical has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The company made radical changes to the schedule.
We need a more radical rethink of the budget.
She had radical surgery and recovered well.
She joined a radical student group in the seventies.
His views got more radical over the years.

senses.head: Complete and far-reaching, especially of a change
examples: The company made radical changes to the schedule.
We need a more radical rethink of the budget.
She had radical surgery and recovered well.

senses.head: Supporting extreme political or social change
examples: She joined a radical student group in the seventies.
His views got more radical over the years.

entries.contrast: Also a noun (a radical). Beyond the political meaning that Russian радикальный shares, English radical often just means thorough and far-reaching: a radical redesign is not a political statement.

entries.meaning: Operated from a distance by radio signals. ---
examples: He flies a radio-controlled plane on weekends.
The gate at the end of the driveway is radio-controlled.
Radio-controlled cars were the big gift that Christmas.
entries.form: compound — noun + participle; often shortened to RC

entries.meaning: Radioactive has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The site is still radioactive forty years later.
They store the radioactive waste underground.
Some of the soil is more radioactive than the air above it.
Social Security is radioactive in an election year.
The topic became radioactive after the scandal.

senses.head: Giving off harmful radiation
examples: The site is still radioactive forty years later.
They store the radioactive waste underground.
Some of the soil is more radioactive than the air above it.

senses.head: So controversial that politicians avoid touching it
examples: Social Security is radioactive in an election year.
The topic became radioactive after the scandal.

entries.meaning: Ragged has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He wore a ragged T-shirt and no shoes.
The flag was ragged at the edges after the storm.
The team's play was ragged in the first quarter.
She took a ragged breath and kept going.
His singing got more ragged toward the end of the tour.

senses.head: Torn, old and in bad condition
examples: He wore a ragged T-shirt and no shoes.
The flag was ragged at the edges after the storm.

senses.head: Uneven and rough, not smooth or controlled
examples: The team's play was ragged in the first quarter.
She took a ragged breath and kept going.
His singing got more ragged toward the end of the tour.

entries.contrast: Two syllables: RAG-id, like rugged and wicked. In run ragged it means worn out from overwork: The twins run me ragged.

entries.meaning: Raging has 2 distinct senses.
examples: A raging fire destroyed the barn.
They had to cross a raging river.
I woke up with a raging headache.
There's a raging debate about the new rules.

senses.head: Very strong and violent, of fire, water or weather
examples: A raging fire destroyed the barn.
They had to cross a raging river.

senses.head: Very intense, of pain, thirst or an argument
examples: I woke up with a raging headache.
There's a raging debate about the new rules.

entries.meaning: With a lot of rain. ---
examples: It was a cold, rainy Tuesday in March.
October was rainier than usual this year.
The whole week is supposed to be rainy.
entries.contrast: Save it for a rainy day means save money for a time when you will need it.

entries.meaning: Higher than the surface around it. ---
examples: We built a raised garden bed out of cedar.
The band played on a raised platform at the end of the room.
Raised lettering runs across the cover.
entries.contrast: Raised voices means loud and angry ones. She was raised in Ohio is the verb, not this adjective.

entries.meaning: Rambling has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He left a rambling voicemail at two in the morning.
The essay is rambling and hard to follow.
Her second speech was even more rambling than the first.
They bought a rambling old farmhouse with six bedrooms.
A rambling rose covers the back fence.

senses.head: Long and confused, with no clear point
examples: He left a rambling voicemail at two in the morning.
The essay is rambling and hard to follow.
Her second speech was even more rambling than the first.

senses.head: Of a house or garden: spread out in an irregular way
examples: They bought a rambling old farmhouse with six bedrooms.
A rambling rose covers the back fence.

entries.meaning: Noisy, full of energy and hard to control, usually of children or animals. ---
examples: Three rambunctious boys tore through the kitchen.
The puppy gets rambunctious right before dinner.
The crowd was more rambunctious than security expected.
entries.contrast: American English. British speakers say rumbustious.

entries.meaning: Spreading fast and out of control. ---
examples: Corruption was more rampant in that department than anywhere else in the city.
Rampant inflation wiped out their savings.
Rumors ran rampant after the announcement.
entries.position: both — often after be or run
entries.contrast: Almost always about something bad that is spreading: rampant inflation, rampant corruption, never rampant kindness.

entries.meaning: Badly built or falling apart; of an organization, thrown together and barely working. ---
examples: They spent the summer in a ramshackle cabin by the river.
The porch looked even more ramshackle up close.
It's a ramshackle operation — nobody knows who's in charge.

entries.meaning: Of fat, oil or butter: old, and tasting or smelling unpleasant. ---
examples: The peanut butter went rancid in the heat.
There's a rancid smell coming from that pan.
Nuts turn rancid faster than most people think.
entries.contrast: Rancid is for fats and oils. Milk goes sour, meat goes bad or is spoiled, bread goes stale.

entries.meaning: Full of bitter, long-lasting anger. ---
examples: The divorce was long and rancorous.
A rancorous debate split the board in half.
Talks grew more rancorous with every week that passed.
entries.form: -ous from rancor — American spelling; British rancour

entries.meaning: Random has 2 distinct senses.
examples: They called ten random names from the list.
The attacks look random, but the police aren't sure.
Each student gets a random seat assignment.
Some random guy started talking to me on the bus.
That was the most random thing he's ever said.

senses.head: Chosen or happening with no plan or pattern
examples: They called ten random names from the list.
The attacks look random, but the police aren't sure.
Each student gets a random seat assignment.

senses.head: Informal: strange, unexpected or out of place
body: (странный, ни с того ни с сего)
examples: Some random guy started talking to me on the bus.
That was the most random thing he's ever said.

entries.contrast: At random is a fixed phrase: We picked names at random. The informal strange sense is common in speech but out of place in formal writing.

entries.meaning: Arranged or assigned by chance, especially in research. ---
examples: It was a randomized controlled trial with 400 patients.
Each group got a randomized list of tasks.
Students took a randomized version of the test.
entries.contrast: American spelling -ized; British writing often has randomised.

entries.meaning: Rank has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He's a rank amateur with a camera.
That's rank hypocrisy and everyone knows it.
It was rank stupidity to drive in that storm.
His gym bag smelled even more rank after a week in the car.
Rank water sat in the bottom of the cooler.

senses.head: Complete and total — used before a noun to stress how bad something is
examples: He's a rank amateur with a camera.
That's rank hypocrisy and everyone knows it.
It was rank stupidity to drive in that storm.

senses.head: Smelling strong and unpleasant
examples: His gym bag smelled even more rank after a week in the car.
Rank water sat in the bottom of the cooler.

entries.position: both — the complete sense only before a noun: a rank amateur
entries.comparison: more/most — more rank, most rank (the smell sense only)
entries.contrast: Also a noun (military rank) and a verb (The team ranks third).

entries.meaning: Given a position on an official list of the best. ---
examples: She's the third-ranked player in the world.
Only ranked teams make the tournament.
He lost to a lower-ranked opponent in the second round.
entries.position: both — usually in compounds before a noun: top-ranked
entries.form: -ed from rank; common in top-ranked, highly ranked, third-ranked

entries.meaning: Holding the highest position in a group; most senior. ---
examples: The ranking officer took over the scene.
She's the ranking Democrat on the committee.
Several high-ranking officials resigned that week.
entries.form: -ing from rank; usual in high-ranking, top-ranking
entries.contrast: Also a noun (the world rankings). Don't confuse it with ranked: the ranking officer is the most senior one, a ranked player has a number next to their name.

entries.meaning: Greedy, taking as much as possible with no concern for anyone else. ---
examples: Rapacious lenders went after older homeowners.
He wrote about the rapacious side of the timber industry.
The company grew more rapacious as it lost market share.

entries.meaning: Happening fast, especially of change or growth. ---
examples: The town saw rapid growth after the plant opened.
She made a rapid recovery from surgery.
Change has been more rapid than anyone predicted.
entries.contrast: Rapid describes changes and processes. For people, cars and answers, American English says fast or quick: a fast runner, not a rapid runner.

entries.meaning: So interested in something that you notice nothing else. ---
examples: The kids listened with rapt attention.
She sat rapt through the whole concert.
A rapt audience filled every seat in the hall.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like wrapped but is a different word. The set phrase is rapt attention.

entries.meaning: Showing great delight and enthusiasm. ---
examples: The band got a rapturous welcome in Chicago.
Critics were even more rapturous about her second novel.
Rapturous applause went on for five minutes.

entries.meaning: Rare has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Snow is rarer here than it used to be.
It's rare for him to call on a weekday.
The museum owns a rare first edition.
He orders his steak rare.
I asked for medium, not rare.

senses.head: Not often seen, found or done
examples: Snow is rarer here than it used to be.
It's rare for him to call on a weekday.
The museum owns a rare first edition.

senses.head: Of beef: cooked only a little, still red inside
examples: He orders his steak rare.
I asked for medium, not rare.

entries.takes: for + noun + to-infinitive — It's rare for him to call
entries.contrast: Russian редкий also covers hair and combs; English uses thin for hair (thinning hair) and fine-toothed for combs. For meat the scale is rare, medium rare, medium, medium well, well done.

entries.meaning: Rarefied has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He moved in the rarefied world of art collecting.
Rare book dealing is an even more rarefied world than art collecting.
Climbers struggle in the rarefied air above 15,000 feet.
The rarefied atmosphere makes every step harder.

senses.head: Belonging to a small, closed world that few people enter
examples: He moved in the rarefied world of art collecting.
Rare book dealing is an even more rarefied world than art collecting.

senses.head: Of air: thin, with less oxygen than usual
examples: Climbers struggle in the rarefied air above 15,000 feet.
The rarefied atmosphere makes every step harder.

entries.form: -ed from rarefy — to make thinner; note the spelling rarefied, not rarified

entries.meaning: Very eager to start something. ---
examples: The team was raring to go by kickoff.
She's raring to get back on the court.
We were up at six and raring to start.
entries.takes: to-infinitive — almost always raring to go
entries.contrast: Nearly always in the fixed phrase raring to go. It never goes before a noun, and it is not related to rare.

entries.meaning: Done or acting too quickly, without thinking about what will happen. ---
examples: Don't make any rash decisions while you're angry.
It was rash of him to quit without another job lined up.
It would be even more rash to sell the house now.
entries.takes: of + person + to-infinitive — It was rash of him to quit
entries.contrast: Also a noun: a skin rash, and a rash of means a sudden series of something bad (a rash of break-ins).

entries.meaning: Rough and harsh in sound, of a voice or of breathing. ---
examples: He has a raspy voice from years of smoking.
Her breathing got raspier through the night.
The singer's raspy tone is her signature.
entries.form: -y from rasp — a rough file, and the sound one makes

entries.meaning: Relating to Rastafari, a religious movement that began in Jamaica in the 1930s. ---
examples: Rastafarian beliefs shaped early reggae.
She studies Rastafarian communities in Jamaica.
The red, gold and green stripes are Rastafarian colors.
entries.form: from Ras Tafari, the name of Haile Selassie before he became emperor
entries.contrast: Always capitalized. Also a noun (a Rastafarian), often shortened to Rasta.

entries.meaning: Based on clear thinking rather than on emotion; able to think clearly. ---
examples: There's a perfectly rational explanation for the noise.
Try to be rational about the money.
Her argument is more rational than his, even if it's less popular.
entries.form: -al from ratio — by way of reason
entries.contrast: Don't mix it up with the noun rationale (ruh-shuh-NAL), which means the reasoning behind a decision.

entries.meaning: Nervous and upset after something unsettling. ---
examples: She sounded rattled on the phone.
The pitcher got rattled after the error.
He was more rattled by the question than he let on.
entries.form: -ed from rattle — what shakes you shakes your nerves

entries.meaning: Old, worn out and in bad condition. ---
examples: He still wears that ratty old hoodie.
The couch is even rattier than I remembered.
Ratty carpet covered the stairs.
entries.contrast: In American English it means worn out. In British English ratty can mean irritable.

entries.meaning: Loud and rough, especially of a crowd, laughter or a party. ---
examples: A raucous crowd filled the bar after the game.
There was raucous laughter from the back of the room.
The party got more raucous as the night went on.

entries.meaning: Rude and sexual in a crude way. ---
examples: The comedian's set was pretty raunchy.
Her jokes get raunchier after midnight.
It's a raunchy movie, not one for the family.

entries.meaning: Badly damaged or almost destroyed. ---
examples: They flew supplies into the ravaged coastal towns.
His face was ravaged by years of hard living.
The ravaged forest will take decades to grow back.

entries.meaning: Extremely hungry. ---
examples: The kids were ravenous after practice.
By dinnertime they were even more ravenous.
He ate like a ravenous teenager.
entries.contrast: Nothing to do with the bird raven. It is much stronger than hungry — closer to starving.

entries.meaning: Completely crazy, or wild with anger. ---
examples: By the third day of delays he was raving mad.
You'd have to be raving mad to swim in that water.
She went stark raving mad trying to fix the printer.
entries.form: fixed phrase — raving used as an intensifier + mad; the full form is stark raving mad
entries.contrast: A fixed phrase, and it goes after a verb, not before a noun. Here mad means crazy, not angry — though people also use the whole phrase for great anger.

entries.meaning: Extremely beautiful. ---
examples: She looked ravishing in the green dress.
The garden is ravishing in June.
He painted the most ravishing sunset I've ever seen.
entries.contrast: Literary and a little old-fashioned, and usually about beauty. The verb ravish has a dark second meaning, but the adjective does not carry it.

entries.meaning: Raw has 4 distinct senses.
examples: Don't eat raw cookie dough.
The fish is served raw, with rice and ginger.
The lab sent us the raw data.
Raw materials cost more this year than last.
His hands were raw from the rope.
My throat felt raw after shouting all night.
It's the rawest song on the album.
The interview was raw and uncomfortable to watch.

senses.head: Not cooked
examples: Don't eat raw cookie dough.
The fish is served raw, with rice and ginger.

senses.head: Not yet processed, cleaned up or analyzed
examples: The lab sent us the raw data.
Raw materials cost more this year than last.

senses.head: Of skin: sore, red and painful
examples: His hands were raw from the rope.
My throat felt raw after shouting all night.

senses.head: Honest and full of strong feeling, with nothing softened
examples: It's the rawest song on the album.
The interview was raw and uncomfortable to watch.

entries.contrast: A raw deal means unfair treatment. Raw meat is uncooked; meat that has gone bad is spoiled.

entries.meaning: Razor-sharp has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The knife is razor-sharp, so be careful.
Razor-sharp rocks line that stretch of the shore.
At ninety she's still razor-sharp.
He has a razor-sharp memory for names.

senses.head: Extremely sharp
examples: The knife is razor-sharp, so be careful.
Razor-sharp rocks line that stretch of the shore.

senses.head: Very quick and precise, of a mind, memory or sense of humor
examples: At ninety she's still razor-sharp.
He has a razor-sharp memory for names.

entries.meaning: Reachable has 2 distinct senses.
examples: I'm reachable by text all weekend.
She's more reachable by text than by phone.
The summit is reachable in a single day.
The goal is ambitious but reachable.

senses.head: Able to be contacted
examples: I'm reachable by text all weekend.
She's more reachable by text than by phone.

senses.head: Able to be got to or achieved
examples: The summit is reachable in a single day.
The goal is ambitious but reachable.

entries.meaning: Opposing social or political change, and wanting things to go back to how they were. ---
examples: The editorial called the ruling reactionary.
He joined a reactionary faction of the party.
Her politics grew more reactionary with age.
entries.contrast: Always a criticism, never a neutral label. It is not the same as reactive: a reactionary politician wants the past back, a reactive one only responds to events.

entries.meaning: Reactive has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Management is reactive — nothing gets fixed until it breaks.
We need to be less reactive and more strategic.
It was a reactive decision made in one afternoon.
Sodium is highly reactive with water.
Store the reactive chemicals in a separate cabinet.

senses.head: Responding to events after they happen instead of planning ahead
examples: Management is reactive — nothing gets fixed until it breaks.
We need to be less reactive and more strategic.
It was a reactive decision made in one afternoon.

senses.head: In chemistry: easily taking part in chemical reactions
examples: Sodium is highly reactive with water.
Store the reactive chemicals in a separate cabinet.

entries.meaning: Readable has 2 distinct senses.
examples: It's a dense subject, but the book is very readable.
She writes the most readable science column around.
The sign is barely readable from the road.
Make the font bigger so it's readable on a phone.

senses.head: Enjoyable and easy to read
examples: It's a dense subject, but the book is very readable.
She writes the most readable science column around.

senses.head: Clear enough to be read
examples: The sign is barely readable from the road.
Make the font bigger so it's readable on a phone.

entries.contrast: Readable praises the writing; legible is only about whether the letters can be made out.

entries.meaning: Already made and ready to use, rather than made to order. ---
examples: We bought a ready-made pie crust.
He had a ready-made excuse waiting.
Ready-made curtains rarely fit these windows.

entries.meaning: Already cooked or prepared, so you can eat it right away. ---
examples: The store sells ready-to-eat meals by the register.
Pack some ready-to-eat snacks for the drive.
The salad is washed and ready-to-eat.

entries.meaning: Of clothing: made in standard sizes rather than for one person. ---
examples: The designer launched a ready-to-wear line last fall.
Ready-to-wear suits usually need some tailoring anyway.
Everything in this part of the store is ready-to-wear.

entries.meaning: Real has 3 distinct senses.
examples: Is the threat real, or is it just talk?
The dream felt more real than the morning did.
The bag is real leather.
Those aren't real diamonds.
The parking downtown is a real problem.
He can be a real pain when he's tired.

senses.head: Actually existing, not imagined or invented
examples: Is the threat real, or is it just talk?
The dream felt more real than the morning did.

senses.head: Genuine, not a copy or an imitation
examples: The bag is real leather.
Those aren't real diamonds.

senses.head: Used before a noun to stress how much something is what it is
examples: The parking downtown is a real problem.
He can be a real pain when he's tired.

entries.position: both — the emphasizing sense only before a noun: a real problem
entries.contrast: Real good and real fast are informal speech; in writing use the adverb really. For real is also informal.

entries.meaning: Happening or shown at the same moment as the event itself. ---
examples: The app gives real-time traffic updates.
We get real-time data from the sensors on the bridge.
Real-time translation is built into the phone.
entries.contrast: Hyphenated before a noun, two separate words after a verb: real-time updates, but The data arrives in real time.

entries.meaning: Realistic has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Let's set a realistic deadline.
Be realistic about how much you can finish by Friday.
Her expectations are more realistic now than they were.
The special effects are surprisingly realistic.
He paints in a realistic style.

senses.head: Sensible about what is actually possible
examples: Let's set a realistic deadline.
Be realistic about how much you can finish by Friday.
Her expectations are more realistic now than they were.

senses.head: Looking or sounding like real life
examples: The special effects are surprisingly realistic.
He paints in a realistic style.

entries.meaning: Realized has 2 distinct senses.
examples: It's a fully realized vision of the city in 2100.
The characters feel like realized people, not sketches.
You pay tax on realized gains, not on paper ones.
Realized losses can offset those gains.

senses.head: Made real and worked out in full
examples: It's a fully realized vision of the city in 2100.
The characters feel like realized people, not sketches.

senses.head: In finance: actually received or lost, not just on paper
examples: You pay tax on realized gains, not on paper ones.
Realized losses can offset those gains.

entries.contrast: Realize is usually a verb (I realized my mistake). As an adjective it turns up in fully realized and in finance, where realized gains are ones you have actually taken.

entries.meaning: At or in the back of something. ---
examples: The rear door doesn't lock properly.
Passengers exit through the rear entrance.
Check the rear tires for wear.
entries.contrast: Also a noun (the rear of the building) and a verb (to rear children). As an adjective it never follows a verb: say The door at the back is locked, not The door is rear.

entries.meaning: Reasonable has 3 distinct senses.
examples: That sounds like a reasonable request.
Be reasonable — he's only nine.
A more reasonable boss would have let it go.
We had a reasonable turnout for a rainy night.
She has a reasonable chance of winning the seat.
The hotel was clean and reasonable.
They charge reasonable prices for repairs.

senses.head: Fair and sensible
examples: That sounds like a reasonable request.
Be reasonable — he's only nine.
A more reasonable boss would have let it go.

senses.head: Fairly good or fairly large, though not outstanding
examples: We had a reasonable turnout for a rainy night.
She has a reasonable chance of winning the seat.

senses.head: Not too expensive
examples: The hotel was clean and reasonable.
They charge reasonable prices for repairs.

entries.meaning: Based on careful thinking and clear argument. ---
examples: She wrote a reasoned response to the criticism.
The judge gave a carefully reasoned opinion.
We need a more reasoned debate about the bill.
entries.contrast: Reasoned is about the argument — carefully built. Reasonable is about the person or the demand — fair and sensible.

entries.meaning: No longer worried, because someone has taken your fear away. ---
examples: She felt reassured after talking to the doctor.
Everyone left the meeting reassured about their jobs.
I was more reassured by her calm tone than by anything she actually said.
entries.contrast: reassured is how you feel; reassuring is the thing that causes it: I felt reassured because her voice was reassuring.

entries.meaning: Making someone feel less worried or afraid. ---
examples: Her voice on the phone was calm and reassuring.
He gave the crowd a reassuring smile.
The nurse's explanation was far more reassuring than the leaflet.
entries.contrast: The -ing form describes the thing that calms you; the -ed form describes the person: a reassuring nurse, a reassured patient.

entries.meaning: Refusing to obey rules or the people in charge. ---
examples: He was a rebellious teenager who skipped class all the time.
The students grew more rebellious as the new rules piled up.
There is something rebellious about the way she dresses.

entries.meaning: Changed so completely that it feels like a new life or a new start. ---
examples: After two weeks off, he felt completely reborn.
The old factory district has been reborn as an arts center.
The team looked reborn in the second half.

entries.meaning: Formal: stubbornly refusing to cooperate or obey. ---
examples: A few recalcitrant senators blocked the bill for a month.
The mule was recalcitrant and would not move.
He got more recalcitrant with every new rule the school added.

entries.meaning: Moving back and away from you, or slowly getting smaller. ---
examples: He is self-conscious about his receding hairline.
We watched the receding taillights disappear around the corner.
The receding floodwaters left mud across the whole street.

entries.meaning: Generally accepted by most people, though not necessarily true. ---
examples: The received wisdom is that you should never put everything in one stock.
She spent her career challenging received ideas about diet.
That view has hardened into received opinion in the field.
entries.contrast: As an adjective it lives in a few fixed phrases — received wisdom, received opinion, received ideas. In I received your email it is just the verb.

entries.meaning: Happening or made a short time ago. ---
examples: In recent years the town has almost doubled in size.
Is there a more recent version of the report?
The damage is recent — it happened during last week's storm.

entries.meaning: Willing to listen to new ideas and think about them. ---
examples: The boss was surprisingly receptive to my idea.
Try to pitch it to a receptive audience first.
Voters are more receptive to the message than they were last year.

entries.meaning: Set back into a wall, ceiling or surface instead of sticking out. ---
examples: The kitchen has recessed lighting in the ceiling.
The door handle is recessed so nothing catches on it.
His eyes were dark and deeply recessed.

entries.meaning: Belonging to a period when the economy is shrinking. ---
examples: The economy is showing recessionary signs again.
Hiring freezes are a classic recessionary move.
Many firms cut travel in the recessionary years after 2008.

entries.meaning: Of a gene: showing up only when a child gets it from both parents. ---
examples: Blue eyes come from a recessive gene.
The trait is recessive, so both parents have to carry it.
Red hair is a recessive characteristic.

entries.meaning: Able to be filled with electricity again and used many times. ---
examples: The flashlight takes rechargeable batteries.
Is this battery rechargeable?
We switched to rechargeable AAs to save money.

entries.meaning: Given by each side to the other, in both directions. ---
examples: The two countries signed a reciprocal trade agreement.
Respect between a teacher and a student should be reciprocal.
Our states have a reciprocal deal on driver's licenses.

entries.meaning: Acting without thinking about the danger or the damage. ---
examples: He was charged with reckless driving.
It would be reckless to spend the whole budget in January.
Her second husband was even more reckless with money than her first.
entries.form: -less from an old verb reck — to care

entries.meaning: Taken back and made usable again, especially old material or land. ---
examples: The table is made of reclaimed wood from an old barn.
Much of the airport sits on reclaimed land.
The water is reclaimed and used to irrigate the golf course.

entries.meaning: Living alone and avoiding other people. ---
examples: The reclusive author has not given an interview in thirty years.
He became more reclusive after his wife died.
She has grown quite reclusive in old age.

entries.meaning: Easy to know again when you see or hear it. ---
examples: Her voice is instantly recognizable.
He wore a hat, but his walk was still recognizable.
The logo is one of the most recognizable in the world.

entries.meaning: Officially accepted, or accepted by everyone as real or good. ---
examples: She is a recognized expert on immigration law.
The certificate is recognized by employers across the country.
Burnout is now a recognized medical condition.
entries.comparison: not gradable — usually graded with widely: a widely recognized expert

entries.meaning: Reconciled has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She is reconciled to living alone.
He seems reconciled to the fact that he will never play again.
I am more reconciled to the move than I was in January.
The brothers were finally reconciled after ten years of silence.
She hoped to be reconciled with her father before he died.

senses.head: Having accepted something unwelcome that cannot be changed
examples: She is reconciled to living alone.
He seems reconciled to the fact that he will never play again.
I am more reconciled to the move than I was in January.

senses.head: Friendly again after a quarrel
examples: The brothers were finally reconciled after ten years of silence.
She hoped to be reconciled with her father before he died.

entries.position: predicative only — after be, become or seem
entries.takes: to + noun or -ing (accepting); with + person (friendly again)

entries.meaning: Of surgery: rebuilding a part of the body that was damaged. ---
examples: She had reconstructive surgery after the accident.
He is a reconstructive surgeon at the children's hospital.
Insurance covered the reconstructive work but not the cosmetic part.

entries.meaning: Better or bigger than anything of its kind before. ---
examples: She swam a record-breaking time in the 200 meters.
The movie had a record-breaking opening weekend.
It was a record-breaking heat wave for July.

entries.meaning: Recorded has 2 distinct senses.
examples: They played recorded music instead of hiring a band.
This call may be recorded for training purposes.
He left a recorded message for the whole staff.
It was the warmest June in recorded history.
There is no recorded case of the disease in this state.

senses.head: Captured on tape, video or a computer so it can be played later
examples: They played recorded music instead of hiring a band.
This call may be recorded for training purposes.
He left a recorded message for the whole staff.

senses.head: Written down in an official record
examples: It was the warmest June in recorded history.
There is no recorded case of the disease in this state.

entries.meaning: Able to be got back after being lost, spent or deleted. ---
examples: Deleted files are usually recoverable for about thirty days.
Only part of the loss is recoverable through insurance.
The data on the burned drive was not recoverable.

entries.meaning: Recovered has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She is fully recovered from the surgery.
He looks recovered, but he still tires by noon.
Police returned the recovered jewelry to its owner.
The recovered files filled three hard drives.

senses.head: Healthy again after an illness or injury
examples: She is fully recovered from the surgery.
He looks recovered, but he still tires by noon.

senses.head: Found and brought back after being lost or stolen
examples: Police returned the recovered jewelry to its owner.
The recovered files filled three hard drives.

entries.meaning: Getting better after an illness, an injury or an addiction. ---
examples: He is a recovering alcoholic and has been sober for six years.
The ward has a quiet lounge for recovering patients.
She counsels recovering addicts at a community center.
entries.position: attributive only — after a verb it is the verb recover, not an adjective: She is recovering well
entries.contrast: A recovering alcoholic keeps the -ing form for life — recovered would suggest the problem is over and gone.

entries.meaning: Done for fun in your free time, not for work or medical need. ---
examples: The town is building a new recreational center by the lake.
Recreational marijuana is legal in several states.
He plays recreational soccer on Sunday mornings.

entries.meaning: Medical: of or through the rectum. ---
examples: The nurse took a rectal temperature.
He is scheduled for a rectal exam next week.
The medicine comes as a rectal suppository.

entries.meaning: Coming back again and again over a long time. ---
examples: She has a recurrent dream about missing a train.
Back pain has been a recurrent problem for him since the fall.
The theme is recurrent throughout the novel.
entries.contrast: recurrent and recurring mean nearly the same thing; recurring is the everyday word and recurrent is the one doctors and critics use.

entries.meaning: Happening again and again, often on a set schedule. ---
examples: Set up a recurring payment so you do not forget the rent.
It is a recurring joke on the show.
She has had recurring headaches since the concussion.

entries.meaning: Able to be treated and used again instead of thrown away. ---
examples: Put all recyclable materials in the blue bin.
Is this container recyclable?
Most glass and aluminum is recyclable.

entries.meaning: Full of healthy energy and normal desires. ---
examples: He is a red-blooded American teenager.
No red-blooded fan would miss that game.
It is the kind of movie that appeals to red-blooded action lovers.
entries.contrast: Usually said of men and often half-joking. It means full of energy and ordinary appetites, not angry or violent.

entries.meaning: Grand and ceremonious, the way important guests are welcomed. ---
examples: They gave the visiting team the red-carpet treatment.
He got a red-carpet welcome at the airport.
It was a red-carpet reception, complete with photographers.
entries.form: compound — color + noun, from the carpet rolled out for important guests

entries.meaning: Red-faced has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The mayor was left red-faced when the numbers turned out to be wrong.
A red-faced official admitted the mistake to reporters.
He came in red-faced and out of breath.
The coach was red-faced with rage by halftime.

senses.head: Embarrassed, especially in public
examples: The mayor was left red-faced when the numbers turned out to be wrong.
A red-faced official admitted the mistake to reporters.

senses.head: With a red face from anger, heat or hard effort
examples: He came in red-faced and out of breath.
The coach was red-faced with rage by halftime.

entries.comparison: not gradable — usually intensified with very or increasingly

entries.meaning: In the act of doing something wrong, so there is no denying it. ---
examples: The guard caught him red-handed with the cash in his pocket.
They were caught red-handed copying answers off a phone.
If you take it, you will get caught red-handed.
entries.position: predicative only — almost always after catch: caught red-handed
entries.form: compound — color + noun + -ed, from the image of blood on a killer's hands
entries.contrast: It lives in one phrase, catch someone red-handed, and never goes before a noun.

entries.meaning: Red-hot has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He pulled the red-hot iron out of the fire with tongs.
Do not touch the burner — it is red-hot.
She is the red-hot favorite for the award.
The company's stock was red-hot all last quarter.

senses.head: Heated until the metal glows red
examples: He pulled the red-hot iron out of the fire with tongs.
Do not touch the burner — it is red-hot.

senses.head: Very exciting, very successful or very much in demand right now
examples: She is the red-hot favorite for the award.
The company's stock was red-hot all last quarter.

entries.meaning: Of a day: important and happy, one you will remember. ---
examples: The day she got her citizenship was a red-letter day.
Graduation is a red-letter day for the whole family.
Mark it on the calendar — it is a red-letter day around here.
entries.position: attributive only — almost always in a red-letter day
entries.form: compound — from the red ink that marked feast days on old calendars

entries.meaning: Slightly red, or red mixed with another color. ---
examples: She has reddish hair and very pale skin.
The sky over the desert turned a reddish orange.
The soil here is reddish and full of clay.
entries.comparison: not gradable — the -ish ending already means somewhat

entries.meaning: Brown with a clear touch of red in it. ---
examples: The dog has a thick reddish-brown coat.
The leaves turn a deep reddish-brown in late October.
The stain on the carpet was reddish-brown and would not come out.
entries.form: compound — two colors joined with a hyphen

entries.meaning: Able to be exchanged for goods, money or a service. ---
examples: The coupon is redeemable for one free coffee.
These points are redeemable at any partner hotel.
The voucher is redeemable in store only.
entries.takes: for + what you get; at + where you use it

entries.meaning: Good enough to make up for everything that is bad about something. ---
examples: The movie's one redeeming quality is the soundtrack.
He has no redeeming features that I can see.
The apartment is tiny, but the view is its redeeming feature.
entries.position: attributive only — almost always with quality, feature or value

entries.meaning: Saving someone from guilt or failure, and giving them a second chance. ---
examples: The novel ends on a redemptive note.
He sees his volunteer work as redemptive.
There is a redemptive quality to the final scene.

entries.meaning: Having red or orange hair. ---
examples: A redheaded boy answered the door.
Both of her kids are redheaded.
He is the redheaded one in the back row.
entries.contrast: The person is a redhead (noun); the adjective keeps the -ed: a redheaded kid.

entries.meaning: Strong and impressive enough to be worth fearing or respecting. ---
examples: She faced a redoubtable opponent in the final.
The redoubtable Mrs. Hayes ran the office for forty years.
He proved a more redoubtable negotiator than anyone expected.
entries.contrast: It means formidable and worth respecting. It has nothing to do with doubt, even though it looks like it.

entries.meaning: Made smaller, lower or cheaper than before. ---
examples: The store sells last season's coats at reduced prices.
Students pay a reduced fare on the city bus.
He works a reduced schedule while he finishes his degree.

entries.meaning: Redundant has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Saying free gift is redundant — a gift is already free.
Cut the second paragraph; it is redundant.
The report gets more redundant with every draft.
The plane has redundant control systems.
Customer data is stored on redundant servers in two states.

senses.head: Repeating something that has already been said, and so not needed
examples: Saying free gift is redundant — a gift is already free.
Cut the second paragraph; it is redundant.
The report gets more redundant with every draft.

senses.head: Built in twice on purpose, as a backup
examples: The plane has redundant control systems.
Customer data is stored on redundant servers in two states.

entries.contrast: In British English made redundant means laid off from a job. Americans do not use it that way — they say laid off.

entries.meaning: Refined has 3 distinct senses.
examples: She has beautifully refined manners.
His taste in music is more refined than mine.
Try to cut back on refined sugar and white flour.
Refined oil is shipped by rail from the coast.
The second version of the design is far more refined.
We use a refined version of the original formula.

senses.head: Polite, cultured and in good taste
examples: She has beautifully refined manners.
His taste in music is more refined than mine.

senses.head: Made pure by industrial processing
examples: Try to cut back on refined sugar and white flour.
Refined oil is shipped by rail from the coast.

senses.head: Improved by many small careful changes
examples: The second version of the design is far more refined.
We use a refined version of the original formula.

entries.meaning: Reflective has 3 distinct senses.
examples: He was in a reflective mood all evening.
The last chapter is calm and reflective.
She has grown more reflective with age.
Runners should wear a reflective vest at night.
The jacket has reflective stripes down the sleeves.
The test scores are reflective of the whole district.
His answer was reflective of a much deeper problem.

senses.head: Thinking quietly and seriously about things
examples: He was in a reflective mood all evening.
The last chapter is calm and reflective.
She has grown more reflective with age.

senses.head: Throwing back light, so it can be seen in the dark
examples: Runners should wear a reflective vest at night.
The jacket has reflective stripes down the sleeves.

senses.head: Showing what something is really like, or being a sign of it
examples: The test scores are reflective of the whole district.
His answer was reflective of a much deeper problem.

entries.takes: of + noun, in the showing sense

entries.meaning: Reflexive has 2 distinct senses.
examples: His reflexive answer was no, and he regretted it later.
She has a reflexive distrust of salespeople.
Myself and herself are reflexive pronouns.
In he hurt himself, the verb takes a reflexive pronoun.

senses.head: Done automatically, without stopping to think
examples: His reflexive answer was no, and he regretted it later.
She has a reflexive distrust of salespeople.

senses.head: Grammar: pointing back to the subject of the verb
examples: Myself and herself are reflexive pronouns.
In he hurt himself, the verb takes a reflexive pronoun.

entries.meaning: Wanting to change a system to make it work better. ---
examples: A reform-minded mayor took office last year.
The new board is more reform-minded than the old one.
Reform-minded teachers pushed for a longer school day.

entries.meaning: Reformed has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He is a reformed smoker and now hates the smell.
She is a reformed shoplifter who counsels teenagers.
The reformed tax code takes effect in January.
Critics say the reformed system is no fairer than the old one.

senses.head: No longer doing the bad thing you used to do
examples: He is a reformed smoker and now hates the smell.
She is a reformed shoplifter who counsels teenagers.

senses.head: Of a system or law: changed so that it works better
examples: The reformed tax code takes effect in January.
Critics say the reformed system is no fairer than the old one.

entries.meaning: Supporting gradual change to a political or religious system. ---
examples: The reformist wing of the party won the vote.
He ran on a reformist platform and lost badly.
Reformist candidates did well in the big cities.
entries.contrast: The same word is also a noun: a reformist is a person who wants reform.

entries.meaning: Rested and full of energy again. ---
examples: I woke up refreshed for the first time in weeks.
A twenty-minute nap left her feeling refreshed.
He came back from vacation more refreshed than anyone expected.
entries.contrast: refreshed is how you feel; refreshing is what causes it: a refreshing nap leaves you refreshed.

entries.meaning: Refreshing has 2 distinct senses.
examples: A glass of cold lemonade is refreshing on a day like this.
We took a refreshing swim in the lake before dinner.
It is refreshing to hear a politician admit a mistake.
Her honesty was more refreshing than anything else that week.

senses.head: Cool and pleasant, making you feel less hot or tired
examples: A glass of cold lemonade is refreshing on a day like this.
We took a refreshing swim in the lake before dinner.

senses.head: Pleasantly different from the usual, in a way you welcome
examples: It is refreshing to hear a politician admit a mistake.
Her honesty was more refreshing than anything else that week.

entries.takes: to-infinitive, after it: It is refreshing to hear that

entries.meaning: Kept cold so that it does not spoil. ---
examples: The vaccine has to travel in a refrigerated truck.
Keep the dough refrigerated until you are ready to bake.
The store added a whole refrigerated section for drinks.

entries.meaning: Grand and dignified, like a king or queen. ---
examples: She has a regal bearing that people notice right away.
The old hotel looks more regal from the street than it does inside.
He gave a regal nod and walked past us.
entries.contrast: regal describes a manner that reminds you of a king (a regal wave); royal says the person or thing really belongs to a king's family (the royal family).

entries.meaning: Organized by strict rules and a strict schedule, often too strict. ---
examples: Her day is highly regimented, down to the minute.
He grew up in a regimented household with a chore chart.
Training camp is more regimented than the regular season.

entries.meaning: Belonging to one part of a country rather than the whole of it. ---
examples: The chain started as a small regional grocery in Ohio.
She won the regional championship in March.
There are regional differences in how people say that word.

entries.meaning: Officially listed, licensed or recorded. ---
examples: She is a registered nurse at the county hospital.
You have to be a registered voter to take part.
The name is a registered trademark.

entries.meaning: Regressive has 2 distinct senses.
examples: A sales tax is regressive because it hits poor families hardest.
Critics call the flat fee deeply regressive.
The policy is a regressive step for women's rights.
His behavior got more regressive the longer he stayed home.

senses.head: Of a tax or fee: taking a bigger share from people who earn less
examples: A sales tax is regressive because it hits poor families hardest.
Critics call the flat fee deeply regressive.

senses.head: Going back to an earlier and worse state
examples: The policy is a regressive step for women's rights.
His behavior got more regressive the longer he stayed home.

entries.meaning: Feeling sorry about something you did or missed. ---
examples: She sounded regretful about missing the wedding.
He gave a regretful shrug and closed the door.
The older he gets, the more regretful he seems about that year.
entries.contrast: regretful is how a person feels; regrettable is a thing that is a shame: a regretful apology for a regrettable mistake.

entries.meaning: Bad enough that people are sorry it happened. ---
examples: The whole incident was regrettable but nobody's fault.
He made a regrettable remark about her weight.
It is regrettable that no one spoke up sooner, and even more regrettable that no one has apologized.

entries.meaning: Regular has 4 distinct senses.
examples: Take the medicine at regular intervals, about six hours apart.
Her heartbeat is strong and regular now.
His visits have become more regular since he retired.
I will just have a regular coffee, nothing fancy.
It is not a holiday — it is a regular workday.
He is one of our regular customers.
The bar has a few regular patrons who come every night.
Walk is a regular verb — its past is walked.
Most English plurals are regular and simply add an s.

senses.head: Happening again and again at even intervals
examples: Take the medicine at regular intervals, about six hours apart.
Her heartbeat is strong and regular now.
His visits have become more regular since he retired.

senses.head: Normal or standard, not special and not large
examples: I will just have a regular coffee, nothing fancy.
It is not a holiday — it is a regular workday.

senses.head: Coming to the same place or doing the same thing often
examples: He is one of our regular customers.
The bar has a few regular patrons who come every night.

senses.head: Grammar: following the normal pattern
examples: Walk is a regular verb — its past is walked.
Most English plurals are regular and simply add an s.

entries.meaning: Controlled by official rules. ---
examples: Banking is a heavily regulated industry.
The market is more regulated now than it was in 2005.
Water quality is closely regulated by the state.

entries.meaning: Having to do with official rules and the bodies that enforce them. ---
examples: The merger still faces a regulatory review.
Regulatory agencies have been slow to act.
There are a few regulatory hurdles to clear first.

entries.meaning: Holding the title or the throne right now. ---
examples: She is the reigning world champion.
The reigning monarch opened parliament on Tuesday.
He is the reigning king of late-night television.
entries.contrast: Spelled from reign (to rule), not raining or reining, though all three sound the same.

entries.meaning: Made stronger by adding extra material or support. ---
examples: The bunker is built of reinforced concrete.
The backpack has reinforced straps at the shoulders.
The door was reinforced with steel plates.

entries.meaning: Rejected has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He keeps a folder of rejected drafts.
Rejected applicants can appeal within thirty days.
She felt hurt and rejected after that phone call.
Kids who feel rejected by classmates often act out.

senses.head: Turned down or refused
examples: He keeps a folder of rejected drafts.
Rejected applicants can appeal within thirty days.

senses.head: Feeling unwanted by other people
examples: She felt hurt and rejected after that phone call.
Kids who feel rejected by classmates often act out.

entries.meaning: Relational has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The app runs on a relational database.
SQL was built for relational data.
The therapist focuses on relational problems rather than symptoms.
Teaching has a strong relational side that no test measures.

senses.head: Computing: storing data in tables that are linked to each other
examples: The app runs on a relational database.
SQL was built for relational data.

senses.head: Having to do with how people get along with each other
examples: The therapist focuses on relational problems rather than symptoms.
Teaching has a strong relational side that no test measures.

entries.meaning: Relative has 2 distinct senses.
examples: After the storm, the relative calm felt strange.
They live in relative comfort compared with their neighbors.
What counts as expensive is relative to how much you earn.
Who, which and that introduce a relative clause.
Whose is a relative pronoun.

senses.head: Judged by comparison with something else, not on its own
examples: After the storm, the relative calm felt strange.
They live in relative comfort compared with their neighbors.
What counts as expensive is relative to how much you earn.

senses.head: Grammar: joining a clause to the noun it describes
examples: Who, which and that introduce a relative clause.
Whose is a relative pronoun.

entries.contrast: The same word is also a common noun: a relative is a member of your family.

entries.meaning: Relentless has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The relentless heat lasted the whole of August.
The pressure on young athletes is relentless.
She is relentless once she decides she wants something.
Their defense got more relentless in the fourth quarter.

senses.head: Never stopping or easing off
examples: The relentless heat lasted the whole of August.
The pressure on young athletes is relentless.

senses.head: Refusing to give up or to show any mercy
examples: She is relentless once she decides she wants something.
Their defense got more relentless in the fourth quarter.

entries.form: -less from relent — to soften or give in

entries.meaning: Connected with the subject at hand, and therefore worth considering. ---
examples: Please bring any relevant documents to the meeting.
That question is not relevant to what we are discussing.
The book feels more relevant now than when it came out.

entries.meaning: Reliable has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She is the most reliable person on the team.
We need a more reliable car for that drive.
Is that a reliable source?
We have reliable figures for only three of the years.

senses.head: Able to be trusted to do what is needed, every time
examples: She is the most reliable person on the team.
We need a more reliable car for that drive.

senses.head: Of information: likely to be correct
examples: Is that a reliable source?
We have reliable figures for only three of the years.

entries.meaning: Needing someone or something in order to manage. ---
examples: The town is heavily reliant on summer tourism.
He has become more reliant on his phone than he would like.
Many older residents are reliant on the one bus line.
entries.position: predicative only — before a noun only inside compounds like self-reliant

entries.meaning: Glad because something you were worried about is over or did not happen. ---
examples: I am so relieved that you are okay.
She gave a relieved laugh when the test came back clean.
He looked more relieved than happy when the verdict was read.
entries.takes: to-infinitive; that-clause; about or at + noun

entries.meaning: Religious has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Her family is very religious and goes to church twice a week.
He became more religious after his illness.
The museum has a whole room of religious art.
Religious holidays are marked on the school calendar.

senses.head: Believing in a religion and practicing it
examples: Her family is very religious and goes to church twice a week.
He became more religious after his illness.

senses.head: Having to do with religion
examples: The museum has a whole room of religious art.
Religious holidays are marked on the school calendar.

entries.meaning: Still there after the rest has gone or been used. ---
examples: Divide the remaining money between the two of you.
The remaining guests stayed to help clean up.
We will deal with the remaining questions tomorrow.

entries.meaning: Unusual enough that people notice and talk about it. ---
examples: She has made a remarkable recovery.
The house is remarkable for its stained-glass windows.
What is most remarkable is how calm he stayed.

entries.meaning: Remedial has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He had to take remedial math his freshman year.
The district pays for remedial reading classes.
The city took remedial action after the flood.
Remedial work on the bridge starts Monday.

senses.head: Of a class: teaching the basics to students who are behind
examples: He had to take remedial math his freshman year.
The district pays for remedial reading classes.

senses.head: Meant to put right something that has gone wrong
examples: The city took remedial action after the flood.
Remedial work on the bridge starts Monday.

entries.meaning: Making you think of someone or something else. ---
examples: The smell was reminiscent of my grandmother's kitchen.
Her singing is reminiscent of early Joni Mitchell.
The lobby is more reminiscent of a hotel than an office.
entries.position: predicative only — after be or seem, almost always with of

entries.meaning: Formal: careless about a duty you should have carried out. ---
examples: It would be remiss of me not to thank the volunteers.
The inspector was remiss in not checking the wiring.
I would be remiss if I did not mention her help.
entries.position: predicative only — after be, often in It would be remiss of me not to...

entries.meaning: Feeling deep guilt about something bad you did. ---
examples: He seemed genuinely remorseful about what he had done.
The judge saw no sign of a remorseful defendant.
She grew more remorseful as the details came out in court.

entries.meaning: Remorseless has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The killer was cold and remorseless on the stand.
He seemed more remorseless with every question the prosecutor asked.
The remorseless rain went on for five days.
There is a remorseless logic to her argument.

senses.head: Feeling no guilt at all about the harm you cause
examples: The killer was cold and remorseless on the stand.
He seemed more remorseless with every question the prosecutor asked.

senses.head: Never letting up
examples: The remorseless rain went on for five days.
There is a remorseless logic to her argument.

entries.meaning: Remote has 4 distinct senses.
examples: They live on a remote island off the coast of Maine.
The cabin was more remote than the photos suggested.
The job is fully remote, with two trips a year.
She has had a remote position since 2020.
There is not the remotest chance he will agree.
The risk is remote but it is real.
He can seem remote until you know him well.
Her father was a remote figure throughout her childhood.

senses.head: Far away from towns and from other people
examples: They live on a remote island off the coast of Maine.
The cabin was more remote than the photos suggested.

senses.head: Done from home or from another city instead of at the office
examples: The job is fully remote, with two trips a year.
She has had a remote position since 2020.

senses.head: Of a chance or possibility: very small
examples: There is not the remotest chance he will agree.
The risk is remote but it is real.

senses.head: Distant and hard to get close to, in manner
examples: He can seem remote until you know him well.
Her father was a remote figure throughout her childhood.

entries.comparison: -er/-est or more/most — remoter or more remote, remotest or most remote

entries.meaning: Operated from a distance by a handheld device or a signal. ---
examples: He got a remote-controlled car for his birthday.
The gate is remote-controlled, so stay in the truck.
They filmed the wedding with a remote-controlled drone.

entries.meaning: Made so it can be taken off and put back. ---
examples: The stroller has a removable seat cover you can wash.
The stickers are removable and will not damage the paint.
It comes with a removable liner for cold weather.

entries.meaning: Removed has 2 distinct senses.
examples: His account of the evening is far removed from what actually happened.
Life in the capital is far removed from village life.
She is my first cousin once removed.
He is a cousin twice removed on my mother's side.

senses.head: Very different or very distant from something
examples: His account of the evening is far removed from what actually happened.
Life in the capital is far removed from village life.

senses.head: Of a cousin: one or two generations apart from you
examples: She is my first cousin once removed.
He is a cousin twice removed on my mother's side.

entries.position: after the noun — in a first cousin once removed; otherwise after a verb, in far removed from
entries.comparison: not gradable — graded with far: far removed
entries.contrast: In a cousin once removed, removed means one generation apart — nobody was taken away.

entries.meaning: Having left the group you belonged to and turned against it. ---
examples: A renegade group broke away from the main party.
The movie is about a renegade cop who ignores every rule.
Renegade soldiers seized the radio station at dawn.
entries.contrast: The same word is also a noun: a renegade is the person who breaks away.

entries.meaning: Renewable has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The state gets a third of its power from renewable sources.
Wind and solar are renewable; coal is not.
The contract is for one year, renewable for two more.
Your permit is renewable online in about ten minutes.

senses.head: Of energy or resources: never running out, because nature replaces it
examples: The state gets a third of its power from renewable sources.
Wind and solar are renewable; coal is not.

senses.head: Able to be extended for another period of time
examples: The contract is for one year, renewable for two more.
Your permit is renewable online in about ten minutes.

entries.meaning: Starting again, and often stronger than before. ---
examples: There is renewed interest in the case after the documentary.
She came back from the break with renewed energy.
Renewed fighting broke out near the border.

entries.meaning: Famous and widely admired for something good. ---
examples: He is one of the most renowned heart surgeons in the country.
The region is renowned for its wine.
She is renowned as a teacher as much as a performer.

entries.meaning: Costing nothing to live in or use. ---
examples: They offered him a rent-free apartment above the shop.
The space is rent-free for the first six months.
The deal includes a rent-free period while the building is fixed up.
entries.contrast: The same form works as an adverb after a verb — They lived there rent-free — and that use is not an adjective.

entries.meaning: Rented out to people for money, or having to do with renting. ---
examples: We picked up the rental car at the airport.
Rental prices downtown have gone up again.
He owns three rental properties across the river.
entries.contrast: The same word is also a noun: a rental is the car or apartment you have rented.

entries.meaning: Repeatable has 2 distinct senses.
examples: An experiment has to be repeatable before anyone believes it.
We want a repeatable process, not one lucky quarter.
His reaction was not repeatable in front of the kids.
She said something about the referee that is not repeatable here.

senses.head: Able to be done again with the same result
examples: An experiment has to be repeatable before anyone believes it.
We want a repeatable process, not one lucky quarter.

senses.head: Polite enough to say out loud
examples: His reaction was not repeatable in front of the kids.
She said something about the referee that is not repeatable here.

entries.meaning: Happening more than once, again and again. ---
examples: Repeated warnings had no effect on him.
She made repeated attempts to reach the office by phone.
He was fired after repeated absences.
entries.contrast: repeated just says it happened more than once; repetitive adds that it is boringly the same.

entries.meaning: Repellent has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The whole idea is repellent to me.
He found the man's politics more repellent than his manners.
The jacket is made of a water-repellent fabric.
The couch is treated with a stain-repellent coating.

senses.head: So unpleasant that it makes you want to keep away
examples: The whole idea is repellent to me.
He found the man's politics more repellent than his manners.

senses.head: Keeping a substance off, usually in a compound
examples: The jacket is made of a water-repellent fabric.
The couch is treated with a stain-repellent coating.

entries.contrast: The same word is also a noun: insect repellent is the spray you put on your skin.

entries.meaning: Sorry for what you did and wanting to make it right. ---
examples: He did not sound the least bit repentant.
A repentant thief returned the money anonymously.
She seemed more repentant once she saw the damage.

entries.meaning: Doing or saying the same thing over and over, usually in a boring way. ---
examples: The work is repetitive but it pays well.
Typing all day can cause repetitive strain injuries.
The second album is more repetitive than the first.

entries.meaning: Able to be swapped for a new one of the same kind. ---
examples: The battery is replaceable, so do not throw the whole thing out.
Everyone here is replaceable except the founder.
The filters are cheap and easily replaceable.

entries.meaning: Filled with something, or having plenty of it. ---
examples: The report is replete with errors.
His speech was replete with quotations from the Bible.
The museum is replete with treasures from the region.
entries.position: predicative only — after be, almost always with with
entries.contrast: Formal and written. In speech Americans say full of.

entries.meaning: Said by the news or by officials to be true, though not proved. ---
examples: The reported number of cases keeps going up.
The reported cause of the fire was a space heater.
Reported crime is down, but that isn't the same as crime being down.
entries.position: attributive only — before a noun (the reported cases); after a verb it is the passive verb, not the adjective

entries.meaning: So wrong that it deserves strong criticism. ---
examples: His behavior at the meeting was reprehensible.
Lying to the families was a reprehensible thing to do.
Nothing is more reprehensible than blaming the victim.

entries.meaning: In art, showing people and things as they really look. ---
examples: He likes representational art better than abstract painting.
Her early work was strictly representational.
The museum has a whole floor of representational painting.

entries.meaning: Representative has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The sample was not representative of the country as a whole.
Is this painting representative of his later work?
We need a more representative group of testers.
The United States has a representative democracy.
Representative government was the whole point of the revolution.

senses.head: Typical of a larger group, so that it shows what the whole group is like
examples: The sample was not representative of the country as a whole.
Is this painting representative of his later work?
We need a more representative group of testers.

senses.head: Working through elected officials who act for the people
examples: The United States has a representative democracy.
Representative government was the whole point of the revolution.

entries.contrast: Also a common noun: a sales representative, our representative in Congress.

entries.meaning: Repressed has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Years of repressed anger came out at once.
He talked about his repressed memories of the accident.
