She describes her family as cold and repressed.
He was the most repressed person I have ever worked with.

senses.head: Pushed down and never expressed, of a feeling or a memory
examples: Years of repressed anger came out at once.
He talked about his repressed memories of the accident.

senses.head: Unable to show feelings or enjoy things, of a person
examples: She describes her family as cold and repressed.
He was the most repressed person I have ever worked with.

entries.meaning: Using force and strict control to keep people from being free. ---

The government grew more repressive after the protests.

entries.meaning: Able to be done again by someone else with the same result. ---

entries.meaning: Having to do with producing babies or young. ---

examples: The museum has a whole reptilian collection.

senses.head: Cold and unpleasant, in the way a snake seems to people

entries.meaning: Republican has 2 distinct senses.

senses.head: Belonging to or supporting the Republican Party of the United States
examples: She comes from a Republican family in Texas.

examples: France has a long republican tradition.
They fought for a republican form of government.

entries.meaning: So wrong or unpleasant that it disgusts you. ---

entries.meaning: Extremely unpleasant to look at, smell or think about. ---

entries.meaning: Known to be honest and to do good work. ---

entries.meaning: That you must do or have, because a rule says so. ---

entries.meaning: Needed for a particular purpose. ---

entries.meaning: Angry and bitter because you feel you have been treated unfairly. ---
examples: He was resentful of his brother's success.

entries.meaning: Reserved has 2 distinct senses.

senses.head: Working at one place all the time instead of visiting
examples: She is our resident expert on tax law.

entries.meaning: Residential has 2 distinct senses.

senses.head: Made up of homes rather than stores, offices or factories
examples: They live in a quiet residential neighborhood.
The whole block is residential, so there are no shops.

senses.head: Where you live on site while you take part in a program
examples: He spent six weeks in a residential treatment program.
The college has a residential requirement for freshmen.

entries.meaning: Left over after most of something is gone. ---

entries.meaning: Resilient has 2 distinct senses.

senses.head: Able to recover quickly after trouble or illness
examples: Kids are more resilient than we give them credit for.

senses.head: Springing back into shape after being bent or pressed
examples: The foam is light and resilient.

entries.meaning: Resistant has 2 distinct senses.

senses.head: Not harmed or affected by something
examples: These bacteria are resistant to most antibiotics.

senses.head: Unwilling to accept something and quietly fighting it
examples: Older staff were resistant to the change.
He is resistant to any kind of therapy.

entries.form: also the second half of compounds: heat-resistant, water-resistant

entries.meaning: Firm about what you have decided, and not changing your mind. ---
examples: She was resolute in her decision to leave.

He gave a resolute answer: no.

entries.meaning: Resonant has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He has a deep, resonant voice.

The film is resonant with memories of childhood.
Her speech was especially resonant for young voters.

senses.head: Deep, clear and continuing, of a sound or a voice
examples: He has a deep, resonant voice.
The old bell gave a resonant hum.

senses.head: Full of a meaning that stays with people
examples: The film is resonant with memories of childhood.
Her speech was especially resonant for young voters.

entries.takes: with + noun; for or with + person, in the 'meaningful' sense

entries.meaning: Resounding has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The show was a resounding success.

There was a resounding crash from the kitchen.
The speech got a resounding cheer.

senses.head: Complete and unmistakable, of a success, a defeat or an answer
examples: The show was a resounding success.
The proposal met with a resounding no.

senses.head: Loud and echoing
examples: There was a resounding crash from the kitchen.
The speech got a resounding cheer.

entries.meaning: Good at finding a way to solve problems with whatever you have. ---
examples: She is the most resourceful person on the team.
Resourceful cooks can make dinner out of almost nothing.
You have to be resourceful when the budget is this small.

entries.meaning: Admired by other people because of what you do or know. ---
examples: He is a widely respected surgeon.
The paper is respected on both sides of the aisle.
She is one of the most respected judges in the state.
entries.contrast: Three words that learners mix up: respected — admired by other people; respectful — behaving politely toward someone; respective — belonging to each one separately.

entries.meaning: Belonging to each of the people or things just named, separately. ---
examples: After the meeting they went back to their respective offices.
The two companies kept their respective names.
Each writer spoke about their respective field.
entries.contrast: Not respectful (polite) and not respected (admired). Respective always goes with a plural noun and means 'each one's own'.

entries.meaning: Having to do with breathing and the lungs. ---
examples: He was treated for a respiratory infection.
Smoke can cause serious respiratory problems.
The virus attacks the respiratory system.

entries.meaning: Looking splendid, bright and colorful. ---
examples: She arrived resplendent in a red silk gown.
The hall was resplendent with flowers.
The general stood on the steps, resplendent in full uniform.
entries.position: both — most often after a verb or right after the noun: the general, resplendent in blue
entries.contrast: Literary. You meet it in writing and in wedding announcements, not in everyday speech.

entries.meaning: Responsive has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The staff was friendly and responsive.
The mayor has to be more responsive to voters.
The tumor was responsive to the new drug.
The steering is light and responsive.

senses.head: Reacting quickly and well to what people need or say
examples: The staff was friendly and responsive.
The mayor has to be more responsive to voters.

senses.head: Reacting well to treatment or to a control
examples: The tumor was responsive to the new drug.
The steering is light and responsive.

entries.meaning: Feeling fresh again because you have slept or relaxed. ---
examples: I felt rested for the first time in weeks.
You'll play better rested.
A short nap left her rested and ready to work.
entries.position: predicative only — before a noun only in the compound well-rested: a well-rested team

entries.meaning: Calm and quiet, so that it helps you relax. ---
examples: We had a restful weekend at the lake.
The room is painted a restful green.
Nothing is more restful than a quiet morning.
entries.contrast: Restful describes the thing that gives you rest; rested describes the person who got it. A restful weekend leaves you rested.

entries.meaning: Unwilling to keep waiting or to be controlled, and beginning to show it. ---
examples: The crowd grew restive as the delay went on.
Restive lawmakers began to question the plan.
The horses were restive before the storm.
entries.contrast: Close to restless, but restive adds impatience with being held back or controlled: a restive crowd is about to stop obeying.

entries.meaning: Restless has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The kids get restless on long drives.
He was restless all evening before the interview.
She had a restless night.
It was a restless sleep full of strange dreams.

senses.head: Unable to stay still or be patient, because you are bored or worried
examples: The kids get restless on long drives.
He was restless all evening before the interview.

senses.head: Broken and without real rest, of a night or of sleep
examples: She had a restless night.
It was a restless sleep full of strange dreams.

entries.meaning: Restorative has 2 distinct senses.
examples: A hot bath is wonderfully restorative.
She took a restorative week off in the mountains.
The school uses restorative justice instead of suspensions.
He does restorative dental work.

senses.head: Making you feel strong and fresh again
examples: A hot bath is wonderfully restorative.
She took a restorative week off in the mountains.

senses.head: Aimed at repairing harm rather than punishing
examples: The school uses restorative justice instead of suspensions.
He does restorative dental work.

entries.meaning: Calm and controlled; not extreme or showy. ---
examples: His reaction was surprisingly restrained.
The design is elegant and restrained.
She gave a restrained smile and said nothing.

entries.meaning: Restricted has 2 distinct senses.
examples: This is a restricted area — you need a badge.
The documents are restricted.
He is on a restricted diet after the surgery.
The team works with a very restricted budget.

senses.head: Controlled, so that only certain people may enter or use it
examples: This is a restricted area — you need a badge.
The documents are restricted.

senses.head: Limited in amount, range or choice
examples: He is on a restricted diet after the surgery.
The team works with a very restricted budget.

entries.meaning: Limiting what people can do, usually more than they think is fair. ---
examples: The dress code is too restrictive.
These are the most restrictive voting laws in the state's history.
Restrictive rules drove the best players away.

entries.meaning: Becoming strong, popular or common again after a weak period. ---
examples: A resurgent auto industry brought jobs back to the city.
The team faces a resurgent rival on Sunday.
Measles is resurgent in states with low vaccination rates.
entries.form: -ent — the adjective behind the noun resurgence

entries.meaning: Done to punish someone for something they did to you first. ---
examples: The country launched a retaliatory strike.
He says the firing was retaliatory.
Retaliatory tariffs hit farmers hardest.

entries.meaning: Not willing to talk about something or to say what you think. ---
examples: He is reticent about his years in the army.
She was oddly reticent during the whole meeting.
Witnesses were more reticent than the police had expected.
entries.contrast: Reticent is about not speaking; reluctant is about not wanting to act. You are reticent about your past but reluctant to leave.

entries.meaning: No longer working, because you have reached the end of your working life. ---
examples: My neighbor is a retired teacher.
Both of my parents are retired now.
He is a retired Navy officer who still gets up at five.

entries.meaning: Retiring has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He is a retiring man who hates parties.
She is shy and retiring in a big group.
The retiring chairman gave a short speech.
They threw a party for the retiring principal.

senses.head: Shy, and staying out of the center of attention
examples: He is a retiring man who hates parties.
She is shy and retiring in a big group.

senses.head: About to leave a job or an office for good
examples: The retiring chairman gave a short speech.
They threw a party for the retiring principal.

entries.position: both — the 'leaving office' sense only before a noun

entries.meaning: Able to be pulled back in or folded away. ---
examples: The stadium has a retractable roof.
Cats have retractable claws.
The blade is retractable, which makes it safer to carry.

entries.meaning: Copying the style of an earlier time on purpose, usually the 1950s to the 1980s. ---
examples: The diner has a retro look, right down to the jukebox.
Her whole outfit is very retro.
Retro video games are selling again.

entries.meaning: Taking effect from a date in the past, not only from today. ---
examples: The raise is retroactive to January 1.
Congress passed a retroactive tax change.
The new rule is not retroactive, so old cases stand.

entries.meaning: Looking back at things that happened or were made in the past. ---
examples: The study is retrospective, based on old medical records.
He took a retrospective look at thirty years on the job.
The team holds a retrospective meeting after every project.
entries.contrast: Also a noun: a retrospective is a show of an artist's work from across their whole career.

entries.meaning: Coming back after being away, or taking part again after a break. ---
examples: Returning students register on Monday.
The returning champion took the court first.
Returning soldiers were met at the airport by their families.

entries.meaning: Able to be used again instead of thrown away. ---
examples: Bring a reusable bag to the store.
The containers are reusable and dishwasher safe.
We switched to reusable water bottles last year.

entries.meaning: Revealing has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The dress was a little too revealing for the office.
She wore something less revealing to the interview.
His answer was very revealing.
It is the most revealing interview she has ever given.

senses.head: Showing a lot of the body, of clothes
examples: The dress was a little too revealing for the office.
She wore something less revealing to the interview.

senses.head: Telling you something important that was not obvious before
examples: His answer was very revealing.
It is the most revealing interview she has ever given.

entries.meaning: Deeply respected, almost in the way holy things are respected. ---
examples: He is revered as the father of the sport.
She is a revered figure in American poetry.
The old cookbook is revered by chefs.

entries.meaning: Showing deep respect, the way people behave in a holy place. ---
examples: The crowd fell into a reverent silence.
He speaks about his old teacher in reverent tones.
The movie takes a reverent approach to its subject.

entries.meaning: Opposite in direction or order to the usual one. ---
examples: Put the names in reverse order.
The truck has a reverse camera.
Critics called the policy reverse discrimination.
entries.contrast: Also a noun (the reverse is true) and a verb (reverse the car). As an adjective it goes only before a noun — for 'the opposite' after a verb, say the opposite.

entries.meaning: Reversible has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The damage is reversible if you stop now.
Most of these side effects are reversible.
It is a reversible jacket — black on one side, red on the other.
Reversible belts save you buying two.

senses.head: Able to be changed back to the way it was
examples: The damage is reversible if you stop now.
Most of these side effects are reversible.

senses.head: Able to be worn with either side outward
examples: It is a reversible jacket — black on one side, red on the other.
Reversible belts save you buying two.

entries.meaning: Changed and corrected from an earlier version. ---
examples: Use the revised edition, not the old one.
The revised figures are much lower.
Here is the revised schedule for next week.
entries.contrast: In American English revise means to change a text or a figure. It does not mean 'study for an exam' — that British use is review or study here.

entries.meaning: So unpleasant that it almost makes you feel sick. ---
examples: The smell in the basement was revolting.
He told a revolting joke at dinner.
That is the most revolting thing I have ever tasted.
entries.contrast: In this everyday sense it has nothing to do with revolt 'to rebel', so the revolting peasants is an old English joke.

entries.meaning: Revolutionary has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The first iPhone was a revolutionary design.
Her way of teaching reading was revolutionary at the time.
Revolutionary leaders took over the capital within a week.
The group had openly revolutionary aims.

senses.head: Completely new and changing the way things are done
examples: The first iPhone was a revolutionary design.
Her way of teaching reading was revolutionary at the time.

senses.head: Having to do with a political revolution
examples: Revolutionary leaders took over the capital within a week.
The group had openly revolutionary aims.

entries.contrast: Also a noun: a revolutionary is a person who fights to overthrow a government.

entries.meaning: Giving you the good feeling that the effort was worth it. ---
examples: Teaching is hard work, but it is rewarding.
It was the most rewarding year of my life.
Small children are exhausting and rewarding to raise.
entries.contrast: It is about satisfaction, not money: a job can be rewarding and still badly paid. For money say well-paid.

entries.meaning: Rhetorical has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Don't answer — it was a rhetorical question.
He ended with a rhetorical question about fairness.
It is a rhetorical device, not a real promise.
Her rhetorical skill won the debate.

senses.head: Asked for effect, not because you want an answer — of a question
examples: Don't answer — it was a rhetorical question.
He ended with a rhetorical question about fairness.

senses.head: Having to do with the art of speaking and writing persuasively
examples: It is a rhetorical device, not a real promise.
Her rhetorical skill won the debate.

entries.meaning: Of the disease in which the body attacks its own joints and they swell and hurt. ---
examples: She was diagnosed with rheumatoid arthritis at thirty.
Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune disease.
He takes a weekly shot for his rheumatoid arthritis.
entries.contrast: In practice you meet it in one phrase, rheumatoid arthritis. The silent rh- is simply 'r'.

entries.meaning: Ending in the same sound as another word or another line. ---
examples: The poem is written in rhyming couplets.
Little kids love rhyming books.
'Cat' and 'hat' are a rhyming pair.

entries.meaning: Having a regular, repeated beat or movement. ---
examples: The rhythmic sound of the waves put me to sleep.
Her breathing was slow and rhythmic.
It is a rhythmic, danceable song.

entries.meaning: Old, weak and likely to break or fall over. ---
examples: We climbed a rickety wooden staircase.
The table is rickety, so don't lean on it.
They crossed on a rickety little bridge.

entries.meaning: Riddled has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The road sign was riddled with bullet holes.
They found the old boat riddled with worm holes.
The report was riddled with errors.
The whole system is riddled with corruption.

senses.head: Full of holes, especially holes made by bullets
examples: The road sign was riddled with bullet holes.
They found the old boat riddled with worm holes.

senses.head: Full of something bad, all the way through
examples: The report was riddled with errors.
The whole system is riddled with corruption.

entries.position: predicative only — after a verb, or right after the noun: a report riddled with errors

entries.meaning: So silly or unreasonable that nobody can take it seriously. ---
examples: Twenty dollars for a cup of coffee is ridiculous.
He looked ridiculous in that hat.
This is the most ridiculous rule in the whole handbook.
entries.contrast: Ridiculous means laughably bad or unreasonable. For something meant to make you laugh, say funny.

entries.meaning: Very common and everywhere, of something bad; with with, full of it. ---
examples: Rumors were rife in the days before the vote.
Corruption is rife in the construction business.
The essay is rife with spelling mistakes.
entries.position: predicative only — never before a noun
entries.contrast: Rife is used only about bad things — rumors, corruption, mistakes — and never goes before a noun.

entries.meaning: Dishonestly arranged in advance so that a particular side wins. ---
examples: He claimed the election was rigged.
It is a rigged game — the house always wins.
The whole contest looked rigged from the start.
entries.form: -ed from rig 'to fix the result dishonestly'

entries.meaning: Right-hand has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Take the right-hand lane at the light.
The switch is on the right-hand side of the door.
She is the governor's right-hand woman.
He was the boss's right-hand man for twenty years.

senses.head: On or toward the right side
examples: Take the right-hand lane at the light.
The switch is on the right-hand side of the door.

senses.head: In right-hand man and right-hand woman: the person you rely on most
examples: She is the governor's right-hand woman.
He was the boss's right-hand man for twenty years.

entries.русский: правый, находящийся справа; правая рука (о человеке)
entries.contrast: Right-hand is about position; right-handed is about the hand a person writes with.

entries.meaning: Having the opinions and values the speaker thinks are decent and correct. ---
examples: No right-minded person would defend that.
Right-minded citizens spoke up at the meeting.
Every right-minded voter should be worried by this.
entries.contrast: Nothing to do with the political right — that is right-wing.

entries.meaning: Belonging to the conservative side in politics. ---
examples: He writes for a right-wing website.
Her views are pretty right-wing for this town.
A right-wing group organized the rally.

entries.meaning: Righteous has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He saw himself as a righteous man.
The sermon was about righteous living.
There was righteous anger in her voice.
Righteous indignation filled the letters page for a week.

senses.head: Morally right and good, often with a religious feeling to it
examples: He saw himself as a righteous man.
The sermon was about righteous living.

senses.head: Of anger: felt to be completely justified
examples: There was righteous anger in her voice.
Righteous indignation filled the letters page for a week.

entries.contrast: The insult is self-righteous: certain of being right and showing it.

entries.meaning: Having the legal or moral right to something — of an owner, an heir or a place. ---
examples: The painting was returned to its rightful owner.
She took her rightful place at the top of the rankings.
He is the rightful heir to the property.

entries.meaning: Rigid has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The case has a rigid plastic shell.
Keep your arm rigid while I wrap it.
The school has rigid rules about phones.
He is too rigid to work well on a team.

senses.head: Stiff and not bending
examples: The case has a rigid plastic shell.
Keep your arm rigid while I wrap it.

senses.head: Very strict and not open to change
examples: The school has rigid rules about phones.
He is too rigid to work well on a team.

entries.meaning: Rigorous has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The drug went through rigorous testing.
She is a rigorous thinker who checks every number.
It is a rigorous program — expect long hours.
They follow a rigorous training schedule all winter.

senses.head: Careful, thorough and exact
examples: The drug went through rigorous testing.
She is a rigorous thinker who checks every number.

senses.head: Demanding and hard to keep up with, of a course or a schedule
examples: It is a rigorous program — expect long hours.
They follow a rigorous training schedule all winter.

entries.meaning: Full of noisy energy, or very great — of a good time or a success. ---
examples: They had a rip-roaring good time at the fair.
The show was a rip-roaring success.
It is a rip-roaring adventure movie with no quiet moments.
entries.contrast: Informal and cheerful. It goes with success, time and adventure, not with people.

entries.meaning: Ripe has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The peaches are finally ripe.
Pick the ripest tomato on the vine.
The market is ripe for change.
Conditions were ripe for a strike.

senses.head: Fully grown and ready to eat, of fruit, vegetables or cheese
examples: The peaches are finally ripe.
Pick the ripest tomato on the vine.

senses.head: Ready for something to happen
examples: The market is ripe for change.
Conditions were ripe for a strike.

entries.meaning: Rising has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Rising prices are hurting families on a fixed income.
We watched the rising water from the porch.
She is a rising star in country music.
He is a rising senior at the high school.

senses.head: Going up in amount, level or price
examples: Rising prices are hurting families on a fixed income.
We watched the rising water from the porch.

senses.head: Becoming more successful or important
examples: She is a rising star in country music.
He is a rising senior at the high school.

entries.contrast: In American schools a rising senior is a student who will be a senior next fall.

entries.meaning: Carrying no chance of loss or harm. ---
examples: There is no such thing as a risk-free investment.
The trial is risk-free — you can cancel any time.
No surgery is completely risk-free.

entries.meaning: Carrying a real chance that something will go wrong. ---
examples: Driving in that storm was risky.
Stocks are riskier than bonds.
It is a risky plan, but it might work.
entries.contrast: Risky and risqué look alike but are different words: risky is about danger, risqué is about being slightly indecent.

entries.meaning: Slightly shocking because it deals with sex. ---
examples: He told a risque joke at the wedding and his wife glared.
The play was risque for 1955.
Her act got more risque as the night went on.
entries.position: both — a risque joke; the show was pretty risque
entries.form: from French; usually printed with the accent, risqué
entries.contrast: A false friend for Russian speakers: risque is about sex and decency, not about danger. Risky business is risky.

entries.meaning: Slightly rude or sexual, in a way that may shock some people. ---
examples: He told a risqué joke at the wedding.
The costumes were a little risqué for a family show.
Her act is the most risqué on the whole tour.
entries.form: from French; often written without the accent, risque, and the ending is said 'kay'
entries.contrast: Not the same word as risky. A risqué joke has nothing to do with danger.

entries.meaning: Done as part of a ceremony, or always done in the same fixed way. ---
examples: Ritual washing comes before the meal.
The dance had a ritual meaning for the village.
There was the ritual exchange of gifts at the door.
entries.contrast: Far more common as a noun (a morning ritual). The adjective goes only before a noun; after a verb use ritualistic.

entries.meaning: Done in a fixed, repeated way, like a ceremony. ---
examples: The team has a ritualistic warm-up before every game.
His hand-washing had become ritualistic.
There is something ritualistic about Sunday dinner at their house.

entries.meaning: Expensive and fashionable. ---
examples: They stayed at a ritzy hotel downtown.
It is the ritziest neighborhood in the city.
The place is too ritzy for jeans.
entries.contrast: Informal and a little dated. Fancy or upscale is what people say now.

entries.meaning: So interesting that you cannot look away. ---
examples: The trial made for riveting television.
Her testimony was absolutely riveting.
It is a riveting account of the escape.
entries.form: -ing from rivet 'to fasten with a metal pin'

entries.meaning: Roaring has 2 distinct senses.
examples: We sat by a roaring fire.
A roaring crowd greeted the team at the airport.
The bake sale was a roaring success.
The 1920s are still called the Roaring Twenties.

senses.head: Making a loud, deep, continuous sound
examples: We sat by a roaring fire.
A roaring crowd greeted the team at the airport.

senses.head: Very great or lively — in a few fixed phrases
examples: The bake sale was a roaring success.
The 1920s are still called the Roaring Twenties.

entries.meaning: Cooked in an oven or over a fire — in the names of dishes. ---
examples: We had roast beef and potatoes.
She ordered the roast chicken.
Roast duck is the house specialty.
entries.contrast: Before a noun, dish names keep the old form: roast beef, roast chicken, roast potatoes. Everywhere else say roasted: The potatoes were roasted, not fried.

entries.meaning: Cooked or browned with dry heat, in an oven or over a fire. ---
examples: Roasted vegetables are the easiest side dish there is.
The peppers were roasted and then peeled.
Try the salad with roasted almonds.
entries.contrast: The everyday form. Only the old dish names use plain roast (roast beef).

entries.meaning: Robotic has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The factory uses a robotic arm for welding.
He had robotic surgery on his knee.
Her voice on the phone was flat and robotic.
He gave a robotic answer and moved on to the next caller.

senses.head: Belonging to or done by robots
examples: The factory uses a robotic arm for welding.
He had robotic surgery on his knee.

senses.head: Stiff and without feeling, like a machine
examples: Her voice on the phone was flat and robotic.
He gave a robotic answer and moved on to the next caller.

entries.meaning: Robust has 3 distinct senses.
examples: He is eighty and still robust.
These plants are robust enough to survive a frost.
We need a more robust password policy.
Sales were robust over the holidays.
It is a robust red wine that stands up to steak.
He likes his coffee dark and robust.

senses.head: Strong and healthy
examples: He is eighty and still robust.
These plants are robust enough to survive a frost.

senses.head: Strong and working well, of a system, an economy or a debate
examples: We need a more robust password policy.
Sales were robust over the holidays.

senses.head: Strong and full, of a taste or smell
examples: It is a robust red wine that stands up to steak.
He likes his coffee dark and robust.

entries.meaning: As low as it can possibly go — almost always of prices. ---
examples: They are selling tickets at rock-bottom prices.
Gas hit rock-bottom rates that winter.
We got a rock-bottom deal on the car.
entries.contrast: As two words it is a noun phrase: He hit rock bottom last year.

entries.meaning: Rocky has 2 distinct senses.
examples: They hiked along a rocky beach.
The trail gets rockier near the top.
The marriage got off to a rocky start.
It has been a rocky year for the company.

senses.head: Covered with rocks, or made of rock
examples: They hiked along a rocky beach.
The trail gets rockier near the top.

senses.head: Full of problems and not at all steady
examples: The marriage got off to a rocky start.
It has been a rocky year for the company.

entries.meaning: Rolling has 2 distinct senses.
examples: We drove past rolling hills and old farms.
The house sits on forty acres of rolling farmland.
The city had rolling blackouts all August.
They announced a rolling schedule of layoffs.

senses.head: Rising and falling in long gentle slopes, of land
examples: We drove past rolling hills and old farms.
The house sits on forty acres of rolling farmland.

senses.head: Happening in stages, one area or group at a time
examples: The city had rolling blackouts all August.
They announced a rolling schedule of layoffs.

entries.meaning: Of ancient Rome, or of the city of Rome today. ---
examples: They found a Roman coin in the field.
Roman roads still run across parts of Europe.
The chapters are numbered with Roman numerals.
entries.contrast: Also a noun for a person (the Romans). With a small letter, roman is the plain upright type you are reading now, as opposed to italic.

entries.meaning: Belonging to the Christian church that has the Pope at its head. ---
examples: She was raised Roman Catholic.
They were married in a Roman Catholic church.
The hospital is Roman Catholic and was founded by nuns.
entries.contrast: Also a noun (He's a Roman Catholic). In everyday speech people usually just say Catholic.

entries.meaning: Of the languages that grew out of Latin — French, Spanish, Italian, Portuguese and Romanian. ---
examples: Spanish and Italian are Romance languages.
She studies Romance philology.
The Romance languages all give nouns a gender.
entries.contrast: A different word from the noun romance 'a love story', and it is always capitalized.

entries.meaning: From Romania, or connected with Romania and its language. ---
examples: He is a Romanian filmmaker living in Berlin.
We had dinner at a Romanian restaurant.
Her grandparents are Romanian.
entries.contrast: Also a noun: the people (a Romanian) and the language (She speaks Romanian).

entries.meaning: Romantic has 3 distinct senses.
examples: They are in a romantic relationship.
He planned a romantic dinner for their anniversary.
Venice at night is impossibly romantic.
It is the most romantic restaurant in town.
He has a romantic view of the old West.
That is a romantic notion of what soldiers actually do.

senses.head: Having to do with love between people
examples: They are in a romantic relationship.
He planned a romantic dinner for their anniversary.

senses.head: Beautiful in a way that makes you think of love
examples: Venice at night is impossibly romantic.
It is the most romantic restaurant in town.

senses.head: Idealistic, and not based on how things really are
examples: He has a romantic view of the old West.
That is a romantic notion of what soldiers actually do.

entries.contrast: Also a noun (a hopeless romantic). Capital Romantic means the poets and composers of the early 1800s.

entries.meaning: Having plenty of space inside. ---
examples: The car is surprisingly roomy in back.
Their new place is roomier than the old one.
I want a roomy bag for the trip.

entries.meaning: Rooted has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The custom is rooted in the nineteenth century.
His fear of water is rooted in one bad afternoon.
I stood rooted to the spot.
She was rooted in place by the noise.

senses.head: Coming from something and firmly fixed in it
examples: The custom is rooted in the nineteenth century.
His fear of water is rooted in one bad afternoon.

senses.head: Unable to move, as if fixed to the ground
examples: I stood rooted to the spot.
She was rooted in place by the noise.

entries.русский: укоренённый, уходящий корнями; приросший к месту
entries.position: both — before a noun with an adverb: a deeply rooted belief
entries.comparison: not gradable — the adverb carries the degree: deeply rooted, firmly rooted
entries.form: -ed from root; also the compound deep-rooted
entries.contrast: Rooted for is a different verb: to root for a team means to cheer for it.

entries.meaning: Rose-colored has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He looks back at the nineties through rose-colored glasses.
Take off the rose-colored glasses and look at the numbers.
The report gives a rose-colored picture of the economy.
She picked a rose-colored fabric for the curtains.
The invitations came on rose-colored card stock.

senses.head: Seeing things as better than they really are
examples: He looks back at the nineties through rose-colored glasses.
Take off the rose-colored glasses and look at the numbers.
The report gives a rose-colored picture of the economy.

senses.head: Pink, the color of a rose
examples: She picked a rose-colored fabric for the curtains.
The invitations came on rose-colored card stock.

entries.position: attributive only — almost always in rose-colored glasses
entries.contrast: American spelling is rose-colored; British writing has rose-coloured or rose-tinted.

entries.meaning: Rosy has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The baby had rosy cheeks after the walk.
Her face was rosy from the cold.
His cheeks looked rosier after a week at the beach.
The company painted a rosy picture of next year.
Things are not as rosy as the press release suggests.

senses.head: Pink and healthy-looking, usually about skin
examples: The baby had rosy cheeks after the walk.
Her face was rosy from the cold.
His cheeks looked rosier after a week at the beach.

senses.head: Hopeful; promising a good future
examples: The company painted a rosy picture of next year.
Things are not as rosy as the press release suggests.

entries.contrast: Rosy drops the e of rose, and the y becomes i in comparison: rosier, rosiest.

entries.meaning: Having pink, healthy-looking cheeks. ---
examples: A rosy-cheeked boy opened the door.
The choir was full of rosy-cheeked kids in scarves.
She played a rosy-cheeked farm girl in the movie.

entries.meaning: Turning around a center point; working by turning. ---
examples: The old phone had a rotary dial.
A rotary engine has no pistons going up and down.
The bakery bakes everything in a rotary oven.
entries.contrast: In New England a rotary is also a noun — a traffic circle. Elsewhere in the US people say traffic circle or roundabout.

entries.meaning: Rotten has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The apples at the bottom of the bag were rotten.
The whole porch is rotten underneath.
Something smells rotten in the fridge.
We had rotten luck with the weather.
That was a rotten thing to say.
I feel rotten about canceling on you.

senses.head: Decayed and no longer good
examples: The apples at the bottom of the bag were rotten.
The whole porch is rotten underneath.
Something smells rotten in the fridge.

senses.head: Very bad or unpleasant
examples: We had rotten luck with the weather.
That was a rotten thing to say.
I feel rotten about canceling on you.

entries.contrast: Rotten fits food, wood and teeth. Milk that has gone bad is spoiled or sour, not rotten.

entries.meaning: Rough has 4 distinct senses.
examples: The wall was rough to the touch.
My hands get rough in the winter.
This road is rougher than the one we took.
She's had a rough year.
It was a rough flight.
Give me a rough estimate.
This is just a rough draft.
Don't be too rough with the puppy.
The neighborhood used to be pretty rough.

senses.head: Not smooth or even to the touch
examples: The wall was rough to the touch.
My hands get rough in the winter.
This road is rougher than the one we took.

senses.head: Difficult or unpleasant to live through
examples: She's had a rough year.
It was a rough flight.

senses.head: Approximate; not finished or exact
examples: Give me a rough estimate.
This is just a rough draft.

senses.head: Using force; not gentle or safe
examples: Don't be too rough with the puppy.
The neighborhood used to be pretty rough.

entries.contrast: The gh is pronounced /f/: rough rhymes with stuff. The adverb roughly also means 'approximately': roughly ten miles.

entries.meaning: Rough and disorderly, but usually without real harm. ---
examples: Rough-and-tumble play is normal for puppies.
He grew up in a rough-and-tumble neighborhood.
She loves the rough-and-tumble world of city politics.

entries.meaning: Going on all day and all night without stopping. ---
examples: The patient needs round-the-clock care.
There was round-the-clock coverage of the trial.
The plant runs on a round-the-clock schedule.
entries.form: compound — preposition phrase used as one word
entries.contrast: Before a noun it is the adjective round-the-clock care; after a verb use the adverb around the clock: They worked around the clock.

entries.meaning: Not direct — going the long way, or said in an indirect way. ---
examples: We took a roundabout route to avoid the highway.
He told me in a roundabout way that I hadn't gotten the job.
That's a roundabout explanation for something very simple.
entries.contrast: In Britain a roundabout is a noun — a traffic circle. As an adjective meaning 'indirect' it is normal American English.

entries.meaning: Rounded has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The table has rounded corners.
Her handwriting is soft and rounded.
Sand the edges until they're rounded.
The school aims to give kids a rounded education.
She wanted a more rounded view of the problem.

senses.head: Curved, with no sharp corners or edges
examples: The table has rounded corners.
Her handwriting is soft and rounded.
Sand the edges until they're rounded.

senses.head: Complete and balanced, covering every side of something
examples: The school aims to give kids a rounded education.
She wanted a more rounded view of the problem.

entries.meaning: Making people excited and enthusiastic. ---
examples: The coach gave a rousing speech at halftime.
The band ended with a rousing version of the anthem.
The bill passed to rousing applause.

entries.meaning: Done regularly as normal procedure; ordinary. ---
examples: It was a routine traffic stop.
She's in for routine surgery on Thursday.
There is nothing routine about this case.
entries.position: both — mostly before a noun: a routine checkup
entries.contrast: The stress is on the second syllable: roo-TEEN. A routine is also a noun — a fixed order of doing things, or a dance or comedy act.

entries.meaning: Moving from place to place instead of staying in one. ---
examples: She works as a roving reporter for the network.
A roving band of musicians played between the tables.
The museum sends a roving exhibit to small towns.
entries.contrast: A roving eye is a set phrase for someone who keeps looking at other people romantically.

entries.meaning: Noisy and rough, in a way that can cause trouble. ---
examples: A rowdy group of fans filled the bar.
The crowd got rowdier after the third quarter.
It was a rowdy wedding, in the best way.

entries.meaning: Royal has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The royal family spent the summer in Scotland.
The palace is still a royal residence.
She received a royal pardon.
Parking downtown is a royal pain.
He made a royal mess of the kitchen.

senses.head: Belonging to or connected with a king or queen
examples: The royal family spent the summer in Scotland.
The palace is still a royal residence.
She received a royal pardon.

senses.head: Complete, total — used before a few words to make them stronger
examples: Parking downtown is a royal pain.
He made a royal mess of the kitchen.

entries.contrast: Royal means 'of a king or queen'; regal means 'looking like royalty'. A royal pain has nothing to do with kings — it just means a very big nuisance.

entries.meaning: Tough and bendy like rubber, usually said about badly cooked food. ---
examples: The calamari was rubbery.
Microwaved eggs come out rubbery.
He cut into a rubbery piece of steak.
entries.contrast: A rubber mat is made of rubber; rubbery chicken only feels like it.

entries.meaning: Red and healthy-looking, said about skin. ---
examples: He had a ruddy face from working outdoors.
Her complexion was ruddy after the hike.
His cheeks looked ruddier than usual.

entries.meaning: Very basic — only the first and simplest level. ---
examples: He has a rudimentary knowledge of Spanish.
The clinic has only rudimentary equipment.
Our plan is still pretty rudimentary.

entries.meaning: Ruffled has 3 distinct senses.
examples: The bird sat there with ruffled feathers.
His hair was ruffled from the wind.
She looked a little ruffled by the question.
Nothing gets him ruffled.
She wore a white ruffled blouse.
The dress has a ruffled hem.

senses.head: Pushed out of place so it is no longer smooth
examples: The bird sat there with ruffled feathers.
His hair was ruffled from the wind.

senses.head: Slightly upset or annoyed
examples: She looked a little ruffled by the question.
Nothing gets him ruffled.

senses.head: Made with ruffles — strips of gathered cloth
examples: She wore a white ruffled blouse.
The dress has a ruffled hem.

entries.contrast: Unruffled is the common opposite of the second sense: She stayed unruffled through the whole meeting.

entries.meaning: Rugged has 3 distinct senses.
examples: The rugged coastline is hard to reach by car.
We hiked through rugged terrain for six hours.
These boots are rugged enough for winter work.
The laptop comes in a rugged case.
He has a rugged, weather-beaten face.
The ad was looking for a rugged type.

senses.head: Rough, rocky and hard to travel across
examples: The rugged coastline is hard to reach by car.
We hiked through rugged terrain for six hours.

senses.head: Strong and built to survive hard use
examples: These boots are rugged enough for winter work.
The laptop comes in a rugged case.

senses.head: Of a man's face: strong-featured in an attractive way
examples: He has a rugged, weather-beaten face.
The ad was looking for a rugged type.

entries.contrast: The -ed is always /ɪd/ and makes a second syllable: RUH-gid, never ruhgd.

entries.meaning: Ruined has 2 distinct senses.
examples: We walked around a ruined castle above the river.
The ruined church is still standing after the fire.
My shoes were ruined by the road salt.
The whole evening was ruined by one phone call.

senses.head: Destroyed, with only broken remains left
examples: We walked around a ruined castle above the river.
The ruined church is still standing after the fire.

senses.head: Spoiled so badly that it is no good any more
examples: My shoes were ruined by the road salt.
The whole evening was ruined by one phone call.

entries.meaning: Causing very serious damage, especially to money or a business. ---
examples: The lawsuit was ruinous for the family business.
They borrowed at ruinous interest rates.
A second bad harvest would be ruinous.

entries.meaning: Having power over a country or an organization. ---
examples: The ruling party lost its majority.
Members of the ruling class sent their children abroad.
The ruling coalition fell apart in March.
entries.contrast: A ruling is also a noun — a judge's or an official's decision.

entries.meaning: Wrinkled and messy, usually said about clothes or bedding. ---
examples: He showed up in a rumpled suit.
The sheets were rumpled where the cat had slept.
Her jacket looked rumpled after the flight.

entries.meaning: Run-down has 2 distinct senses.
examples: They bought a run-down house on the edge of town.
The whole block looks run-down.
I've been feeling run-down since the trip.
You look run-down — take a day off.

senses.head: In bad condition because nobody has taken care of it
examples: They bought a run-down house on the edge of town.
The whole block looks run-down.

senses.head: Tired and slightly unwell
examples: I've been feeling run-down since the trip.
You look run-down — take a day off.

entries.contrast: A rundown, written as one word with the stress on run, is a noun meaning a quick summary: Give me the rundown.

entries.meaning: Ordinary, with nothing special about it. ---
examples: It's a run-of-the-mill office job.
The food was run-of-the-mill diner food.
This is no run-of-the-mill thunderstorm.

entries.meaning: Of a sentence: made of two sentences joined without the right punctuation. ---
examples: Her essay was full of run-on sentences.
Fix the run-on sentence in the second paragraph.
A comma splice is one kind of run-on error.
entries.contrast: A grammar term: a run-on sentence pushes two sentences together with no period and no conjunction.

entries.meaning: Runaway has 3 distinct senses.
examples: The shelter takes in runaway teens.
A runaway horse blocked the road for an hour.
A runaway truck hit the barrier on the hill.
Runaway inflation wiped out their savings.
The movie was a runaway hit.
She won the primary in a runaway victory.

senses.head: Having escaped or left home without permission
examples: The shelter takes in runaway teens.
A runaway horse blocked the road for an hour.

senses.head: Out of control and impossible to stop
examples: A runaway truck hit the barrier on the hill.
Runaway inflation wiped out their savings.

senses.head: Won very easily; extremely successful
examples: The movie was a runaway hit.
She won the primary in a runaway victory.

entries.contrast: A runaway is also a noun — a child or teenager who has left home.

entries.meaning: Running has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The cabin has no running water.
Rinse the rice under running water.
It's a running joke in our family.
Keep a running total as you shop.
They have a running argument about the thermostat.

senses.head: Of water: flowing, especially from a tap
examples: The cabin has no running water.
Rinse the rice under running water.

senses.head: Continuing over a long time, with new parts added
examples: It's a running joke in our family.
Keep a running total as you shop.
They have a running argument about the thermostat.

entries.contrast: In running shoes and running track, running is a noun used as a modifier, not an adjective. Three days running is an adverb meaning 'in a row'.

entries.meaning: Runny has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The sauce came out runny.
I like my eggs a little runny.
This batter is runnier than the recipe says.
She has a runny nose and a cough.
My eyes get runny every spring.

senses.head: More liquid than it should be
examples: The sauce came out runny.
I like my eggs a little runny.
This batter is runnier than the recipe says.

senses.head: Of a nose or eyes: producing liquid because of a cold or an allergy
examples: She has a runny nose and a cough.
My eyes get runny every spring.

entries.meaning: In or about the countryside, away from cities. ---
examples: She grew up in rural Kansas.
Rural hospitals are closing all over the state.
The area north of the lake is still very rural.
entries.contrast: Rural is a neutral fact of geography; rustic adds old-fashioned charm. A city restaurant can look rustic, never rural.

entries.meaning: Rushed has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The ending of the movie felt rushed.
We ate a rushed breakfast and ran for the train.
I felt rushed the whole morning.
Don't let them make you feel rushed.

senses.head: Done too fast, without enough time to do it well
examples: The ending of the movie felt rushed.
We ate a rushed breakfast and ran for the train.

senses.head: Of a person: forced to hurry
examples: I felt rushed the whole morning.
Don't let them make you feel rushed.

entries.meaning: Belonging to the Orthodox church of Russia. ---
examples: They were married in a Russian Orthodox church in Brooklyn.
His grandmother is Russian Orthodox.
Russian Orthodox Christmas falls on January 7.
entries.contrast: Russian православный on its own is Orthodox or Eastern Orthodox; Russian Orthodox names the Russian church in particular. Both words take a capital letter.

entries.meaning: Using Russian as an everyday language. ---
examples: The clinic is looking for a Russian-speaking nurse.
There is a large Russian-speaking community in Brighton Beach.
She joined a Russian-speaking book club.
entries.contrast: Russian-speaking is about the language, not the country: a Russian-speaking family may be from Kazakhstan or Israel. After a verb say They speak Russian.

entries.meaning: Plain and old-fashioned in a country way that people find charming. ---
examples: The restaurant has a rustic look — bare wood and iron lamps.
We rented a rustic cabin with a wood stove.
The bread is dense and rustic.
entries.contrast: Rustic is a compliment about style — plain and country-like. Rural is only about location.

entries.meaning: Rusty has 2 distinct senses.
examples: A rusty nail was sticking out of the board.
The gate gets rustier every year.
My Spanish is pretty rusty.
He's rusty after two years off the ice.

senses.head: Covered with rust
examples: A rusty nail was sticking out of the board.
The gate gets rustier every year.

senses.head: Of a skill: weaker than it was because you have not practiced
examples: My Spanish is pretty rusty.
He's rusty after two years off the ice.

entries.meaning: Willing to hurt people to get what you want; showing no pity. ---
examples: He was ruthless with anyone who slowed the project down.
It's a ruthless business.
She made a ruthless cut to the budget.
entries.form: -less — literally 'without ruth', an old word for pity

entries.meaning: From or relating to Rwanda. ---
examples: The Rwandan team qualified for the tournament.
He teaches Rwandan history at the community college.
Her husband is Rwandan.
entries.contrast: A Rwandan is also the noun for a person from Rwanda.

entries.meaning: Having very long, curved upper teeth — said of certain extinct cats. ---
examples: The museum has a saber-toothed cat skeleton.
Kids always want to see the saber-toothed tiger.
Saber-toothed predators died out about ten thousand years ago.
entries.contrast: American spelling is saber; British writing has sabre-toothed.

entries.meaning: So sweet and sentimental that it feels fake. ---
examples: The movie ends on a saccharine note.
He sang it in a saccharine voice.
The card's message was a little saccharine for my taste.
entries.contrast: The adjective ends in -e: saccharine. Saccharin, with no e, is the noun for the artificial sweetener.

entries.meaning: Sacred has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The mountain is sacred to several tribes.
The choir sang sacred music at the service.
Sunday dinner is sacred in this family.
Nothing was sacred in his comedy.

senses.head: Connected with religion and treated with religious respect
examples: The mountain is sacred to several tribes.
The choir sang sacred music at the service.

senses.head: Too important to change, break or joke about
examples: Sunday dinner is sacred in this family.
Nothing was sacred in his comedy.

entries.takes: to + person or group (sacred to the Lakota)
entries.contrast: The -ed is /ɪd/ and makes a second syllable: SAY-krid. Sacred covers religion and deep respect; holy is stronger and almost always religious.

entries.meaning: Offered up or given up, especially so that something else is saved. ---
examples: The manager became the sacrificial lamb after a bad season.
Ancient texts describe a sacrificial altar on the hill.
He made a sacrificial move to protect his queen.
entries.contrast: A sacrificial lamb is a set phrase for the person blamed or given up so that others are protected.

entries.meaning: Treating something holy — or something people deeply respect — with disrespect. ---
examples: Wearing shoes inside the temple would be sacrilegious.
Putting ketchup on it is practically sacrilegious in Chicago.
The church called the painting sacrilegious.
entries.contrast: Watch the spelling: sacrilegious has -rileg-, not -relig-, even though it is about religion.

entries.meaning: So important that nobody is allowed to change or question it. ---
examples: In this office, Friday afternoons are sacrosanct.
The contract is not sacrosanct — we can renegotiate.
He treats his grandmother's recipe as sacrosanct.

entries.meaning: Enjoying other people's pain or fear. ---
examples: The coach had a sadistic sense of humor.
It felt sadistic to make them run in that heat.
He plays a sadistic villain in the new series.

entries.meaning: Not hurt and no longer in danger, after something risky. ---
examples: The hikers were found safe and sound the next morning.
Call me when you get there safe and sound.
All three kids came back safe and sound.
entries.position: predicative only — after be, arrive, get home and similar verbs
entries.contrast: A fixed phrase, always in this order and only after a verb: They got home safe and sound, never a safe and sound child.

entries.meaning: Wise, in a calm and experienced way. ---
examples: She gave me some sage advice about buying a house.
The column is full of sage observations.
A sage nod was all the answer I got.
entries.contrast: Sage is also a noun — the herb, and a word for a wise old person. As an adjective it sounds slightly literary; everyday English says wise.

entries.meaning: Sagging has 2 distinct senses.
examples: We had to replace the sagging porch roof.
The old mattress was sagging in the middle.
Sagging sales forced the store to close.
They tried to lift the team's sagging morale.

senses.head: Hanging down in the middle under its own weight
examples: We had to replace the sagging porch roof.
The old mattress was sagging in the middle.

senses.head: Falling or getting weaker, about sales, prices or spirits
examples: Sagging sales forced the store to close.
They tried to lift the team's sagging morale.

entries.meaning: Of or from the Sahara desert. ---
examples: A cloud of Saharan dust reached Florida last summer.
The plant survives in Saharan conditions.
Saharan nights can be surprisingly cold.
entries.contrast: Sub-Saharan Africa means the part of the continent south of the desert, and is far more common in the news than Saharan alone.

entries.meaning: Extremely good, patient and forgiving. ---
examples: She had saintly patience with the twins.
Nobody is saintly at six in the morning.
He was saintly about the whole mess.
entries.contrast: Saintly ends in -ly but is an adjective, not an adverb: saintly patience, never He smiled saintly.

entries.meaning: Full of sexual detail, in a way meant to shock or excite. ---
examples: The tabloid ran the salacious details on page one.
The book was banned as salacious in 1928.
He kept the story alive with salacious rumors.
entries.contrast: Salacious is about sexual detail served up for gossip. It is stronger and far more disapproving than racy.

entries.meaning: Paid a fixed yearly salary rather than by the hour. ---
examples: Salaried employees don't punch a clock.
She moved from an hourly job to a salaried position.
The company has about two hundred salaried staff.
entries.contrast: A salaried worker is paid a fixed amount per year; an hourly worker is paid by the hour. In the US the difference decides who gets overtime.

entries.meaning: Standing out as the most noticeable or important. ---
examples: Let me go over the salient points of the contract.
The most salient fact is that nobody was home.
Her age is not salient here — her experience is.
entries.contrast: Nothing to do with salt. It means 'standing out as important', and is most often met in the salient points.

entries.meaning: Containing salt; made of a salt solution. ---
examples: The nurse flushed the line with saline solution.
Wash the wound with a saline rinse.
The lake is highly saline.
entries.contrast: Saline is a technical word from medicine and chemistry. Food that tastes of salt is salty, never saline.

entries.meaning: With salt added, for taste or to keep it from spoiling. ---
examples: Use salted butter for the topping.
A bowl of salted peanuts came with the drinks.
Salted caramel is on every dessert menu now.
entries.contrast: Salted means salt was added — salted butter. Salty describes the taste: The soup is too salty.

entries.meaning: Salty has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The soup is too salty.
Ocean air feels salty on your skin.
This batch is saltier than the last one.
He's still salty about not getting picked.
Don't get salty with me — I warned you.

senses.head: Tasting of salt, or containing a lot of it
examples: The soup is too salty.
Ocean air feels salty on your skin.
This batch is saltier than the last one.

senses.head: Annoyed or bitter about something, in American slang
examples: He's still salty about not getting picked.
Don't get salty with me — I warned you.

entries.takes: about + noun or -ing — in the slang sense
entries.contrast: The slang sense is everywhere in American speech: Why are you so salty? means 'Why are you so annoyed?'

entries.meaning: From or relating to El Salvador. ---
examples: There's a great Salvadoran bakery on the corner.
She's Salvadoran on her mother's side.
Salvadoran pupusas are worth the drive.
entries.contrast: Salvadoran is the usual American form; Salvadorian also appears. The country's name keeps the article: El Salvador.

entries.meaning: Still able to be saved, repaired or rescued. ---
examples: Only the engine was salvageable after the fire.
Is the friendship still salvageable?
They sorted the wet books into salvageable and ruined piles.

entries.meaning: Same has 2 distinct senses.
examples: We've lived on the same street for twenty years.
She asked me the same question twice.
Your jacket is the same as mine.
The town looks the same as it did in 1990.
He's still the same old Dave.

senses.head: Not another one; exactly this one and no other
examples: We've lived on the same street for twenty years.
She asked me the same question twice.
Your jacket is the same as mine.

senses.head: Not changed from before
examples: The town looks the same as it did in 1990.
He's still the same old Dave.

entries.position: both — always with the, this or that: the same street, They look the same
entries.takes: as + noun or clause (the same as mine)
entries.contrast: Always the same, never a same. Compare with as, not like and never than: the same as mine. Russian такой же and одинаковый are both the same: Our phones are the same.

entries.meaning: From or relating to Samoa or American Samoa. ---
examples: The team's best lineman is Samoan.
We went to a Samoan church service on the island.
She teaches Samoan dance on Saturdays.
entries.contrast: A Samoan is also the noun for a person, and Samoan is the name of the language.

entries.meaning: Acting as if you are morally better than other people. ---
examples: Spare me the sanctimonious lecture about recycling.
He gets sanctimonious whenever the topic comes up.
The editorial struck a sanctimonious tone.
entries.contrast: Sanctimonious is always an insult — it means acting morally better than everyone else. The neutral words are devout and religious.

entries.meaning: Sandy has 2 distinct senses.
examples: We found a long sandy beach south of town.
The soil here is sandy and dries out fast.
The path got sandier closer to the dunes.
He has sandy hair and freckles.
Her eyebrows are sandy, almost blond.

senses.head: Covered with sand, or made mostly of sand
examples: We found a long sandy beach south of town.
The soil here is sandy and dries out fast.
The path got sandier closer to the dunes.

senses.head: Of hair: light yellowish brown
examples: He has sandy hair and freckles.
Her eyebrows are sandy, almost blond.

entries.meaning: Sane has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The court found him sane enough to stand trial.
Long walks are what keeps me sane.
Let's set a sane deadline for once.
A saner approach would be to test it first.

senses.head: Mentally healthy; not mentally ill
examples: The court found him sane enough to stand trial.
Long walks are what keeps me sane.

senses.head: Sensible and reasonable
examples: Let's set a sane deadline for once.
A saner approach would be to test it first.

entries.contrast: The noun is sanity. In everyday speech insane often just means 'crazy' or even 'amazing': That concert was insane.

entries.meaning: Cheerfully confident that things will turn out well. ---
examples: She's sanguine about the company's chances.
Analysts are less sanguine than they were in March.
He took a sanguine view of the delay.
entries.contrast: A formal word. Everyday English says optimistic or hopeful.

entries.meaning: Sanitary has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The kitchen failed a sanitary inspection.
Sanitary conditions in the camp were poor.
Eating off that counter isn't very sanitary.
They keep the prep area sanitary.

senses.head: Having to do with keeping places clean and free of disease
examples: The kitchen failed a sanitary inspection.
Sanitary conditions in the camp were poor.

senses.head: Clean enough to be safe
examples: Eating off that counter isn't very sanitary.
They keep the prep area sanitary.

entries.contrast: Russian санитарный matches only the technical sense. English also uses sanitary to mean 'clean enough to be safe': That counter isn't sanitary.

entries.meaning: Sanitized has 2 distinct senses.
examples: All the equipment is sanitized between classes.
The tray came out sanitized and still warm.
The textbook gives a sanitized version of the war.
It was a sanitized retelling for children.

senses.head: Cleaned thoroughly so that germs are killed
examples: All the equipment is sanitized between classes.
The tray came out sanitized and still warm.

senses.head: With the unpleasant or embarrassing parts taken out
examples: The textbook gives a sanitized version of the war.
It was a sanitized retelling for children.

entries.contrast: American spelling is -ized; British writing has sanitised.

entries.meaning: Too sentimental, in a silly and slightly embarrassing way. ---
examples: We watched a sappy Christmas movie.
The card was sappy, but I kept it.
His toast got sappier with every glass of wine.
entries.contrast: An American informal word; the British equivalent is soppy. It teases rather than attacks.

entries.meaning: Saying the opposite of what you mean, to mock or criticize. ---
examples: 'Great job,' he said, sarcastic as ever.
Don't be sarcastic with your teacher.
She made a sarcastic comment about my parking.
entries.contrast: Sarcastic is saying the opposite of what you mean in order to mock someone. Ironic is wider and usually aimed at no one.

entries.meaning: Mocking in a dark, unamused way. ---
examples: He gave a sardonic smile and went back to his coffee.
The narrator has a sardonic sense of humor.
Her tone was dry and sardonic.
entries.contrast: Sardonic is darker and quieter than sarcastic — a sardonic smile mocks without a word being said.

entries.meaning: Having to do with clothes and the way someone dresses. ---
examples: His sartorial choices got more attention than his speech.
The piece is about sartorial trends in menswear.
She arrived in full sartorial splendor.
entries.contrast: A formal, often playful word. It describes choices, style and splendor — never a person directly: his sartorial taste, not a sartorial man.

entries.meaning: Sassy has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Don't get sassy with your grandmother.
He was a sassy five-year-old.
She showed up in a sassy red dress.
The ad copy is sassier than anything they've run before.

senses.head: Cheeky and rude, especially about answering back
examples: Don't get sassy with your grandmother.
He was a sassy five-year-old.

senses.head: Lively, bold and confident, often about style
examples: She showed up in a sassy red dress.
The ad copy is sassier than anything they've run before.

entries.contrast: An American word. About a child it is a complaint; about an adult or a style it is usually a compliment.

entries.meaning: Of the devil; evil in a religious sense. ---
examples: The town panicked over rumors of a satanic cult.
The band leaned into satanic imagery.
He called the whole scheme satanic.

entries.meaning: Using humor and exaggeration to criticize people or institutions. ---
examples: The magazine runs a satirical column every week.
It's a satirical novel about Wall Street.
The piece is satirical, not a real news report.
entries.contrast: Satiric is a rarer form of the same word. Do not confuse it with satisfactory or with sarcastic, which is about a person's tone, not a work.

entries.meaning: Good enough for the purpose, but no better than that. ---
examples: The repair work was satisfactory.
We need a satisfactory explanation by Friday.
Her condition is listed as satisfactory.
entries.contrast: Satisfactory means 'good enough', not 'good' — a satisfactory grade is barely passing. Satisfying is about pleasure: a satisfying meal.

entries.meaning: Saturated has 2 distinct senses.
examples: My jacket was saturated by the time I got home.
The ground is saturated after three days of rain.
The market is saturated with delivery apps.
Butter is high in saturated fat.
The photo has deep, saturated colors.

senses.head: Completely soaked through
examples: My jacket was saturated by the time I got home.
The ground is saturated after three days of rain.

senses.head: Holding as much as it possibly can
examples: The market is saturated with delivery apps.
Butter is high in saturated fat.
The photo has deep, saturated colors.

entries.meaning: Bold and cheeky, often in a flirty way. ---
examples: She sent him a saucy postcard from Miami.
The show is famous for its saucy jokes.
His answer was a little saucier than the judge liked.
entries.contrast: Nothing to do with sauce on food. It is a slightly old-fashioned, playful word for 'cheeky' or 'a little risqué'.

entries.meaning: From or relating to Saudi Arabia. ---
examples: The Saudi delegation arrived on Tuesday.
He works for a Saudi airline.
Most of the students in the program are Saudi.
entries.contrast: Saudi alone is the usual adjective; Saudi Arabian is also correct. A Saudi is the noun for a person.

entries.meaning: Cooked quickly in a pan with a little butter or oil. ---
examples: The steak came with sauteed mushrooms.
Add the sauteed onions to the pot.
She served sauteed spinach with lemon.
entries.contrast: Often written with the accent: sautéed. It means fried quickly in a little fat, not deep-fried.

entries.meaning: Savage has 3 distinct senses.
examples: The dog gave him a savage bite.
It was a savage storm, even for February.
The review was savage.
She wrote a savage takedown of the proposal.
His reply was savage.
That comeback was straight-up savage.

senses.head: Very violent or fierce
examples: The dog gave him a savage bite.
It was a savage storm, even for February.

senses.head: Extremely harsh, about criticism
examples: The review was savage.
She wrote a savage takedown of the proposal.

senses.head: Brutally blunt in a way people find funny, in slang
examples: His reply was savage.
That comeback was straight-up savage.

entries.contrast: Calling people savage in the old sense of 'primitive' is offensive today. The living uses are 'very violent' and, in slang, 'brutally blunt'.

entries.meaning: Savory has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Do you want something sweet or savory for breakfast?
The bakery makes savory hand pies.
The broth was deep and savory.
Mushrooms add a savory note to the sauce.

senses.head: Salty or spicy rather than sweet
examples: Do you want something sweet or savory for breakfast?
The bakery makes savory hand pies.

senses.head: Tasting good in a rich, salty way
examples: The broth was deep and savory.
Mushrooms add a savory note to the sauce.

entries.contrast: American spelling savory; British savoury. Not savory about a person or a business means shady: a less than savory character.

entries.meaning: Cut short with a saw, especially of a shotgun. ---
examples: Police recovered a sawed-off shotgun from the trunk.
He kept a sawed-off broom handle behind the counter.
The workbench stands on sawed-off table legs.
entries.contrast: American sawed-off; British sawn-off. Used of a person it is an informal, rude way of saying 'short'.

entries.meaning: Of the Saxons, a Germanic people who settled in England, or of Saxony in Germany. ---
examples: The village church has a Saxon tower.
He wrote his thesis on Saxon law.
The porcelain is Saxon, from the Meissen works.
entries.contrast: In American English Anglo-Saxon is far more common; Saxon on its own is mostly historical.

entries.meaning: Able to grow much larger without breaking or being redesigned. ---
examples: The model isn't scalable beyond a few hundred users.
They wanted a scalable business, not a boutique.
We picked a more scalable database this time.
entries.contrast: Common in business and technology: something scalable can grow much bigger without being rebuilt.

entries.meaning: Covered with scales, or with dry, flaking skin. ---
examples: The lizard's scaly back caught the light.
My elbows get scaly in the winter.
His skin was scalier than the doctor expected.
entries.contrast: Spelled scaly, with no e before the -y.

entries.meaning: Shocking and morally wrong; causing public outrage. ---
examples: The memo revealed scandalous spending.
It's scandalous that the building is still unsafe.
She wrote a book about the family's scandalous past.
entries.contrast: Russian скандальный can mean simply 'quarrelsome'; English scandalous always involves shock or disgrace. A noisy neighbor is difficult, not scandalous.

entries.meaning: From or relating to Scandinavia. ---
examples: The store sells Scandinavian furniture.
Her grandparents were Scandinavian.
He's taking a Scandinavian literature class.
entries.contrast: Scandinavian usually means Denmark, Norway and Sweden. Nordic is wider and takes in Finland and Iceland too.

entries.meaning: Scant has 2 distinct senses.
examples: There is scant evidence for either theory.
The report got scant attention from the press.
Add a scant teaspoon of salt.
We finished in a scant three hours.

senses.head: Barely any; much less than is needed
examples: There is scant evidence for either theory.
The report got scant attention from the press.

senses.head: Just a little under the amount named
examples: Add a scant teaspoon of salt.
We finished in a scant three hours.

entries.contrast: Scant goes straight before a noun, often before a number: a scant two weeks. After a verb use scarce or not enough.

entries.meaning: Scanty has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The evidence is scanty at best.
They lived on scanty rations that winter.
She wore a scanty costume for the number.
The outfits got scantier as the show went on.

senses.head: Too small in amount
examples: The evidence is scanty at best.
They lived on scanty rations that winter.

senses.head: Of clothing: covering very little of the body
examples: She wore a scanty costume for the number.
The outfits got scantier as the show went on.

entries.contrast: About information scanty is close to scant, but scant only stands before a noun. About clothing only scanty works.

entries.meaning: Not available in the amount people need; hard to get. ---
examples: Affordable apartments are scarce downtown.
Water became scarcer every week of the drought.
Good news has been scarce this year.
entries.contrast: Scarce is about supply — there is not enough of it. Rare is about how seldom something occurs: a rare bird, but scarce housing. The adverb scarcely means 'hardly'.

entries.meaning: Bright, strong red. ---
examples: She wore a scarlet coat to the parade.
The maples turn scarlet in October.
The book's cover is plain scarlet.
entries.contrast: Scarlet is a bright red leaning to orange; crimson leans to purple. Scarlet fever is a children's illness.

entries.meaning: Scarred has 2 distinct senses.
examples: His hands were scarred from years of kitchen work.
The old table is scarred with knife marks.
She was scarred by the divorce.
A whole generation was scarred by the war.

senses.head: Marked with scars
examples: His hands were scarred from years of kitchen work.
The old table is scarred with knife marks.

senses.head: Emotionally damaged by something painful
examples: She was scarred by the divorce.
A whole generation was scarred by the war.

entries.form: -ed from scar, with the r doubled
entries.contrast: Do not confuse scarred with scared (испуганный). They sound different too: SKAHRD against SKAIRD.

entries.meaning: Frightening. ---
examples: That was the scariest part of the ride.
It's scary how fast kids grow.
We watched a scary movie with all the lights on.
entries.contrast: Scary is the thing that frightens you; scared is how you feel. Russian страшный covers both: a scary movie leaves you scared.

entries.meaning: Extremely harsh in its criticism. ---
examples: The Times ran a scathing review.
She sent a scathing email to the whole department.
His report was more scathing than anyone expected.
entries.form: -ing from scathe, an old verb meaning 'to harm'
entries.contrast: Almost always about words: a scathing review, scathing criticism. People are not usually called scathing.

entries.meaning: Forgetful and disorganized. ---
examples: I've been so scatterbrained since the baby came.
He's a brilliant but scatterbrained professor.
She left the keys in the door again — totally scatterbrained.

entries.meaning: Scattered has 3 distinct senses.
examples: Toys were scattered all over the floor.
Her family is scattered across three states.
Scattered showers are expected this afternoon.
There were scattered power outages overnight.
I'm a little scattered today — I didn't sleep.
He sounded scattered on the phone.

senses.head: Spread out over an area instead of being together
examples: Toys were scattered all over the floor.
Her family is scattered across three states.

senses.head: Happening here and there rather than everywhere, about weather and outages
examples: Scattered showers are expected this afternoon.
There were scattered power outages overnight.

senses.head: Of a person: unable to keep track of things
examples: I'm a little scattered today — I didn't sleep.
He sounded scattered on the phone.

entries.meaning: Done in a broad, unfocused way, with no real plan. ---
examples: Their marketing is scattershot — a little of everything.
He took a scattershot approach to job hunting.
The essay is scattershot but full of good lines.
entries.form: compound — verb + noun, from the way shotgun pellets spread out
entries.contrast: An American word, and a criticism: it says an effort had no focus, not that it was fast.

entries.meaning: Having beautiful natural views. ---
examples: We took the scenic route along the coast.
There's a scenic overlook two miles up the road.
The drive through the pass is the most scenic part of the trip.
entries.contrast: The scenic route is the longer, prettier way — Americans often say it as a joke after getting lost.

entries.meaning: Given a pleasant smell, usually on purpose. ---
examples: She lit a scented candle.
We bought scented soap for the guest bathroom.
He hates scented laundry detergent.
entries.contrast: Scented means a smell was added on purpose; fragrant means it smells good on its own. American products are labeled unscented or fragrance-free.

entries.meaning: Planned to happen at a particular time. ---
examples: The scheduled departure is 6:40.
Scheduled maintenance will close the line tonight.
The meeting ran past its scheduled end.
entries.contrast: Americans say SKEJ-ool; the British say SHED-yool. A scheduled flight is a regular service, not a charter.

entries.meaning: Shown as a simple diagram, with only the main parts. ---
examples: The manual includes a schematic drawing of the circuit.
He gave a schematic outline of the plan.
The characters are schematic — more types than people.
entries.contrast: A schematic is also a noun — a wiring or circuit diagram. About writing, schematic is a criticism: too simple to feel real.

entries.meaning: Making secret plans to get what you want, usually by tricking people. ---
examples: The show is full of scheming lawyers and crooked cops.
His scheming brother had already sold half the land.
She is far more scheming than she lets on.

entries.meaning: Schizophrenic has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He was treated at the clinic for schizophrenic episodes.
The book explains what schizophrenic symptoms actually look like.
Her brother is schizophrenic and has been stable for years.
The company's schizophrenic marketing sells luxury and thrift in the same ad.
Policy on the region has been schizophrenic for a decade.

senses.head: Having or relating to schizophrenia, a serious mental illness
examples: He was treated at the clinic for schizophrenic episodes.
The book explains what schizophrenic symptoms actually look like.
Her brother is schizophrenic and has been stable for years.

senses.head: Pulling in two opposite directions at once
examples: The company's schizophrenic marketing sells luxury and thrift in the same ad.
Policy on the region has been schizophrenic for a decade.

entries.contrast: The loose sense 'contradictory' offends many people, since it borrows a real illness as a metaphor. In writing, prefer contradictory or inconsistent.

entries.meaning: So sentimental that it feels fake or embarrassing. ---
examples: The ending is schmaltzy, but I cried anyway.
He sang a schmaltzy ballad in a rented tuxedo.
Their second album is even schmaltzier than the first.

entries.meaning: Having to do with schools, studying and grades. ---
examples: Players have to keep up their scholastic standing to stay on the team.
She won a scholastic award for her work in chemistry.
The league covers scholastic sports across three states.

entries.meaning: Affecting every part of a school. ---
examples: The principal called a schoolwide assembly for Friday morning.
They ran a schoolwide survey about the new lunch menu.
The phone ban is schoolwide, not just in the math wing.

entries.meaning: Scientific has 2 distinct senses.
