examples: The journal publishes scientific research on sleep.
There is no scientific evidence for any of this.
She left teaching for a scientific career at a lab in Boston.
He takes a scientific approach to picking a fantasy roster.
Tasting ten brands in one night is not exactly scientific.
Their hiring is more scientific than it used to be.

senses.head: Having to do with science
examples: The journal publishes scientific research on sleep.
There is no scientific evidence for any of this.
She left teaching for a scientific career at a lab in Boston.

senses.head: Careful and organized, based on testing rather than guessing
examples: He takes a scientific approach to picking a fantasy roster.
Tasting ten brands in one night is not exactly scientific.
Their hiring is more scientific than it used to be.

entries.meaning: Brilliantly lively and interesting. ---
examples: She is a scintillating speaker who never uses notes.
The conversation was hardly scintillating.
His scintillating second half won the game.
entries.contrast: Often used sarcastically about something boring: a scintillating lecture on tax forms.

entries.meaning: Burned on the surface, or dried out and browned by heat. ---
examples: Nothing was left but scorched fields and black smoke.
The shirt had a scorched mark where the iron sat too long.
By August the lawn was completely scorched.

entries.meaning: Scorching has 2 distinct senses.
examples: We walked four blocks in the scorching afternoon sun.
It was scorching by ten in the morning.
They played the whole game in scorching heat.
The paper ran a scorching review of the restaurant.
She sent a scorching email to the whole department.

senses.head: Extremely hot
examples: We walked four blocks in the scorching afternoon sun.
It was scorching by ten in the morning.
They played the whole game in scorching heat.

senses.head: Fiercely critical
examples: The paper ran a scorching review of the restaurant.
She sent a scorching email to the whole department.

entries.meaning: With no points scored, in a game or a part of a game. ---
examples: The match ended in a scoreless tie.
Both teams were scoreless through three quarters.
The pitcher threw five scoreless innings.

entries.meaning: Showing that you think someone or something deserves no respect. ---
examples: She gave him a scornful look and walked out.
He is openly scornful of anyone who studies for the test.
The critics were more scornful of the sequel than of the original.

entries.meaning: Growing in thin, uneven, untidy patches. ---
examples: He showed up with a scraggly beard and no jacket.
A few scraggly pines grew along the ridge.
The lawn looked scragglier every week we skipped it.
entries.contrast: Ends in -ly but is an adjective, not an adverb.

entries.meaning: Scrambled has 2 distinct senses.
examples: I had scrambled eggs and toast for breakfast.
She likes her eggs scrambled, not fried.
The diner serves scrambled eggs all day.
The letters came through scrambled and nobody could read them.
The channel is scrambled unless you pay for it.

senses.head: Cooked by beating the eggs together and stirring them in a pan
examples: I had scrambled eggs and toast for breakfast.
She likes her eggs scrambled, not fried.
The diner serves scrambled eggs all day.

senses.head: Mixed up out of order, or coded so that it cannot be read or heard
examples: The letters came through scrambled and nobody could read them.
The channel is scrambled unless you pay for it.

entries.meaning: Fighting hard and never giving up, especially against bigger opponents. ---
examples: They are a scrappy team that wins games they should lose.
He was a scrappy kid who never backed down.
The scrappier of the two candidates took the debate.
entries.contrast: In American English this is praise — small but tough. British scrappy means 'messy, thrown together', which is an insult.

entries.meaning: Scratchy has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The blanket is warm but scratchy.
She hated the scratchy tag inside the collar.
This sweater is scratchier than the wool one.
His voice was scratchy after two nights of shouting.
The recording is scratchy, but you can hear the words.

senses.head: Rough enough against the skin to itch
examples: The blanket is warm but scratchy.
She hated the scratchy tag inside the collar.
This sweater is scratchier than the wool one.

senses.head: Rough and uneven in sound
examples: His voice was scratchy after two nights of shouting.
The recording is scratchy, but you can hear the words.

entries.meaning: Unpleasantly thin and weak-looking. ---
examples: He was a scrawny teenager who ate constantly.
A scrawny cat was waiting on the porch.
The chicken they served was even scrawnier than the last one.
entries.contrast: Scrawny is unkind; slim and slender are compliments.

entries.meaning: Crazy in a funny, unpredictable way, used above all of comedy. ---
examples: We watched a screwball comedy from the 1930s.
The plot takes a screwball turn in the second act.
She has a screwball sense of humor that wins people over.
entries.form: compound — screw + ball, first a baseball pitch
entries.contrast: Also a noun: a screwball is an oddball, and in baseball a pitch that breaks the wrong way.

entries.meaning: Written out in advance instead of said or done spontaneously. ---
examples: Network television still runs mostly scripted dramas.
His apology sounded scripted.
The town hall felt more scripted than the debate did.

entries.meaning: Untidy and worn-looking. ---
examples: A scruffy dog followed us the whole way home.
He turned up scruffy and an hour late.
The neighborhood looks scruffier than it did ten years ago.

entries.meaning: Extremely good to eat. ---
examples: Her grandmother makes a scrumptious peach pie.
Everything on the table looked scrumptious.
The bread was warm and absolutely scrumptious.
entries.contrast: Warm and a little old-fashioned; delicious is the neutral word.

entries.meaning: Careful to do everything correctly and honestly, down to small details. ---
examples: She is scrupulous about paying people on time.
The report was based on scrupulous record keeping.
He is more scrupulous than anyone else in that office.

entries.meaning: Sculpted has 2 distinct senses.
examples: A sculpted stone lion sits at each end of the bridge.
The doors are covered in sculpted panels.
He has the sculpted arms of someone who lives at the gym.
Her cheekbones look sculpted.

senses.head: Shaped by carving or modeling
examples: A sculpted stone lion sits at each end of the bridge.
The doors are covered in sculpted panels.

senses.head: Firm and clearly shaped, as if carved, said of a body or a face
examples: He has the sculpted arms of someone who lives at the gym.
Her cheekbones look sculpted.

entries.meaning: Insulting and almost certainly untrue, said or written to damage someone. ---
examples: The campaign spread scurrilous rumors about his family.
She sued the site over a scurrilous article.
The attacks grew more scurrilous as the vote got closer.

entries.meaning: Traveling by sea, or living by work at sea. ---
examples: The Portuguese were a great seafaring nation.
He came from a long line of seafaring men.
The museum tells the story of the town's seafaring past.
entries.form: compound — sea + faring, from fare 'to travel'

entries.meaning: Sealed has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Bring the form back in a sealed envelope.
The meat comes in a sealed plastic tray.
Every window in the building is sealed shut.
His juvenile record is sealed.
The indictment stayed sealed until the arrest.

senses.head: Closed so tightly that nothing can get in or out
examples: Bring the form back in a sealed envelope.
The meat comes in a sealed plastic tray.
Every window in the building is sealed shut.

senses.head: Closed by a court or an official so that the public cannot see it
examples: His juvenile record is sealed.
The indictment stayed sealed until the arrest.

entries.meaning: Seamless has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The handoff between the two crews was seamless.
They promise a seamless transfer of your old files.
The new checkout is more seamless than the old one.
The pipe is drawn as a single seamless tube.
She wore a seamless knit dress.

senses.head: Moving from one part to the next with no gap, break or trouble
examples: The handoff between the two crews was seamless.
They promise a seamless transfer of your old files.
The new checkout is more seamless than the old one.

senses.head: Made in one piece, with no sewn or welded joins
examples: The pipe is drawn as a single seamless tube.
She wore a seamless knit dress.

entries.meaning: Trying hard to find out the truth about someone or something. ---
examples: She gave him a long, searching look.
The reporter asked a few searching questions about the money.
The book is a searching account of his own failures.

entries.meaning: Browned fast over high heat on the outside. ---
examples: The special is seared tuna with a sesame crust.
Serve the steak seared on both sides but still pink inside.
A seared scallop should be dark gold, not gray.

entries.meaning: Searing has 2 distinct senses.
examples: A searing pain shot down his leg.
They crossed the desert in searing heat.
The wind off the pavement was searing.
The film is a searing portrait of life on the border.
She wrote a searing letter to the board.

senses.head: Burning hot, or painful like a burn
examples: A searing pain shot down his leg.
They crossed the desert in searing heat.
The wind off the pavement was searing.

senses.head: Sharply critical or emotionally intense
examples: The film is a searing portrait of life on the border.
She wrote a searing letter to the board.

entries.meaning: Sick to your stomach because of the movement of a boat. ---
examples: Half the passengers were seasick within an hour.
Take a pill before you board if you get seasick.
He looked seasick the whole way across.

entries.meaning: Happening in, or changing with, a particular time of year. ---
examples: The store hires seasonal workers every November.
Seasonal allergies hit him hard in the spring.
Demand for the product is highly seasonal.
entries.contrast: Seasonal means 'tied to a season'; seasoned means 'experienced' or 'flavored'.

entries.meaning: Seasoned has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She is a seasoned negotiator who has seen every trick.
Even seasoned climbers turn back in that weather.
The soup was perfectly seasoned.
Use lightly seasoned ground beef for the filling.

senses.head: Having a lot of experience at something
examples: She is a seasoned negotiator who has seen every trick.
Even seasoned climbers turn back in that weather.

senses.head: Given flavor with salt, pepper or herbs
examples: The soup was perfectly seasoned.
Use lightly seasoned ground beef for the filling.

entries.position: both — the 'experienced' sense goes before a noun

entries.meaning: Sitting down, or done while sitting. ---
examples: Please remain seated until the plane reaches the gate.
The class ends with a seated stretch.
She was already seated when I got there.

entries.meaning: In good enough condition to sail safely. ---
examples: The inspector declared the boat seaworthy.
It took two years to make the old schooner seaworthy again.
Nobody would call that raft a seaworthy vessel.

entries.meaning: Quiet and private, far from other people. ---
examples: They rented a secluded cabin in the mountains.
There is a secluded beach on the far side of the island.
The back patio is more secluded than the front porch.

entries.meaning: Second has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Her office is the second door on the left.
He struck out in the second inning.
This is the second time this week.
Give him a second chance.
Would you like a second helping?

senses.head: Coming right after the first
examples: Her office is the second door on the left.
He struck out in the second inning.
This is the second time this week.

senses.head: One more of the same kind
examples: Give him a second chance.
Would you like a second helping?

entries.contrast: Also a noun (a second of time) and a verb (to second a motion). In I finished second it is the adverb.

entries.meaning: Not quite as good as the best one. ---
examples: He wore his second-best suit to the interview.
Their offer was the second-best on the table.
Taking the bus is second-best, but it works.
entries.contrast: Also a noun in settle for second best, written without the hyphen.

entries.meaning: Second-class has 2 distinct senses.
examples: They were treated like second-class citizens in their own country.
No student should get a second-class education because of a zip code.
He rode in a second-class car all the way to Chicago.
The magazine went out at second-class postage rates.

senses.head: Treated as less important, with fewer rights than other people
examples: They were treated like second-class citizens in their own country.
No student should get a second-class education because of a zip code.

senses.head: Of the cheaper grade of travel or mail
examples: He rode in a second-class car all the way to Chicago.
The magazine went out at second-class postage rates.

entries.meaning: Clearly not very good. ---
examples: It was a second-rate hotel with a good view.
He spent years writing second-rate thrillers.
The food is fine; the service is second-rate.

entries.meaning: Not in the starting lineup, or not in the top group. ---
examples: The second-string quarterback finished the game.
They sent a second-string delegation to the talks.
He spent two seasons as a second-string catcher.
entries.form: compound — second + string, from the lineup of players

entries.meaning: In the second year of a course, a job or a career. ---
examples: She is a second-year law student.
The team is built around a second-year point guard.
Second-year residents take the night shifts.

entries.meaning: Secondary has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Cost is secondary to safety here.
The plot is secondary; you watch it for the acting.
Those are secondary concerns we can handle later.
He teaches at the secondary level.
Fewer than half of them finished secondary school.

senses.head: Less important than something else
examples: Cost is secondary to safety here.
The plot is secondary; you watch it for the acting.
Those are secondary concerns we can handle later.

senses.head: Of the school years between elementary school and college
examples: He teaches at the secondary level.
Fewer than half of them finished secondary school.

entries.meaning: Secret has 2 distinct senses.
examples: They held a secret meeting in the back office.
He had a secret second phone.
The vote is secret, so nobody sees your ballot.
There is a secret door behind the bookcase.
She kept the letters in a secret compartment.

senses.head: Known to only a few people and deliberately kept from everyone else
examples: They held a secret meeting in the back office.
He had a secret second phone.
The vote is secret, so nobody sees your ballot.

senses.head: Hidden so that other people cannot find it
examples: There is a secret door behind the bookcase.
She kept the letters in a secret compartment.

entries.contrast: Also a noun: keep a secret. The person who holds things back is secretive, not secret.

entries.meaning: Having to do with the work of a secretary. ---
examples: She took a secretarial course after high school.
The job is mostly secretarial duties and scheduling.
He was hired for secretarial work at a law firm.

entries.meaning: Keeping your plans and feelings to yourself. ---
examples: He was secretive about where the money came from.
The company is famously secretive about new products.
She got more secretive as the divorce dragged on.
entries.contrast: Secretive describes a person or an organization that hides things; secret describes the thing that is hidden.

entries.meaning: Coming from the split between religious or political groups, often violently. ---
examples: Sectarian violence broke out again in the capital.
The country is still divided along sectarian lines.
He warned that the debate was becoming more sectarian than practical.

entries.meaning: Not connected with religion or the church. ---
examples: Public schools here are secular by law.
He writes secular music for a church choir to sing.
The country has grown more secular over two generations.

entries.meaning: Secure has 3 distinct senses.
examples: Keep the files on a secure server.
The building is more secure than it looks.
She finally found a secure job with benefits.
Make sure the ladder is secure before you climb.
Check that the straps are secure.
Kids need to feel secure at home.
He is secure in the knowledge that his family backs him.

senses.head: Safe from attack, theft or danger
examples: Keep the files on a secure server.
The building is more secure than it looks.
She finally found a secure job with benefits.

senses.head: Firmly fixed so that it will not move or come loose
examples: Make sure the ladder is secure before you climb.
Check that the straps are secure.

senses.head: Feeling confident and not worried
examples: Kids need to feel secure at home.
He is secure in the knowledge that his family backs him.

entries.meaning: Calm, slow and rather formal. ---
examples: They went for a sedate walk around the pond.
The party was a sedate affair with classical music.
Life on the island is more sedate than in the city.
entries.contrast: Also a verb: to sedate a patient is to give them a calming drug. The adjective does not mean 'drugged'.

entries.meaning: Having the effect of calming a person down or making them sleepy. ---
examples: The drug has a mild sedative effect.
Sedative properties make it useful before surgery.
They warned him about the sedative side effects.
entries.form: -ive from the same root as sedate
entries.contrast: Much more common as a noun: the doctor gave her a sedative.

entries.meaning: Involving a lot of sitting and very little exercise. ---
examples: Twelve hours at a desk makes for a sedentary job.
A sedentary lifestyle raises your risk of heart disease.
He has gotten more sedentary since he started working from home.

entries.meaning: Formed from layers of sand, mud or shells pressed together over time. ---
examples: Sandstone and limestone are sedimentary rocks.
The canyon walls show bands of sedimentary layers.
Oil is usually found in sedimentary basins.

entries.meaning: Encouraging people to rebel against the government. ---
examples: He was arrested for printing seditious pamphlets.
The speech was condemned as seditious.
The later letters are more seditious than anything he published.

entries.meaning: Seductive has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She sang the whole song in a low, seductive voice.
He gave her a seductive smile across the room.
There is something seductive about a simple answer.
The argument is more seductive than it is sound.

senses.head: Sexually attractive in a deliberate way
examples: She sang the whole song in a low, seductive voice.
He gave her a seductive smile across the room.

senses.head: Tempting, because it makes a bad idea look good
examples: There is something seductive about a simple answer.
The argument is more seductive than it is sound.

entries.meaning: Thin enough that you can see what is behind or under it. ---
examples: She wore a see-through blouse over a tank top.
The shower curtain is almost see-through.
They packed everything in see-through bags for security.
entries.contrast: Used of clothing and thin fabric; for glass and water the word is clear or transparent.

entries.meaning: Seeded has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The top-seeded team lost in the first round.
She is seeded third at the Open this year.
Keep off the newly seeded lawn.
A freshly seeded field needs water twice a day.

senses.head: Ranked among the top players or teams in a tournament
examples: The top-seeded team lost in the first round.
She is seeded third at the Open this year.

senses.head: Planted with seed
examples: Keep off the newly seeded lawn.
A freshly seeded field needs water twice a day.

entries.meaning: Grown without seeds or pits. ---
examples: Get the seedless grapes, not the ones with pits.
Seedless watermelon is easier to feed to kids.
The green ones are seedless.

entries.meaning: Run-down and slightly dishonest or unsafe. ---
examples: They stayed in a seedy motel off the highway.
The bar has a seedy reputation.
The block gets seedier the closer you get to the station.

entries.meaning: Appearing to be true, though it may not be. ---
examples: Her seeming calm hid a lot of panic.
Despite his seeming indifference, he read every word.
The seeming contradiction disappears once you read the footnote.
entries.contrast: Never after a verb — you cannot say the calm was seeming. The adverb seemingly is far more common.

entries.meaning: Seething has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He sat through the whole meeting seething.
She was seething with resentment by the end of the trip.
The market was a seething mass of people.
The river below was seething and brown.

senses.head: Extremely angry but holding it in
examples: He sat through the whole meeting seething.
She was seething with resentment by the end of the trip.

senses.head: Full of crowded, restless movement
examples: The market was a seething mass of people.
The river below was seething and brown.

entries.meaning: Kept apart by race, sex or class, usually unfairly. ---
examples: His parents grew up in a segregated school system.
Housing in the city is still deeply segregated.
Some districts are more segregated now than they were in 1970.

entries.meaning: Seismic has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The bridge was built to the latest seismic standards.
Seismic activity picked up under the volcano.
The ruling was a seismic shift in the law.
Streaming had a seismic effect on the music business.

senses.head: Having to do with earthquakes
examples: The bridge was built to the latest seismic standards.
Seismic activity picked up under the volcano.

senses.head: Enormous and sudden, said of change
examples: The ruling was a seismic shift in the law.
Streaming had a seismic effect on the music business.

entries.meaning: Chosen as the best, and open to only a few. ---
examples: Only a select few were invited to the dinner.
The wine list includes some select California reds.
He plays on a select travel team.
entries.contrast: Also a common verb (select a file). As an adjective it goes only before a noun.

entries.meaning: Picked out from a larger group. ---
examples: The volume prints his selected essays from twenty years.
The sale runs on selected items only.
Selected students get to sit in on the seminar.
entries.contrast: Selected means someone picked them out; select means they are the best. Selected poems is a sample, a select group is an elite.

entries.meaning: Selective has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She is very selective about who she works with.
The college is more selective than it was a decade ago.
He has a selective memory about that night.
The policy amounts to selective enforcement.

senses.head: Choosing carefully, and taking only a few
examples: She is very selective about who she works with.
The college is more selective than it was a decade ago.

senses.head: Affecting or including some things but not others
examples: He has a selective memory about that night.
The policy amounts to selective enforcement.

entries.meaning: So interested in your own life that you barely notice other people. ---
examples: He is too self-absorbed to ask how anyone else is doing.
The narrator is a self-absorbed twenty-year-old.
She gets more self-absorbed every time she is in a play.

entries.meaning: Carrying your own name and address, so that it can be mailed back to you. ---
examples: Include a self-addressed stamped envelope with your entry.
They mailed the results back in the self-addressed envelope.
The form asks for a self-addressed postcard.

entries.meaning: Working to make yourself look more important than you are. ---
examples: The memoir is a long, self-aggrandizing account of one lucky deal.
He made a self-aggrandizing speech about his own generosity.
Each retelling gets more self-aggrandizing.

entries.meaning: Having taken a job or a role without anyone asking you to. ---
examples: He is the self-appointed guardian of the block's parking spots.
A self-appointed committee rewrote the bylaws.
She acts as the self-appointed spokesperson for the neighborhood.

entries.meaning: Calmly confident in your own abilities. ---
examples: She walked into the room self-assured and unhurried.
He gave a self-assured answer to a hostile question.
He is more self-assured on stage than he is in conversation.
entries.contrast: Self-assured is a compliment; self-satisfied and smug are not.

entries.meaning: Able to see your own faults and how you come across to others. ---
examples: For a nineteen-year-old he is remarkably self-aware.
The show is self-aware about how silly its own premise is.
She got more self-aware after a year of therapy.

entries.meaning: Thinking only about yourself and what you want. ---
examples: He is too self-centered to notice that she was upset.
It was a self-centered thing to say at a funeral.
Teenagers can be more self-centered than they mean to be.
entries.contrast: American self-centered; British writing spells it self-centred.

entries.meaning: Admitted by the person themselves, usually about a fault or a habit. ---
examples: He is a self-confessed workaholic.
The book was written by a self-confessed amateur.
She is a self-confessed fan of bad reality TV.

entries.meaning: Self-conscious has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She is self-conscious about her accent.
He gave a self-conscious laugh and looked at the floor.
I felt more self-conscious in that room than anywhere else.
The film is full of self-conscious references to old westerns.
The prose is self-conscious in a way that gets tiring.

senses.head: Uncomfortably aware of how other people are seeing you
examples: She is self-conscious about her accent.
He gave a self-conscious laugh and looked at the floor.
I felt more self-conscious in that room than anywhere else.

senses.head: Deliberately aware of its own style, said of art and writing
examples: The film is full of self-conscious references to old westerns.
The prose is self-conscious in a way that gets tiring.

entries.contrast: A false friend: it does not mean 'сознательный'. It means uncomfortable about how you look or sound.

entries.meaning: Self-contained has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Each episode is a self-contained story.
The guest house is self-contained, with its own kitchen.
He is a quiet, self-contained man who reads all evening.
She seemed perfectly self-contained at the party.

senses.head: Complete in itself, with everything it needs inside it
examples: Each episode is a self-contained story.
The guest house is self-contained, with its own kitchen.

senses.head: Keeping to yourself and not needing other people's company
examples: He is a quiet, self-contained man who reads all evening.
She seemed perfectly self-contained at the party.

entries.meaning: Containing two statements that cannot both be true. ---
examples: His testimony was self-contradictory from the first page.
The rule is self-contradictory: it bans what the next line requires.
That is a self-contradictory way to describe a free market.

entries.meaning: Working against the very thing you are trying to achieve. ---
examples: Cutting the training budget to save money is self-defeating.
He is stuck in a self-defeating cycle of quitting and starting over.
Their strategy turned out to be more self-defeating than risky.

entries.meaning: Making light of your own abilities or achievements. ---
examples: His speech was funny and self-deprecating.
She made a self-deprecating joke about her cooking.
He is more self-deprecating in interviews than he is in person.
entries.contrast: Usually charming rather than sad: it is making fun of yourself before anyone else can.

entries.meaning: Harming yourself by the way you behave. ---
examples: Drinking before every shift was self-destructive and he knew it.
The band fell apart in a self-destructive spiral.
His choices got more self-destructive after the injury.

entries.meaning: Organized and driven by the person doing it, without a teacher or a boss. ---
examples: The course is self-directed, with deadlines you set yourself.
He opened a self-directed retirement account.
Graduate work is more self-directed than college.

entries.meaning: Able to make yourself do what needs doing without being pushed. ---
examples: You have to be self-disciplined to work from home.
She is the most self-disciplined runner on the team.
He is a quiet, self-disciplined kid.

entries.meaning: Having learned by reading and studying alone rather than at a school. ---
examples: He was a self-educated engineer who never finished high school.
She is largely self-educated in music theory.
The library was full of self-educated readers.

entries.meaning: Not wanting attention or credit for what you have done. ---
examples: He is so self-effacing that nobody knew he had funded the whole thing.
She gave a short, self-effacing answer and changed the subject.
The coach is more self-effacing than most people in the job.

entries.meaning: Working for yourself rather than for a company. ---
examples: She has been self-employed since 2015.
Self-employed people pay their taxes quarterly.
He left the firm to become a self-employed consultant.

entries.meaning: Obviously true without needing any proof. ---
examples: We hold these truths to be self-evident.
It is self-evident that the two numbers cannot both be right.
The answer is not as self-evident as he thinks.

entries.meaning: Clear on its own, with no explanation needed. ---
examples: The instructions are self-explanatory.
Most of the buttons are self-explanatory once you open the app.
The chart is more self-explanatory than the paragraph under it.
entries.русский: не требующий пояснений, понятный сам по себе

entries.meaning: Running its own affairs without being controlled from outside. ---
examples: The territory has been self-governing since 1979.
Each self-governing district sets its own school calendar.
The profession is largely self-governing.

entries.meaning: Acting as if you matter far more than you do. ---
examples: A self-important little man checked our badges twice.
The email was long and self-important.
He gets more self-important with every promotion.

entries.meaning: Chosen by yourself rather than forced on you by someone else. ---
examples: He missed his own self-imposed deadline by a month.
She spent a year in self-imposed exile in Maine.
The company works under a self-imposed limit on overtime.

entries.meaning: Brought on by your own actions. ---
examples: The whole crisis was self-induced.
He blamed his self-induced panic on too much coffee.
It was a self-induced injury from lifting too much too fast.

entries.meaning: Self-indulgent has 2 distinct senses.
examples: A whole Saturday in bed felt gloriously self-indulgent.
He has a self-indulgent streak when it comes to gadgets.
The director's cut is self-indulgent at three and a half hours.
Critics called the album more self-indulgent than his last one.

senses.head: Letting yourself have whatever you want, more than is good for you
examples: A whole Saturday in bed felt gloriously self-indulgent.
He has a self-indulgent streak when it comes to gadgets.

senses.head: Too long or too pleased with itself, said of art and writing
examples: The director's cut is self-indulgent at three and a half hours.
Critics called the album more self-indulgent than his last one.

entries.meaning: Wrapped up in your own problems and feelings. ---
examples: He was too self-involved that year to see what she was going through.
The characters are all young and self-involved.
Grief made her more self-involved than usual.
entries.contrast: A close synonym of self-absorbed; American writers use both.

entries.meaning: Rich or successful through your own work, starting with nothing. ---
examples: He likes to call himself a self-made millionaire.
She is a self-made businesswoman from a mill town.
The magazine ran a list of self-made founders under thirty.

entries.meaning: Calm and in control of yourself under pressure. ---
examples: She stayed self-possessed through two hours of questions.
He is a self-possessed witness who never raises his voice.
The younger sister is more self-possessed than either parent.

entries.meaning: Called that by the person themselves, with nobody else agreeing. ---
examples: A self-proclaimed expert ran the whole workshop.
The self-proclaimed king of neighborhood barbecue lost the contest.
He is a self-proclaimed political outsider with thirty years in office.
entries.contrast: Usually skeptical: the writer is signaling that only this person makes the claim.

entries.meaning: Carrying its own engine or motor instead of being pushed or pulled. ---
examples: The army bought a battery of self-propelled guns.
He mows the hill with a self-propelled mower.
A self-propelled barge came up the channel.

entries.meaning: Able to manage without help from other people. ---
examples: Living alone made him self-reliant fast.
She raised three self-reliant daughters.
The town is more self-reliant than it was before the mill closed.

entries.meaning: Having proper pride in yourself and your standards. ---
examples: No self-respecting barbecue joint serves that sauce.
No self-respecting editor would let that headline through.
Any self-respecting fan knows the whole roster.
entries.contrast: Nine times out of ten it follows no: no self-respecting cook would buy that.

entries.meaning: Sure that you are more moral than everyone else, and showing it. ---
examples: He gave a self-righteous lecture about recycling.
The tone of the letter is self-righteous and a little cruel.
She gets more self-righteous every time the subject comes up.

entries.meaning: Giving up your own comfort or wishes for other people. ---
examples: Her mother was a self-sacrificing woman who worked two jobs.
It was a self-sacrificing decision that cost him the promotion.
Nurses on that ward are more self-sacrificing than anyone knows.

entries.meaning: Too pleased with yourself, in a way that annoys other people. ---
examples: He gave a self-satisfied smile when the numbers came in.
She looked self-satisfied after winning the argument.
The whole article is smug and self-satisfied.

entries.meaning: Where customers serve themselves instead of being served. ---
examples: We stopped at a self-service gas station outside Reno.
The cafeteria is self-service, so grab a tray.
Self-service checkout lanes move faster at this hour.

entries.meaning: Done to help yourself, while pretending to help others. ---
examples: His apology sounded self-serving.
It was a self-serving decision dressed up as generosity.
Nothing is more self-serving than helping only when the cameras are on.

entries.meaning: Using a title or description that you gave yourself. ---
examples: A self-styled expert took over the meeting.
He is a self-styled reformer with no record to show for it.
The self-styled king of late-night radio signed off for good.
entries.position: attributive only — never after a verb
entries.contrast: Always doubtful: the speaker gives the title because the person claims it, not because it is earned.

entries.meaning: Able to provide everything you need without help from outside. ---
examples: The farm is almost self-sufficient in vegetables.
She learned to be self-sufficient at a young age.
The country is more self-sufficient in energy than it was ten years ago.

entries.meaning: Able to keep itself going without outside help or money. ---
examples: The project is self-sustaining now and needs no more grants.
A self-sustaining chain reaction starts in a fraction of a second.
Her garden is small but self-sustaining.

entries.meaning: Caring only about yourself and not about other people. ---
examples: Don't be selfish — share the cookies with your sister.
It was a selfish thing to do, and he knew it.
He gets more selfish the longer he lives alone.

entries.meaning: Thinking about other people's needs before your own. ---
examples: Her years of work with refugees were entirely selfless.
It was a selfless act of courage.
The nurses did the most selfless work of anyone that winter.

entries.meaning: Having to do with the meaning of words. ---
examples: The difference is purely semantic.
They spent an hour on a semantic detail.
Semantic analysis of the contract turned up two readings.
entries.contrast: Semantics is the noun: it's just semantics means the argument is about words, not about facts.

entries.meaning: Less formal than a black-tie event, but dressier than everyday clothes. ---
examples: The invitation says semi-formal, so wear a jacket.
It was a semi-formal dinner at the club.
We kept the tone of the meeting semi-formal.
entries.contrast: American dictionaries prefer semiformal, with no hyphen; the two spellings are the same word.

entries.meaning: Happening twice a year. ---
examples: The semiannual report comes out in June and December.
The store runs a semiannual sale on coats.
She goes in for a semiannual checkup.
entries.contrast: Semiannual means twice a year, like biannual; biennial means every two years.

entries.meaning: Partly automatic: one action by the operator, the rest by the machine. ---
examples: A semiautomatic rifle fires one round per trigger pull.
The press is semiautomatic: you load it and it does the rest.
Semiautomatic transmissions were rare on American cars.

entries.meaning: Shaped like half a circle. ---
examples: The seats form a semicircular row around the stage.
A semicircular window sits above the front door.
The driveway in front of the house is semicircular.

entries.meaning: Dressier than everyday clothes, but short of black tie. ---
examples: He wore a semiformal suit to the reception.
The wedding is semiformal — no jeans.
Semiformal attire means a dark suit or a cocktail dress.
entries.contrast: The usual American spelling; semi-formal with a hyphen is the same word.

entries.meaning: Early and so important that later work grows out of it. ---
examples: Her seminal paper changed the whole field.
That record is a seminal album of early punk.
The book is one of the seminal works of the period.
entries.contrast: Not a semi- word: seminal comes from seed and means first and influential, not half of anything.

entries.meaning: Lasting a long time but not forever. ---
examples: She uses a semipermanent hair color that washes out in a month.
The trailers became semipermanent housing for the crew.
Semipermanent makeup lasts about a year.

entries.meaning: Of a stone: valuable, but less so than a diamond or a ruby. ---
examples: The ring is set with semiprecious stones.
Amethyst is a semiprecious gem.
She keeps a tray of semiprecious beads for her jewelry.

entries.meaning: Slightly sweet: less sugar than sweet chocolate or wine, more than bitter. ---
examples: The recipe calls for a cup of semisweet chocolate chips.
We ordered a semisweet white wine.
This chocolate is semisweet, not bitter.

entries.meaning: Belonging to the group of peoples and languages that includes Hebrew and Arabic. ---
examples: Hebrew and Arabic are Semitic languages.
The inscription is written in a Semitic script.
The course covers the Semitic peoples of the ancient Near East.
entries.contrast: Always capitalized. Semitic names a family of languages and peoples; anti-Semitic is used only of hostility toward Jews.

entries.meaning: Having to do with a senator or the Senate. ---
examples: He announced his senatorial campaign in the spring.
Senatorial courtesy decides which judges get a hearing.
A senatorial district in this state covers everything.

entries.meaning: From Senegal, or having to do with Senegal. ---
examples: A Senegalese restaurant opened on Main Street.
The Senegalese team won on penalties.
Her mother is Senegalese.
entries.contrast: The same word is the noun, and it does not change in the plural: a Senegalese, the Senegalese.

entries.meaning: Confused and forgetful because of old age. ---
examples: He joked that he was going senile, but nobody laughed.
Senile dementia was the old name for the condition.
She seemed more senile each time we visited.
entries.contrast: Offensive about a person today — doctors say has dementia. The word survives in the fixed term senile dementia.

entries.meaning: Senior has 3 distinct senses.
examples: She's a senior editor at the paper.
Two more senior officers reviewed the case.
He is senior to me by three years.
Senior citizens ride the city bus for free.
Ask about the senior discount before you pay.
My senior year was the best one.
The senior class voted to go to Chicago.
Senior prom is the third Friday in May.

senses.head: Higher in rank, or longer in the job, than other people
examples: She's a senior editor at the paper.
Two more senior officers reviewed the case.
He is senior to me by three years.

senses.head: Older; meant for older people
examples: Senior citizens ride the city bus for free.
Ask about the senior discount before you pay.

senses.head: Of the last year of high school or college
examples: My senior year was the best one.
The senior class voted to go to Chicago.
Senior prom is the third Friday in May.

entries.takes: to + noun — senior to everyone else on the team
entries.contrast: After senior use to, never than: She is senior to me, not senior than me.

entries.meaning: Sensational has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The food at that place is sensational.
She gave a sensational performance on opening night.
The paper ran a sensational headline about the mayor.
The trial got more sensational with every witness.
Sensational coverage of the crash upset the families.

senses.head: Extremely good; wonderful
examples: The food at that place is sensational.
She gave a sensational performance on opening night.

senses.head: Written or presented to shock and excite people
examples: The paper ran a sensational headline about the mayor.
The trial got more sensational with every witness.
Sensational coverage of the crash upset the families.

entries.contrast: A sensational dinner is wonderful; sensational reporting is cheap and shocking. The noun it goes with tells you which.

entries.meaning: Using shocking stories and details to attract attention. ---
examples: The coverage was sensationalistic and thin on facts.
He hosts a sensationalistic talk show.
Local news has gotten more sensationalistic since the ratings dropped.

entries.meaning: Senseless has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The senseless killing shocked the whole town.
It was a senseless waste of money.
Arguing about it now is senseless.
He was knocked senseless by the fall.
The blow left her senseless on the floor.

senses.head: Having no purpose or meaning; stupid
examples: The senseless killing shocked the whole town.
It was a senseless waste of money.
Arguing about it now is senseless.

senses.head: Unconscious
examples: He was knocked senseless by the fall.
The blow left her senseless on the floor.

entries.contrast: Not the opposite of sensitive. And the second meaning survives mostly in knocked senseless and beaten senseless.

entries.meaning: Having to do with the senses — sight, hearing, touch, taste and smell. ---
examples: Sensory nerves carry signals to the brain.
The museum has a sensory room for small children.
Sensory overload hits me in big stores.

entries.meaning: Connected with physical, often sexual pleasure. ---
examples: Her voice on the record is low and sensual.
They danced a slow, sensual tango.
The film is more sensual than the novel it came from.
entries.contrast: Sensual usually points to physical, often sexual pleasure; sensuous to pleasure the senses take in art, music or food.

entries.meaning: Giving pleasure to the senses. ---
examples: She loves the sensuous texture of velvet.
His poems are full of sensuous detail — smell, color, sound.
The soup was rich and sensuous.
entries.contrast: Keep it apart from sensual: sensuous is about pleasure in colors, sounds and textures, with no sexual meaning attached.

entries.meaning: Able to feel and be aware of things. ---
examples: Whales are sentient beings.
The movie asks whether the robot is sentient.
The law protects sentient animals from cruelty.

entries.meaning: Sentimental has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He gets sentimental after two beers.
The ending is sentimental, but I cried anyway.
She's more sentimental about the old house than I am.
The ring has sentimental value.
I keep the letters for sentimental reasons.

senses.head: Showing tender feelings, often more than the situation deserves
examples: He gets sentimental after two beers.
The ending is sentimental, but I cried anyway.
She's more sentimental about the old house than I am.

senses.head: Valued for the memories attached to it, not for the money
examples: The ring has sentimental value.
I keep the letters for sentimental reasons.

entries.meaning: Separate has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The kids have separate rooms now.
Keep the raw chicken separate from the salad.
We arrived in two separate cars.
That's a separate question, and we'll get to it.
Her work life and her home life are completely separate.

senses.head: Not joined to, or not together with, something else
examples: The kids have separate rooms now.
Keep the raw chicken separate from the salad.
We arrived in two separate cars.

senses.head: Different; not the same one
examples: That's a separate question, and we'll get to it.
Her work life and her home life are completely separate.

entries.contrast: The adjective ends in a schwa — SEP-ruht; the verb is SEP-uh-rayt. Same spelling, two pronunciations.

entries.meaning: Separated has 2 distinct senses.
examples: They've been separated for about a year.
My parents are separated, not divorced.
The twins were separated at birth.
The two wings of the school are separated by a courtyard.

senses.head: No longer living together as a couple, but not divorced
examples: They've been separated for about a year.
My parents are separated, not divorced.

senses.head: Kept apart from something or someone else
examples: The twins were separated at birth.
The two wings of the school are separated by a courtyard.

entries.contrast: Separate is a plain state — apart or different. Separated says something pulled them apart, and of a couple it means living apart but not yet divorced.

entries.meaning: Wanting a region to break away and become its own country. ---
examples: A separatist movement grew in the north.
Separatist fighters took the airport.
He joined a small separatist party in his twenties.

entries.meaning: Infected with harmful bacteria. ---
examples: The wound turned septic within two days.
She was rushed in with septic shock.
An untreated cut like that can go septic.
entries.contrast: A septic tank uses an older sense — bacteria break the waste down. Nothing there is infected.

entries.meaning: Following one after another in a fixed order. ---
examples: The files are stored in sequential order.
The tickets have sequential numbers.
The training is sequential: you can't skip a step.

entries.meaning: Covered with small shiny disks sewn onto the cloth. ---
examples: She wore a sequined dress to the party.
A sequined jacket caught the stage lights.
The costumes were heavily sequined.

entries.meaning: From Serbia, or having to do with Serbia and its language. ---
examples: Serbian is written in two alphabets.
We went to a Serbian film festival downtown.
Her husband is Serbian.

entries.meaning: Happening by luck, and turning out well. ---
examples: Our meeting was completely serendipitous.
It was a serendipitous discovery in the back of the archive.
Nothing is more serendipitous than finding the right book by accident.

entries.meaning: Completely calm and peaceful. ---
examples: She stayed serene through the whole hearing.
A serene lake at dawn is worth the early start.
The garden is more serene on a weekday morning.

entries.meaning: Serial has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Police were hunting a serial killer.
He's a serial entrepreneur — this is his fifth company.
She called him a serial liar to his face.
Write down the serial number on the back.
The novel first appeared in serial form.

senses.head: Doing the same thing again and again
examples: Police were hunting a serial killer.
He's a serial entrepreneur — this is his fifth company.
She called him a serial liar to his face.

senses.head: Forming or belonging to a series
examples: Write down the serial number on the back.
The novel first appeared in serial form.

entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like cereal, the breakfast food — different word, same pronunciation.

entries.meaning: Having a row of small points along the edge, like a saw. ---
examples: Use a serrated knife for bread.
The leaves have serrated edges.
The blade is serrated near the handle.

entries.meaning: Serviceable has 2 distinct senses.
examples: His Spanish is serviceable — he can order dinner and ask directions.
The hotel was plain but serviceable.
Only two of the trucks are still serviceable.
The old boots are serviceable for another winter.

senses.head: Good enough to do the job, though nothing special
examples: His Spanish is serviceable — he can order dinner and ask directions.
The hotel was plain but serviceable.

senses.head: Still in working condition; usable
examples: Only two of the trucks are still serviceable.
The old boots are serviceable for another winter.

entries.meaning: Too eager to obey and please, like a servant. ---
examples: His servile manner around the boss made everyone uncomfortable.
She refused to be servile to anyone.
The letter struck a servile tone that embarrassed the whole department.

entries.meaning: Set has 3 distinct senses.
examples: We meet at a set time every Monday.
The restaurant offers a set menu for thirty dollars.
There's no set rule about how long it takes.
Are you all set?
We're set to leave at six.
He's set in his ways and won't try anything new.
She's set on going to law school.
They were dead set against the plan.

senses.head: Fixed or arranged in advance
examples: We meet at a set time every Monday.
The restaurant offers a set menu for thirty dollars.
There's no set rule about how long it takes.

senses.head: Ready
examples: Are you all set?
We're set to leave at six.

senses.head: Determined about something, or unwilling to change
examples: He's set in his ways and won't try anything new.
She's set on going to law school.
They were dead set against the plan.

entries.position: both — the ready meaning only after a verb
entries.comparison: not gradable — though more set in his ways is common
entries.takes: on + -ing; against + noun — set on leaving, set against the idea
entries.contrast: Mostly a verb and a noun. As an adjective it lives in a few patterns: a set time, all set, set in his ways, set on going.

entries.meaning: Settled has 2 distinct senses.
examples: They finally feel settled in the new town.
Once the kids were settled, she went back to school.
The weather looks settled for the weekend.
The market is settled after a rough month.

senses.head: Living a regular life in one place
examples: They finally feel settled in the new town.
Once the kids were settled, she went back to school.

senses.head: Calm and unlikely to change
examples: The weather looks settled for the weekend.
The market is settled after a rough month.

entries.meaning: Severe has 3 distinct senses.
examples: She's in severe pain.
The storm did severe damage to the pier.
This winter was more severe than last.
The judge handed down a severe sentence.
He gave me a severe look over his glasses.
Her hair was pulled back in a severe bun.
The building's lines are severe and gray.

senses.head: Very bad or serious
examples: She's in severe pain.
The storm did severe damage to the pier.
This winter was more severe than last.

senses.head: Strict and harsh
examples: The judge handed down a severe sentence.
He gave me a severe look over his glasses.

senses.head: Very plain, with no decoration
examples: Her hair was pulled back in a severe bun.
The building's lines are severe and gray.

entries.meaning: Cut off, or cut completely through. ---
examples: Surgeons reattached the severed finger.
A severed cable left the whole block dark.
He still talks about those severed friendships.

entries.meaning: Treating one sex as less able or less important than the other. ---
examples: That joke was sexist and everyone knew it.
The dress code is openly sexist.
Ads from the fifties look more sexist every year.

entries.meaning: Sexual has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Sexual attraction is not the same thing as love.
The novel deals with sexual relationships openly.
Sexual equality at work is still a fight.
Most plants use sexual reproduction.

senses.head: Having to do with sex or physical attraction
examples: Sexual attraction is not the same thing as love.
The novel deals with sexual relationships openly.

senses.head: Having to do with the two sexes, or with reproduction
examples: Sexual equality at work is still a fight.
Most plants use sexual reproduction.

entries.contrast: A false friend: Russian сексуальный often means sexy. English sexual is the neutral, technical word — a sexy dress, never a sexual dress.

entries.meaning: Sexy has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He looked sexy in that jacket.
It's the sexiest song on the album.
Budget reform is not a sexy topic.
They needed a sexier name for the product.

senses.head: Sexually attractive
examples: He looked sexy in that jacket.
It's the sexiest song on the album.

senses.head: Informal: exciting and interesting to people
examples: Budget reform is not a sexy topic.
They needed a sexier name for the product.

entries.meaning: Shabby has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He wore a shabby coat with a torn pocket.
The lobby looked shabbier than in the photos.
That was shabby treatment after twenty years on the job.
It's a shabby way to treat a friend.

senses.head: Worn out and untidy from long use
examples: He wore a shabby coat with a torn pocket.
The lobby looked shabbier than in the photos.

senses.head: Unfair and mean
examples: That was shabby treatment after twenty years on the job.
It's a shabby way to treat a friend.

entries.meaning: Protected from direct sunlight. ---
examples: We found a shaded spot for the picnic.
The path is shaded most of the way up.
The shaded seats at the ballpark sell out first.

entries.meaning: Shadowy has 2 distinct senses.
examples: A shadowy corridor led down to the basement.
The room stays shadowy even at noon.
A shadowy figure was standing by the gate.
The money came from a shadowy offshore fund.

senses.head: Full of shadows and hard to see into
examples: A shadowy corridor led down to the basement.
The room stays shadowy even at noon.

senses.head: Mysterious and secretive
examples: A shadowy figure was standing by the gate.
The money came from a shadowy offshore fund.

entries.meaning: Shady has 2 distinct senses.
examples: We sat on a shady bench by the river.
The north side of the yard is shadier.
That deal sounds shady to me.
He made his money in some shady business out west.

senses.head: Sheltered from the sun; giving shade
examples: We sat on a shady bench by the river.
The north side of the yard is shadier.

senses.head: Informal: probably dishonest
examples: That deal sounds shady to me.
He made his money in some shady business out west.

entries.meaning: Covered with long, thick, untidy hair. ---
examples: A shaggy dog followed us all the way home.
His hair was long and shaggy.
The pony's coat gets shaggier every winter.

entries.meaning: Upset and unsteady after a shock. ---
examples: She was badly shaken by the accident.
He looked shaken when he came out of the office.
The driver was more shaken than hurt.
entries.contrast: Shaken is how a person feels after a shock; shaky describes hands, a voice or anything unsteady.

entries.meaning: Shaky has 3 distinct senses.
examples: My hands were shaky after the second coffee.
He answered in a shaky voice.
Don't put the vase on that shaky table.
The ladder felt shakier the higher I went.
The evidence is shaky at best.
The team got off to a shaky start.

senses.head: Trembling, and hard to control
examples: My hands were shaky after the second coffee.
He answered in a shaky voice.

senses.head: Not firm or steady
examples: Don't put the vase on that shaky table.
The ladder felt shakier the higher I went.

senses.head: Weak and not to be relied on
examples: The evidence is shaky at best.
The team got off to a shaky start.

entries.meaning: Pretending to be real, and meant to fool people. ---
examples: The election was a sham vote with one candidate.
They were arrested over a sham marriage.
Sham charities take the money and disappear.
entries.contrast: Almost always before a noun. The same word is a noun: the whole trial was a sham.

entries.meaning: Showing in your face that you are ashamed. ---
examples: He gave a shamefaced apology and sat down.
She looked shamefaced when the teacher read her note out loud.
The shamefaced players walked off the field.

entries.meaning: So bad that the people responsible should be ashamed. ---
examples: It was a shameful way to end a long career.
Conditions in the camp are shameful.
Nothing was more shameful than the cover-up that followed.
entries.contrast: Shameful describes the act; ashamed describes the person: a shameful lie, but he felt ashamed.

entries.meaning: Doing something bad or embarrassing without any shame at all. ---
examples: That was a shameless plug for his own book.
Shameless lying got him through the interview.
She is shameless about asking for favors.

entries.meaning: Having no clear shape or form. ---
examples: She wore a shapeless gray sweater.
The clay was still a shapeless lump.
His argument was shapeless and hard to follow.

entries.meaning: Having an attractive shape. ---
examples: The dancer had long, shapely legs.
A shapely vase stood on the mantel.
The hedge is shapelier since the gardener came.
entries.comparison: -er/-est or more/most — shapelier, shapeliest; more shapely, most shapely
entries.contrast: An adjective, though it ends in -ly: shapely legs, never she walked shapely.

entries.meaning: Used, owned or felt by two or more people. ---
examples: We have a shared bathroom down the hall.
A shared interest in old movies brought them together.
Their shared history makes every argument worse.

entries.meaning: Sharp has 6 distinct senses.
examples: Careful — that knife is sharp.
Use the sharpest scissors in the drawer.
He cut his hand on a sharp piece of metal.
There's a sharp turn at the bottom of the hill.
The city saw a sharp rise in rents.
Prices took a sharp drop in May.
She still has a sharp mind at ninety.
His sharp eyes caught the typo on page one.
He's sharper than anyone else in the room.
I felt a sharp pain in my side.
A sharp stab of cold air hit us at the door.
Her tone got sharp toward the end.
There was a sharp exchange at the school board meeting.
The recipe calls for sharp cheddar.
The wine has a sharp finish.

senses.head: Having an edge or a point that cuts easily
examples: Careful — that knife is sharp.
Use the sharpest scissors in the drawer.
He cut his hand on a sharp piece of metal.

senses.head: Sudden and large, of a change or a turn
examples: There's a sharp turn at the bottom of the hill.
The city saw a sharp rise in rents.
Prices took a sharp drop in May.

senses.head: Quick to notice or understand things
examples: She still has a sharp mind at ninety.
His sharp eyes caught the typo on page one.
He's sharper than anyone else in the room.

senses.head: Sudden and severe, of a pain
examples: I felt a sharp pain in my side.
A sharp stab of cold air hit us at the door.

senses.head: Harsh and critical
examples: Her tone got sharp toward the end.
There was a sharp exchange at the school board meeting.

senses.head: Strong and slightly bitter, of a taste or smell
examples: The recipe calls for sharp cheddar.
The wine has a sharp finish.

entries.contrast: Sharp is also an adverb in time phrases — at seven o'clock sharp — and in music a sharp note is slightly too high.

entries.meaning: Good at noticing small details. ---
examples: A sharp-eyed reader spotted the error.
You have to be sharp-eyed to find the bird in that photo.
A more sharp-eyed editor would have caught it.

entries.meaning: Shattered has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Shattered glass covered the sidewalk.
He swept up the shattered plate.
She was shattered by the news.
The family is still shattered a year later.

senses.head: Broken into many small pieces
examples: Shattered glass covered the sidewalk.
He swept up the shattered plate.

senses.head: Deeply upset, with your life or hopes broken
examples: She was shattered by the news.
The family is still shattered a year later.

entries.contrast: In British English shattered also means exhausted. Americans say wiped out for that.

entries.meaning: So shocking or destructive that it breaks something apart. ---
examples: The verdict was a shattering blow to the family.
Shattering news came late that night.
There was a shattering crash from the kitchen.

entries.meaning: Made so that it will not break into pieces. ---
examples: The lenses in these glasses are shatterproof.
Shatterproof glass keeps the kids safe.
We bought shatterproof ornaments after the cat arrived.

entries.meaning: Shaved has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He has a shaved head and a gray beard.
Her legs were freshly shaved.
Shaved ice with syrup is summer around here.
The salad comes with shaved Parmesan on top.

senses.head: With the hair cut off close to the skin
examples: He has a shaved head and a gray beard.
Her legs were freshly shaved.

senses.head: Cut into very thin slices
examples: Shaved ice with syrup is summer around here.
The salad comes with shaved Parmesan on top.

entries.meaning: Embarrassed because you have done something silly or wrong. ---
examples: He gave me a sheepish grin and apologized.
She looked sheepish about forgetting my birthday.
The sheepish look on his face said everything.

entries.meaning: With the shell taken off. ---
examples: The recipe calls for a cup of shelled walnuts.
Buy shelled pistachios if you're in a hurry.
Shelled peas cook in five minutes.
entries.contrast: In hard-shelled and soft-shelled the word means the opposite — having a shell of that kind.

entries.meaning: Sheltered has 2 distinct senses.
examples: We ate lunch in a sheltered corner of the yard.
The bay is sheltered from the north wind.
She had a sheltered childhood in a small town.
He's led a more sheltered life than he admits.

senses.head: Protected from wind, rain or sun
examples: We ate lunch in a sheltered corner of the yard.
The bay is sheltered from the north wind.

senses.head: Kept away from anything difficult or unpleasant in life
examples: She had a sheltered childhood in a small town.
He's led a more sheltered life than he admits.

entries.meaning: Constantly moving or changing. ---
examples: Shifting sands buried the road overnight.
The shifting politics of the region make planning hard.
Their shifting stories made the police suspicious.

entries.meaning: Lazy, with no ambition to do anything. ---
examples: He called his nephew shiftless and lazy.
A shiftless crew showed up an hour late.
The main character is a shiftless dreamer who finishes nothing.
entries.form: -less from an old sense of shift, meaning effort

entries.meaning: Looking or sounding dishonest. ---
examples: He had shifty eyes and a nervous laugh.
The salesman seemed shifty from the first minute.
The longer he talked, the shiftier he sounded.

entries.meaning: Shining with a soft, moving light. ---
examples: She wore a shimmery blue dress.
The lake looked shimmery in the heat.
This eyeshadow is more shimmery than I expected.

entries.meaning: Shining has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Her eyes were shining with tears.
A shining moon lit the whole road.
She's a shining example of how to do this job.
That was the one shining moment of the season.

senses.head: Giving out or reflecting light
examples: Her eyes were shining with tears.
A shining moon lit the whole road.

senses.head: Excellent; standing out from everything around it
examples: She's a shining example of how to do this job.
That was the one shining moment of the season.

entries.position: both — the excellent meaning only before a noun
entries.contrast: Shining often carries approval — a shining example. Shiny only describes a surface: shiny shoes.

entries.meaning: Smooth and bright, reflecting the light. ---
examples: His shoes were black and shiny.
The new coin is shinier than the old one.
Kids grab whatever is shiniest on the shelf.

entries.meaning: Happening or used on a ship. ---
examples: They met during a shipboard romance.
Shipboard life takes some getting used to.
The crew ran shipboard drills every morning.

entries.meaning: Neat, clean and in good order. ---
examples: The garage is finally shipshape.
She left the kitchen shipshape.
Everything on deck was shipshape before we sailed.

entries.meaning: Very bad, or very unkind. ---
examples: We had a shitty week.
That was a shitty thing to say to her.
The second hotel was even shittier than the first.
entries.contrast: Vulgar. Fine among friends, never at work or in writing — use lousy or crummy there.

entries.meaning: Shoddy has 2 distinct senses.
examples: They used shoddy materials and the roof leaked by spring.
The second contractor's work was even shoddier.
That's shoddy treatment of a loyal customer.
He gave a shoddy excuse for breaking his promise.

senses.head: Badly made or badly done
examples: They used shoddy materials and the roof leaked by spring.
The second contractor's work was even shoddier.

senses.head: Unfair and dishonest
examples: That's shoddy treatment of a loyal customer.
He gave a shoddy excuse for breaking his promise.

entries.meaning: Wearing no shoes. ---
examples: Shoeless kids ran across the hot sand.
He answered the door shoeless and half asleep.
Guests arrive shoeless and leave their boots by the door.

entries.meaning: Shopworn has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The last box was shopworn and marked down.
They sell shopworn furniture at half price.
The speech was full of shopworn phrases.
That argument is shopworn by now.

senses.head: Dirty or damaged from sitting on display in a store
examples: The last box was shopworn and marked down.
They sell shopworn furniture at half price.

senses.head: No longer fresh or original
examples: The speech was full of shopworn phrases.
That argument is shopworn by now.

entries.meaning: Shorn has 2 distinct senses.
examples: A shorn sheep looks half its size.
His shorn head made him look ten years younger.
The king was left shorn of all real power.
The bill passed shorn of its best provisions.

senses.head: Cut very short, of hair or wool
examples: A shorn sheep looks half its size.
His shorn head made him look ten years younger.

senses.head: Stripped of something you used to have
examples: The king was left shorn of all real power.
The bill passed shorn of its best provisions.

entries.meaning: Having short hair or short fur. ---
examples: A short-haired terrier is easier to groom.
She's been short-haired since college.
Short-haired breeds shed less in the house.

entries.meaning: Without enough people to do the work. ---
examples: We're short-handed tonight, so expect a wait.
The kitchen has been short-handed all month.
They played short-handed for two minutes.
entries.contrast: In hockey a team is short-handed while a player sits in the penalty box. At an office, short-staffed is the everyday word.

entries.meaning: Lasting only a short time. ---
examples: Their happiness was short-lived.
It was a short-lived TV show from the nineties.
The truce proved short-lived.
entries.contrast: Two pronunciations are standard in the US: short-LYVD and short-LIVD.

entries.meaning: Of simple food cooked quickly to order in a diner. ---
examples: He worked as a short-order cook for years.
The diner has a short-order menu — eggs, burgers, fries.
Short-order cooking is all speed and timing.

entries.meaning: Reaching only a short distance, or covering only the near future. ---
examples: Short-range missiles were moved to the border.
The forecast is only a short-range guess.
We made short-range plans and left the rest open.

entries.meaning: Having to do with the near future only. ---
examples: Short-run profits look good, but the debt keeps growing.
The tax cut is a short-run fix.
Short-run costs rose while output fell.
entries.contrast: As an adverb phrase it splits and drops the hyphen: in the short run.

entries.meaning: Without enough employees. ---
examples: The clinic is badly short-staffed.
We've been short-staffed since two nurses quit.
A short-staffed ER means long waits.

entries.meaning: Quick to get angry. ---
examples: He's short-tempered before his first coffee.
A short-tempered boss keeps everyone quiet.
She gets more short-tempered when she's tired.

entries.meaning: Shortsighted has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Cutting the training budget is shortsighted.
It was a shortsighted decision that cost them the contract.
Nothing is more shortsighted than ignoring the repairs.
He's shortsighted and can't read the board without glasses.
She's been shortsighted since grade school.

senses.head: Not thinking about what will happen later
examples: Cutting the training budget is shortsighted.
It was a shortsighted decision that cost them the contract.
Nothing is more shortsighted than ignoring the repairs.

senses.head: Unable to see distant things clearly
examples: He's shortsighted and can't read the board without glasses.
She's been shortsighted since grade school.

entries.contrast: For the eye condition Americans normally say nearsighted; in the US shortsighted usually means bad planning.

entries.meaning: Attracting attention, often too much of it. ---
examples: The ring is a little showy for the office.
Showy red flowers fill the front bed.
His second car is even showier than the first.

entries.meaning: Cut or torn into thin strips. ---
examples: Add a cup of shredded cheese on top.
Shredded documents filled three garbage bags.
The lettuce comes shredded in a bag.

entries.meaning: Good at judging people and situations, and at using that to your advantage. ---
examples: She's a shrewd negotiator.
That was a shrewd guess.
He's shrewder about money than his brother.

entries.meaning: Shrill has 2 distinct senses.
examples: A shrill whistle cut through the noise.
Her voice got shriller as she got angrier.
The debate turned shrill within ten minutes.
Shrill attacks from both sides drowned out the facts.

senses.head: High and unpleasantly loud
examples: A shrill whistle cut through the noise.
Her voice got shriller as she got angrier.

senses.head: Loud and angry in a way that stops people listening
examples: The debate turned shrill within ten minutes.
Shrill attacks from both sides drowned out the facts.

entries.meaning: Dried out and covered in wrinkles. ---
examples: I found two shriveled apples at the back of the drawer.
The flowers on the windowsill were brown and shriveled.
Without water the seedlings looked more shriveled every morning.
entries.contrast: American spelling keeps one l: shriveled, shriveling. The British spelling shrivelled is common in books printed in the UK.

entries.meaning: Smaller than it used to be, often in a way that looks wrong. ---
examples: He pulled a shrunken wool sweater out of the dryer.
Her grandfather seemed shrunken after the illness.
The company is trying to run on a shrunken budget.
entries.form: an old past participle of shrink
entries.contrast: The verb's ordinary past participle is shrunk (my sweater has shrunk); shrunken is the adjective: a shrunken sweater.

entries.meaning: Shut has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Make sure the windows are shut before you leave.
Her eyes were tightly shut.
The lid won't stay shut.
The pharmacy is shut on Sundays.
By ten the whole town is shut.

senses.head: Closed, not open
examples: Make sure the windows are shut before you leave.
Her eyes were tightly shut.
The lid won't stay shut.

senses.head: Not open for business
examples: The pharmacy is shut on Sundays.
By ten the whole town is shut.

entries.position: predicative only — the door is shut; before a noun use closed
entries.contrast: Don't say a shut door — before a noun Americans say a closed door. The verb is the same in all three forms: shut, shut, shut.

entries.meaning: Shuttered has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The main street is lined with shuttered stores.
They bought a shuttered factory and turned it into lofts.
The restaurant has been shuttered since March.
The house sat dark and shuttered all winter.
We walked past rows of shuttered windows.

senses.head: Closed down, out of business for good
examples: The main street is lined with shuttered stores.
They bought a shuttered factory and turned it into lofts.
The restaurant has been shuttered since March.

senses.head: With the shutters closed over the windows
examples: The house sat dark and shuttered all winter.
We walked past rows of shuttered windows.

entries.meaning: Of Siam, the old name of Thailand — now used mostly in fixed phrases. ---
examples: They have two Siamese cats with bright blue eyes.
The museum has a room of Siamese art.
My grandmother still calls conjoined twins Siamese twins.
entries.contrast: Siam is the old name of Thailand, so the modern word for the country is Thai. Siamese survives mainly in Siamese cat; for Siamese twins doctors now say conjoined twins.

entries.meaning: Of or from Siberia. ---
examples: A Siberian husky needs a lot of exercise.
The cold front brought Siberian air all the way to Texas.
Her family is Siberian, from a village near Irkutsk.
entries.comparison: not gradable — but very Siberian when it means 'bitterly cold'
entries.contrast: The person is the noun a Siberian. Americans often use it loosely for extreme cold: Siberian temperatures in Chicago.

entries.meaning: Of or from Sicily. ---
examples: This is my great-aunt's Sicilian recipe for eggplant.
The pizza place does a thick Sicilian crust.
Both of his parents are Sicilian.
entries.contrast: The person is the noun a Sicilian. Sicily is part of Italy, so someone can be both Italian and Sicilian.

entries.meaning: Sickening has 2 distinct senses.
examples: It was sickening to watch him blame the kids.
The details that came out in court were sickening.
There is something sickening about that much waste.
A sickening smell of gas filled the hallway.
The car hit the guardrail with a sickening thud.

senses.head: So bad or cruel that it shocks and disgusts you
examples: It was sickening to watch him blame the kids.
The details that came out in court were sickening.
There is something sickening about that much waste.

senses.head: Making you feel physically ill
examples: A sickening smell of gas filled the hallway.
The car hit the guardrail with a sickening thud.

entries.meaning: Sickly has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He was a sickly kid who missed half of third grade.
The kitten was the sickliest of the litter.
She looked pale and sickly after the flight.
The waiting room was painted a sickly green.
The punch had a sickly sweet taste.

senses.head: Often ill and not strong
examples: He was a sickly kid who missed half of third grade.
The kitten was the sickliest of the litter.
She looked pale and sickly after the flight.

senses.head: Unpleasant in a weak, too-sweet or washed-out way
examples: The waiting room was painted a sickly green.
The punch had a sickly sweet taste.

entries.comparison: -er/-est or more/most — sicklier, sickliest; also more sickly, most sickly
entries.contrast: Despite the -ly, sickly is an adjective, not an adverb. It is not the same as sick: a sick child is ill today, a sickly child is ill again and again.

entries.meaning: Extremely funny. ---
examples: His impression of the principal was sidesplitting.
We watched a sidesplitting comedy about a family road trip.
The second act is more sidesplitting than the first.
entries.form: compound — noun + -ing participle, from the idea of laughing until your sides hurt
entries.contrast: Also written side-splitting. It is strong praise, so save it for something truly funny.

entries.meaning: Pointing or facing toward the side. ---
examples: She gave him a sideways look and said nothing.
The crab made a quick sideways move.
He answered with a sideways nod toward the door.
entries.contrast: sideways is much more often an adverb (he stepped sideways, turn it sideways). As an adjective it goes only before a noun.

entries.meaning: Of or from Sierra Leone. ---
examples: The Sierra Leonean team qualified for the first time.
She writes about Sierra Leonean music for a magazine.
Our new neighbors are Sierra Leonean.
entries.contrast: Two words, both capitalized, and the person is the noun a Sierra Leonean. The country is Sierra Leone, with no -an.

entries.meaning: With a signature on it. ---
examples: Bring a signed copy of the lease to the office.
The contract isn't signed yet.
He keeps a signed baseball on his desk.
entries.contrast: The g is silent: SYND, one syllable.

entries.meaning: Significant has 2 distinct senses.
examples: There has been a significant drop in traffic deaths.
The repair will cost a significant amount of money.
This is the most significant change to the law in thirty years.
She gave her husband a significant look across the table.
It is significant that he never mentioned the money.

senses.head: Large or important enough to matter
examples: There has been a significant drop in traffic deaths.
The repair will cost a significant amount of money.
This is the most significant change to the law in thirty years.

senses.head: Carrying a meaning that is not said out loud
examples: She gave her husband a significant look across the table.
It is significant that he never mentioned the money.

entries.contrast: In research statistically significant means only that the result is unlikely to be chance — not that it is large.

entries.meaning: Of the Sikh religion, which began in the Punjab, or of its followers. ---
examples: There is a Sikh temple on the edge of town.
Many Sikh men wear a turban.
His family is Sikh.
entries.contrast: Pronounced SEEK, like the verb seek. It is also the noun for a member of the religion (a Sikh); the religion itself is Sikhism.

entries.meaning: Silent has 3 distinct senses.
examples: The house was silent except for the clock.
The new dishwasher is almost completely silent.
We stood in a silent line outside the door.
The company has been silent about the layoffs.
He stayed silent for the whole meeting.
The b in 'climb' is silent.
She wrote her thesis on silent films.

senses.head: Making no sound at all
examples: The house was silent except for the clock.
The new dishwasher is almost completely silent.
We stood in a silent line outside the door.

senses.head: Saying nothing, especially about something people expect you to speak about
examples: The company has been silent about the layoffs.
He stayed silent for the whole meeting.

senses.head: Not pronounced, or made without recorded sound
examples: The b in 'climb' is silent.
She wrote her thesis on silent films.

entries.takes: about or on + noun, in the 'saying nothing' sense

entries.meaning: Silky has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The puppy has silky black ears.
This shampoo leaves your hair silkier.
She ran her hand over the silky fabric.
He has a silky radio voice.
