The sauce was rich and silky.

senses.head: Soft and smooth to the touch, like silk
examples: The puppy has silky black ears.
This shampoo leaves your hair silkier.
She ran her hand over the silky fabric.

senses.head: Smooth and pleasant in sound or taste
examples: He has a silky radio voice.
The sauce was rich and silky.

entries.meaning: Able to talk people into things with charming, persuasive speech. ---
examples: A silver-tongued lawyer got the whole case thrown out.
He was the silver-tongued one; his brother just nodded.
Even the most silver-tongued salesman couldn't move that car.
entries.position: attributive only — mostly before a noun
entries.contrast: It is half a compliment: a silver-tongued speaker is smooth, and often a little too smooth to trust.

entries.meaning: Silvery has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The lake looked silvery under the moon.
He has a full head of silvery hair.
The fish flashed silvery in the net.
Her silvery laugh carried across the yard.
Somewhere below, a silvery bell rang twice.

senses.head: Shining pale gray, like silver
examples: The lake looked silvery under the moon.
He has a full head of silvery hair.
The fish flashed silvery in the net.

senses.head: Clear and light in sound
examples: Her silvery laugh carried across the yard.
Somewhere below, a silvery bell rang twice.

entries.meaning: Simple-minded has 2 distinct senses.
examples: That is a simple-minded answer to a hard question.
Their plan is simple-minded: build more parking and hope.
The movie treats its audience as simple-minded.
He plays a sweet, simple-minded farmhand.

senses.head: Too simple to deal with something complicated
examples: That is a simple-minded answer to a hard question.
Their plan is simple-minded: build more parking and hope.

senses.head: Not clever, and easy to fool
examples: The movie treats its audience as simple-minded.
He plays a sweet, simple-minded farmhand.

entries.contrast: Used about a person it is an insult, and about someone with a disability it is offensive; say has a learning disability instead.

entries.meaning: Made easier to understand or to use, with the hard parts taken out. ---
examples: The bank sent out a simplified version of the contract.
We read a simplified edition of the novel in class.
The new form is much more simplified than the old one.

entries.meaning: Treating something complicated as if it were easy, and so getting it wrong. ---
examples: That's a simplistic view of what caused the war.
His answer was simplistic, and the reporters said so.
Blaming one department is the most simplistic explanation there is.
entries.contrast: Not a fancy word for simple. Simple is usually good (a simple plan); simplistic is always a criticism — it means too simple to be true.

entries.meaning: Simulated has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Pilots train in a simulated landing before they ever fly.
The lab ran a simulated power outage.
Students take a simulated exam in the first week.
The seats are simulated leather.
She wore a ring with a simulated diamond.

senses.head: Made by a computer or a machine to copy real conditions
examples: Pilots train in a simulated landing before they ever fly.
The lab ran a simulated power outage.
Students take a simulated exam in the first week.

senses.head: Made to look like a more expensive material
examples: The seats are simulated leather.
She wore a ring with a simulated diamond.

entries.position: attributive only — mostly before a noun

entries.meaning: Happening at exactly the same time as something else. ---
examples: The band played simultaneous shows in three cities by video.
The conference offers simultaneous translation into four languages.
The launch was simultaneous with the announcement in Tokyo.
entries.position: attributive only — mostly before a noun; after a verb use at the same time
entries.form: -ous from Latin simul, 'at the same time'
entries.contrast: Americans say sy-muhl-TAY-nee-uhs; the British start it sim-. The adverb is simultaneously, and it is what you usually need after a verb.

entries.meaning: Really meaning what you say, with nothing put on. ---
examples: Her apology sounded sincere.
He is sincere about wanting to help.
Of all the speeches that night, hers was the most sincere.
entries.contrast: The fixed phrases keep an old superlative: my sincerest apologies, sincerest thanks. Letters end Sincerely, not Sincere.

entries.meaning: Sinful has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The sermon called gossip sinful.
He grew up in a house where dancing was sinful.
They treat waste as more sinful than anything else.
That chocolate cake is downright sinful.
A nap at two in the afternoon feels sinful.

senses.head: Morally wrong, especially in a religious sense
examples: The sermon called gossip sinful.
He grew up in a house where dancing was sinful.
They treat waste as more sinful than anything else.

senses.head: So rich or enjoyable that it feels like cheating — used as a joke
examples: That chocolate cake is downright sinful.
A nap at two in the afternoon feels sinful.

entries.meaning: Of or from Singapore. ---
examples: We had Singaporean noodles at a stand downtown.
The fund is run by a Singaporean bank.
Her husband is Singaporean.
entries.contrast: The person is the noun a Singaporean. The country is Singapore, with no -an.

entries.meaning: Single has 3 distinct senses.
examples: Not a single person showed up.
He answered every single question.
One single mistake cost them the game.
She's been single since the divorce.
It's a hard schedule for a single parent.
The room has two single beds.
I booked a single room for Thursday night.

senses.head: Only one, and no more — often for emphasis
examples: Not a single person showed up.
He answered every single question.
One single mistake cost them the game.

senses.head: Not married and not in a relationship
examples: She's been single since the divorce.
It's a hard schedule for a single parent.

senses.head: Meant for one person
examples: The room has two single beds.
I booked a single room for Thursday night.

entries.position: attributive only — a single mistake; but she is single in the 'not married' sense
entries.contrast: a single ticket in the US means one ticket; the British one-way ticket is a one-way in American English.

entries.meaning: Of a jacket or coat: closing with one row of buttons. ---
examples: He wore a plain single-breasted navy suit.
The jacket is single-breasted, with two buttons.
A single-breasted coat is easier to wear open.

entries.meaning: Made of only one cell. ---
examples: Bacteria are single-celled organisms.
Life on Earth was single-celled for billions of years.
We looked at a single-celled alga under the microscope.
entries.position: attributive only — mostly before a noun
entries.contrast: The scientific word is unicellular; single-celled is what a textbook or a teacher says.

entries.meaning: Done by one person with no help. ---
examples: His single-handed rescue of the crew made the news.
It was a single-handed sail across the Atlantic.
The report credits her with a single-handed turnaround.
entries.contrast: After a verb use the adverb: she did it single-handedly, not she did it single-handed.

entries.meaning: Giving all your attention to one goal and nothing else. ---
examples: She is single-minded about getting into medical school.
It took single-minded work to finish the bridge on time.
He is the most single-minded person on the team.

entries.meaning: Typed with no blank line between the lines of text. ---
examples: He handed in four single-spaced pages.
The résumé should be single-spaced.
A single-spaced letter is hard to mark up.

entries.meaning: Singular has 2 distinct senses.
examples: 'Child' is singular and 'children' is plural.
The verb has to agree with a singular subject.
Singular 'they' is now standard in American writing.
She has a singular gift for calming a room.
The building is a singular piece of American design.

senses.head: In grammar: naming one, not more than one
examples: 'Child' is singular and 'children' is plural.
The verb has to agree with a singular subject.
Singular 'they' is now standard in American writing.

senses.head: Unusual and remarkable — formal
examples: She has a singular gift for calming a room.
The building is a singular piece of American design.

entries.contrast: The grammar sense is the everyday one. The 'remarkable' sense is formal and goes before a noun: a singular talent.

entries.meaning: Giving the feeling that something evil or harmful is going on. ---
examples: There was something sinister about the empty parking garage.
He plays a quiet, sinister landlord.
The second letter was more sinister than the first.

entries.meaning: Of or like a sister — warm, protective and close. ---
examples: She gave him a sisterly pat on the shoulder.
There is a sisterly feeling between the two teams.
That was the most sisterly thing anyone did for me all year.
entries.contrast: Despite the -ly, this is an adjective, not an adverb. The male pair is brotherly.

entries.meaning: Endless and hopeless, because the work undoes itself. ---
examples: Keeping the kitchen clean with three kids is a Sisyphean task.
Answering that inbox is Sisyphean labor.
He described the cleanup as a Sisyphean effort with no end date.
entries.position: attributive only — mostly before a noun
entries.form: from Sisyphus, the Greek king made to roll a rock uphill forever
entries.contrast: Capitalized, because it comes from a name. Russian has the same image: сизифов труд.

entries.meaning: Sitting has 2 distinct senses.
examples: No sitting senator has lost that seat in forty years.
The sitting judge recused herself.
It is rare for a sitting mayor to be challenged in the primary.
Measure the chair from the floor in a sitting position.
The stretch can be done from a sitting pose.

senses.head: Holding the office right now
examples: No sitting senator has lost that seat in forty years.
The sitting judge recused herself.
It is rare for a sitting mayor to be challenged in the primary.

senses.head: Done in a seated position
examples: Measure the chair from the floor in a sitting position.
The stretch can be done from a sitting pose.

entries.contrast: The president is sitting is the verb, not this adjective. Note the idiom a sitting duck — an easy target. Sitting room for living room is chiefly British.

entries.meaning: Situated has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The cabin is situated on twelve acres of woods.
We stayed at a hotel situated right on the beach.
The plant is situated between two rivers.
After the sale they were comfortably situated.
Small farms are badly situated to survive a dry year.

senses.head: Standing in a particular place — formal, common in ads and reports
examples: The cabin is situated on twelve acres of woods.
We stayed at a hotel situated right on the beach.
The plant is situated between two rivers.

senses.head: In a particular position, especially about money — with well or badly
examples: After the sale they were comfortably situated.
Small farms are badly situated to survive a dry year.

entries.position: after the noun — a house situated on the lake; also after be
entries.takes: a place phrase: on, in, near + noun
entries.contrast: Don't put it before a noun — not a situated house. In everyday speech located or plain is sounds less formal: The hotel is on the beach.

entries.meaning: Coming after fifty-nine others in a series. ---
examples: We threw a party for my mother's sixtieth birthday.
This is the museum's sixtieth year.
She was the sixtieth caller and won the tickets.
entries.contrast: sixty counts, sixtieth puts in order: sixty years but the sixtieth year. It is also the noun for the fraction 1/60: a sixtieth of a second.

entries.meaning: Fairly large. ---
examples: They left a sizable tip.
A sizable crowd waited outside the courthouse.
The grant covers a sizable part of the cost.
entries.position: attributive only — mostly before a noun
entries.contrast: American writing drops the e: sizable. The spelling sizeable is usual in Britain.

entries.meaning: Sizzling has 3 distinct senses.
examples: The waiter brought out a sizzling plate of fajitas.
Bacon was sizzling in the pan when I came downstairs.
We crossed the sizzling parking lot in flip-flops.
The forecast calls for another sizzling weekend.
The two leads have sizzling chemistry.
The band opened with a sizzling guitar solo.

senses.head: Cooking with the hissing sound of hot fat
examples: The waiter brought out a sizzling plate of fajitas.
Bacon was sizzling in the pan when I came downstairs.

senses.head: Extremely hot
examples: We crossed the sizzling parking lot in flip-flops.
The forecast calls for another sizzling weekend.

senses.head: Exciting, full of energy or passion
examples: The two leads have sizzling chemistry.
The band opened with a sizzling guitar solo.

entries.meaning: Skeletal has 3 distinct senses.
examples: The X-ray showed no skeletal damage.
The class covers the skeletal system.
The dog they rescued was skeletal.
He came back from the hospital looking skeletal.
The office runs on a skeletal staff over the holidays.
All I have so far is a skeletal outline.

senses.head: Of the bones of the body
examples: The X-ray showed no skeletal damage.
The class covers the skeletal system.

senses.head: So thin that the bones show
examples: The dog they rescued was skeletal.
He came back from the hospital looking skeletal.

senses.head: Cut back to the bare minimum
examples: The office runs on a skeletal staff over the holidays.
All I have so far is a skeletal outline.

entries.meaning: Doubting that something is true, honest or going to work. ---
examples: The neighbors were skeptical about the new parking plan.
He gave me a skeptical look.
Voters are more skeptical than they were a year ago.
entries.takes: about or of + noun or -ing; that-clause
entries.contrast: American spelling starts with sk-; the British write sceptical. It means doubting, not pessimistic.

entries.meaning: Sketchy has 2 distinct senses.
examples: That website looks sketchy — don't put your card in.
We walked home through a sketchy part of town.
The deal got sketchier the more he explained it.
Details of the crash are still sketchy.
My memory of that summer is pretty sketchy.

senses.head: Not to be trusted; a little dangerous or dishonest — informal
examples: That website looks sketchy — don't put your card in.
We walked home through a sketchy part of town.
The deal got sketchier the more he explained it.

senses.head: Giving only a rough idea, without the details
examples: Details of the crash are still sketchy.
My memory of that summer is pretty sketchy.

entries.contrast: The 'suspicious' sense is everyday American slang and is what you will hear most: a sketchy guy, a sketchy neighborhood.

entries.meaning: Skewed has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The results were skewed by two huge donations.
The sample is skewed toward older voters.
Their coverage is more skewed than they admit.
The picture over the couch was skewed.
One skewed shelf threw off the whole wall.

senses.head: Twisted away from a fair or true picture
examples: The results were skewed by two huge donations.
The sample is skewed toward older voters.
Their coverage is more skewed than they admit.

senses.head: Sitting at a crooked angle
examples: The picture over the couch was skewed.
One skewed shelf threw off the whole wall.

entries.takes: toward or in favor of + noun; by + noun for the cause

entries.meaning: Doing something well, because of training and practice. ---
examples: She is a skillful negotiator.
He is skillful at getting kids to talk.
That was the most skillful piece of driving I've ever seen.
entries.contrast: American spelling has two l's: skillful. The British write skilful.

entries.meaning: Of milk: with the cream taken off. ---
examples: I take my coffee with skim milk.
The recipe calls for a cup of skim milk.
Does this latte have skim milk in it?
entries.contrast: In the US it is skim milk; the British say skimmed milk. Don't confuse it with the verb skim — to read something quickly.

entries.meaning: Skimpy has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She said the costume was too skimpy for a school play.
He showed up in skimpy running shorts.
The portions were skimpy for the price.
This year's benefits package is skimpier than last year's.

senses.head: Of clothes: very small, covering very little
examples: She said the costume was too skimpy for a school play.
He showed up in skimpy running shorts.

senses.head: Not as much as you need or expect
examples: The portions were skimpy for the price.
This year's benefits package is skimpier than last year's.

entries.meaning: Only on the surface, not real or lasting. ---
examples: Beauty is only skin-deep.
His politeness is skin-deep — watch how he treats waiters.
The changes at the company turned out to be skin-deep.
entries.position: predicative only — mostly after a verb
entries.contrast: It comes from the saying Beauty is only skin-deep, and it is still used mostly in that shape: only skin-deep.

entries.meaning: Fitting as closely as skin. ---
examples: The cyclists wore skin-tight suits.
Her dress was black and skin-tight.
He can't stand skin-tight sleeves.
entries.contrast: Usually written as one word in American English: skintight. Both spellings are correct.

entries.meaning: Skinny has 3 distinct senses.
examples: He was a skinny kid with big glasses.
The cat got skinnier every week until we took her to the vet.
He wears skinny jeans and high-tops.
A skinny tie looks odd with that suit.
She ordered a skinny vanilla latte.
Can you make that one skinny?

senses.head: Very thin, often too thin
examples: He was a skinny kid with big glasses.
The cat got skinnier every week until we took her to the vet.

senses.head: Of clothes: cut very narrow
examples: He wears skinny jeans and high-tops.
A skinny tie looks odd with that suit.

senses.head: Of a coffee drink: made with nonfat milk — informal
examples: She ordered a skinny vanilla latte.
Can you make that one skinny?

entries.contrast: skinny is blunt and can sting; slim and slender are compliments, thin is neutral.

entries.meaning: Fitting as closely as skin. ---
examples: The dancers wore skintight black leggings.
That shirt is skintight on him now.
She bought a skintight swimsuit for the meet.
entries.contrast: The same word as skin-tight; American writing usually closes it up.

entries.meaning: Skittish has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The horse is skittish around loud trucks.
Our rescue dog was skittish for the first month.
Investors are skittish about the new tariffs.
Buyers got more skittish as the rates went up.

senses.head: Of an animal: nervous and easily frightened
examples: The horse is skittish around loud trucks.
Our rescue dog was skittish for the first month.

senses.head: Of people or markets: nervous and quick to back out
examples: Investors are skittish about the new tariffs.
Buyers got more skittish as the rates went up.

entries.meaning: Of the light blue of a clear sky. ---
examples: She painted the nursery sky-blue.
He wore a sky-blue shirt with no tie.
The team's away jerseys are sky-blue.

entries.meaning: Slack has 3 distinct senses.
examples: The rope went slack and the boat drifted.
Keep the line a little slacker or it will snap.
January is the slack season at the store.
Demand has been slack since the spring.
Security at the gate has gotten slack.
He was fired for slack record-keeping.

senses.head: Loose, not pulled tight
examples: The rope went slack and the boat drifted.
Keep the line a little slacker or it will snap.

senses.head: With little business or activity
examples: January is the slack season at the store.
Demand has been slack since the spring.

senses.head: Not careful enough about doing a job properly
examples: Security at the gate has gotten slack.
He was fired for slack record-keeping.

entries.contrast: The noun is in cut me some slack (go easy on me), and slacks means dress pants.

entries.meaning: Killed, especially violently — formal and journalistic. ---
examples: The city named a park after the slain officer.
Families of the slain students spoke at the hearing.
The report lists the names of the slain soldiers.
entries.contrast: Everyday English says killed; slain survives in news writing, in the Bible and in fantasy. After a verb say was killed, not was slain.

entries.meaning: Saying untrue things that damage someone's good name. ---
examples: He called the accusation slanderous and hired a lawyer.
The radio host made slanderous remarks about the sheriff.
Her second statement was more slanderous than the first.
entries.contrast: In American law slander is spoken and libel is written, so a magazine article is libelous, not slanderous.

entries.meaning: Slanted has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The attic has a slanted ceiling.
Her handwriting is small and slanted.
The coverage was badly slanted toward the developer.
Both sides say the questions were slanted.

senses.head: Sloping, not straight up and down or flat
examples: The attic has a slanted ceiling.
Her handwriting is small and slanted.

senses.head: Presented in an unfair way that favors one side
examples: The coverage was badly slanted toward the developer.
Both sides say the questions were slanted.

entries.takes: toward or against + noun, in the 'biased' sense

entries.meaning: Done in a hurry and without care. ---
examples: The paint job was slapdash — you can see the tape lines.
He turned in a slapdash report an hour before the deadline.
This repair is even more slapdash than the last one.
entries.form: compound — slap + dash, the sound of working too fast

entries.meaning: Funny in a physical way — falling down, pies in the face, running into doors. ---
examples: The kids love the slapstick humor in those old shorts.
It's a slapstick comedy with three chase scenes.
He does a slapstick routine with a ladder and a bucket.
entries.form: compound — slap + stick, the paddle clowns hit each other with
entries.contrast: Slapstick is much more often a noun: the movie is pure slapstick. As an adjective it goes before words like comedy, humor and routine.

entries.meaning: Slashed has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He came out to four slashed tires.
The painting was found slashed in the basement.
The store advertised slashed prices on winter coats.
Libraries are working with slashed budgets.

senses.head: Cut with long, violent cuts
examples: He came out to four slashed tires.
The painting was found slashed in the basement.

senses.head: Cut sharply, about prices or budgets
examples: The store advertised slashed prices on winter coats.
Libraries are working with slashed budgets.

entries.meaning: Owning enslaved people, or allowing people to be owned. ---
examples: Most of the early presidents came from slaveholding families.
The compromise kept the number of slaveholding states even.
The museum sits on a former slaveholding plantation.
entries.position: attributive only — mostly before a noun
entries.contrast: A word from American history, used about the South before the Civil War. The noun for the person is a slaveholder; writers today often prefer enslaver.

entries.meaning: Of the Slavic peoples or their languages. ---
examples: Russian and Polish are both Slavic languages.
She teaches Slavic literature at a state university.
The neighborhood is old and heavily Slavic.
entries.contrast: Slavic covers a language family and the peoples who speak it, so a Russian, a Pole and a Serb are all Slavic. Don't confuse it with slavish, which means copying without thought.

entries.meaning: Slavish has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The building is a slavish copy of a Paris train station.
His writing is a slavish imitation of Hemingway.
The party demands slavish loyalty.
She warned against slavish devotion to the rankings.

senses.head: Copying something exactly, with no ideas of your own
examples: The building is a slavish copy of a Paris train station.
His writing is a slavish imitation of Hemingway.

senses.head: Obeying or admiring someone far too much
examples: The party demands slavish loyalty.
She warned against slavish devotion to the rankings.

entries.position: attributive only — mostly before a noun
entries.contrast: Not the same as Slavic (of the Slavs), and the two are pronounced differently: SLAY-vish and SLAH-vik.

entries.meaning: Sleazy has 2 distinct senses.
examples: It was a sleazy move to read her texts.
He got rich running a sleazy loan business.
They stayed at a sleazy motel off the highway.
The bar got sleazier after the new owners took over.

senses.head: Dishonest and morally dirty
examples: It was a sleazy move to read her texts.
He got rich running a sleazy loan business.

senses.head: Cheap, dirty and a little dangerous
examples: They stayed at a sleazy motel off the highway.
The bar got sleazier after the new owners took over.

entries.meaning: Sleek has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The horse had a sleek brown coat.
She pulled her hair back into a sleek ponytail.
They drove up in a sleek black sedan.
The new phone is even sleeker than the last one.

senses.head: Smooth, shiny and healthy-looking
examples: The horse had a sleek brown coat.
She pulled her hair back into a sleek ponytail.

senses.head: Elegant, with clean lines and no clutter
examples: They drove up in a sleek black sedan.
The new phone is even sleeker than the last one.

entries.meaning: Asleep right now. ---
examples: Don't wake the sleeping baby.
He stepped over two sleeping dogs to get to the door.
Careful — there are sleeping kids in the next room.
entries.contrast: After a verb, the baby is sleeping is the verb; the adjective there is asleep: the baby is asleep. In sleeping bag and sleeping pill the word says what it is for, not that it sleeps.

entries.meaning: Spent without sleep, or unable to sleep. ---
examples: I spent a sleepless night waiting for the call.
Three sleepless weeks with a newborn left them both foggy.
She lay sleepless until the sky turned gray.

entries.meaning: Sleepy has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The medicine makes me sleepy.
He gets sleepier right after lunch.
They retired to a sleepy town on the coast.
It was a sleepy Sunday afternoon.

senses.head: Wanting to go to sleep
examples: The medicine makes me sleepy.
He gets sleepier right after lunch.

senses.head: Quiet, with very little going on
examples: They retired to a sleepy town on the coast.
It was a sleepy Sunday afternoon.

entries.meaning: Made with no sleeves. ---
examples: She wore a sleeveless summer dress.
The dress code says no sleeveless shirts.
His jersey is sleeveless.

entries.meaning: Slender has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She has long, slender fingers.
The dancer was tall and slender.
The second vase is more slender than the first.
The bill passed by a slender majority.
They are living on a slender income.

senses.head: Thin in a graceful, attractive way
examples: She has long, slender fingers.
The dancer was tall and slender.
The second vase is more slender than the first.

senses.head: Small in amount, and barely enough
examples: The bill passed by a slender majority.
They are living on a slender income.

entries.comparison: -er/-est or more/most — slenderer, slenderest; more often more slender, most slender
entries.contrast: slender is a compliment, like slim; skinny is blunt and thin is neutral.

entries.meaning: Cut into thin flat pieces. ---
examples: Buy a pound of sliced turkey at the deli.
Top it with sliced almonds.
The bread comes sliced.
entries.contrast: It is in the American joke the best thing since sliced bread — the greatest invention there is.

entries.meaning: Slick has 3 distinct senses.
examples: The roads were slick with freezing rain.
The deck gets slicker than it looks after a shower.
That was a slick piece of editing.
The company put out a slick thirty-second ad.
A slick salesman talked them into the extended warranty.
His answers were too slick to believe.

senses.head: Smooth and slippery, usually because it is wet
examples: The roads were slick with freezing rain.
The deck gets slicker than it looks after a shower.

senses.head: Done smoothly and well
examples: That was a slick piece of editing.
The company put out a slick thirty-second ad.

senses.head: Smooth in a way that makes you suspicious
examples: A slick salesman talked them into the extended warranty.
His answers were too slick to believe.

entries.meaning: Sliding has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The kitchen has a sliding glass door to the deck.
Push the sliding panel to the left.
The van has a sliding side door.
The clinic charges on a sliding scale based on income.
Daycare fees follow a sliding scale.

senses.head: That opens by sliding instead of swinging
examples: The kitchen has a sliding glass door to the deck.
Push the sliding panel to the left.
The van has a sliding side door.

senses.head: Changing with the circumstances, about a rate or a scale
examples: The clinic charges on a sliding scale based on income.
Daycare fees follow a sliding scale.

entries.meaning: Slight has 2 distinct senses.
examples: There's a slight delay on the eastbound train.
She has a slight accent.
I don't have the slightest idea where he went.
He is a slight man with quick movements.
She looked too slight to carry the pack.

senses.head: Very small in degree
examples: There's a slight delay on the eastbound train.
She has a slight accent.
I don't have the slightest idea where he went.

senses.head: Thin and delicate in build
examples: He is a slight man with quick movements.
She looked too slight to carry the pack.

entries.position: attributive only — a slight delay; the 'thin' sense also goes after a verb
entries.contrast: The superlative lives in two fixed phrases: not in the slightest (not at all) and the slightest idea. There is also a noun and a verb slight, meaning an insult.

entries.meaning: Slimy has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The rocks by the creek are slimy.
The lettuce at the bottom of the bag had gone slimy.
There's something slimy about that landlord.
He is the slimiest guy in the office.

senses.head: Covered with something wet, thick and unpleasant
examples: The rocks by the creek are slimy.
The lettuce at the bottom of the bag had gone slimy.

senses.head: Friendly in a false, unpleasant way
examples: There's something slimy about that landlord.
He is the slimiest guy in the office.

entries.meaning: Slippery has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The steps get slippery when it rains.
Wet leaves make the sidewalk slipperier than ice.
He is a slippery witness who changes his story.
'Fair' is a slippery word in this contract.

senses.head: Hard to stand on or hold, because it is smooth or wet
examples: The steps get slippery when it rains.
Wet leaves make the sidewalk slipperier than ice.

senses.head: Not to be trusted, and hard to pin down
examples: He is a slippery witness who changes his story.
'Fair' is a slippery word in this contract.

entries.comparison: -er/-est or more/most — slipperier, slipperiest; also more slippery, most slippery
entries.contrast: a slippery slope means one small step that leads to something much worse.

entries.meaning: Done carelessly, without attention to the details. ---
examples: The inspector called the wiring slipshod and dangerous.
Slipshod record-keeping cost the clinic its license.
This draft is more slipshod than anything he's turned in before.

entries.meaning: Going up or down at an angle instead of lying flat. ---
examples: The house sits on a gently sloping lawn.
Watch your head under the sloping ceiling.
The field is sloping, so the water runs to the road.
entries.comparison: not gradable — but gently sloping, steeply sloping

entries.meaning: Sloppy has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The report was full of sloppy math.
Their defense got sloppier in the fourth quarter.
He came to dinner in a sloppy old sweatshirt.
Her handwriting is sloppy but readable.

senses.head: Done carelessly and full of mistakes
examples: The report was full of sloppy math.
Their defense got sloppier in the fourth quarter.

senses.head: Messy or loose-looking
examples: He came to dinner in a sloppy old sweatshirt.
Her handwriting is sloppy but readable.

entries.meaning: Drunk — informal. ---
examples: He got completely sloshed at the reception.
Half the wedding party was sloshed by nine.
You don't want to be sloshed when your boss shows up.
entries.form: -ed from slosh, the sound of liquid moving around
entries.contrast: Slang, and slightly old-fashioned but still understood. It goes after a verb only — never a sloshed man.

entries.meaning: Lazy, unwilling to work or move. ---
examples: He wrote about a slothful nephew who never left the couch.
Two weeks of vacation left me slothful.
The sermon called idleness the most slothful kind of sin.
entries.contrast: Formal and a little old-fashioned — everyday English says lazy. Sloth is also one of the seven deadly sins, and the name of the animal.

entries.meaning: Of or from Slovakia. ---
examples: He plays for a Slovakian hockey club.
We tried a Slovakian dumpling dish at the festival.
Her mother is Slovakian.
entries.contrast: Slovak is the shorter adjective and the name of the language and the people; Slovakian usually means 'of the country'. Slovakia is not Slovenia.

entries.meaning: Of or from Slovenia. ---
examples: The Slovenian Alps are full of small ski towns.
She translates Slovenian poetry.
Both coaches are Slovenian.
entries.contrast: Slovenia borders Italy and Austria; Slovakia is farther east. The short form Slovene is also used for the language.

entries.meaning: Messy and careless about how you look or work. ---
examples: The sergeant called his uniform slovenly.
She has slovenly habits in the kitchen.
His desk is the most slovenly one on the floor.
entries.contrast: Despite the -ly, this is an adjective, not an adverb. It has nothing to do with Slovenian.

entries.meaning: Slow has 4 distinct senses.
examples: Traffic was slow the whole way home.
She's the slowest runner on the team, and she still finished.
Recovery after the surgery was slow.
He was slow to answer my email.
Tuesday nights are slow at the restaurant.
It's been a slow month for sales.
The kitchen clock is five minutes slow.
My watch runs slow in the cold.

senses.head: Not moving quickly
examples: Traffic was slow the whole way home.
She's the slowest runner on the team, and she still finished.

senses.head: Taking a long time to happen or to get done
examples: Recovery after the surgery was slow.
He was slow to answer my email.

senses.head: With little business or activity
examples: Tuesday nights are slow at the restaurant.
It's been a slow month for sales.

senses.head: Of a clock or watch: showing a time earlier than the real one
examples: The kitchen clock is five minutes slow.
My watch runs slow in the cold.

entries.contrast: The adverb is slowly: drive slowly. Drive slow and go slow are heard in speech and on signs, but write slowly.

entries.meaning: Slow-moving has 2 distinct senses.
examples: A slow-moving storm is sitting over the valley.
We were stuck behind a slow-moving tractor.
The store marked down its slow-moving inventory.
It is a slow-moving case that has been in court for years.

senses.head: Moving slowly
examples: A slow-moving storm is sitting over the valley.
We were stuck behind a slow-moving tractor.

senses.head: Going forward or selling slowly
examples: The store marked down its slow-moving inventory.
It is a slow-moving case that has been in court for years.

entries.meaning: Slow to understand things. ---
examples: The play makes the sheriff look slow-witted.
I felt slow-witted after three hours of jet lag.
He writes the villain as cruel and the henchman as slow-witted.
entries.contrast: An insult — use it about a character in a book, not about a person you know.

entries.meaning: Sluggish has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The engine is sluggish on cold mornings.
I feel sluggish if I skip breakfast.
Home sales have been sluggish all spring.
The economy looks more sluggish than it did in January.

senses.head: Moving or working more slowly than it should
examples: The engine is sluggish on cold mornings.
I feel sluggish if I skip breakfast.

senses.head: With little growth or activity, about business
examples: Home sales have been sluggish all spring.
The economy looks more sluggish than it did in January.

entries.meaning: Of speech: with the words running together and hard to make out. ---
examples: His speech was slurred and the nurse called the doctor.
She left a slurred message at two in the morning.
Slurred words can be a sign of a stroke.

entries.meaning: Covered with or made of half-melted snow. ---
examples: The sidewalks were gray and slushy.
Wear boots — the driveway is slushy.
The roads get slushier once the plows come through.

entries.meaning: Small has 3 distinct senses.
examples: They live in a small apartment near the park.
Do you have this shirt in a smaller size?
She has two small children at home.
I remember that song from when I was small.
It's a small problem — we can fix it today.
That is a small price to pay for a quiet street.

senses.head: Not big in size or amount
examples: They live in a small apartment near the park.
Do you have this shirt in a smaller size?

senses.head: Young
examples: She has two small children at home.
I remember that song from when I was small.

senses.head: Not important
examples: It's a small problem — we can fix it today.
That is a small price to pay for a quiet street.

entries.contrast: small is a plain measurement; little often adds feeling (a little cabin sounds fond). Use small after how: How small is it?

entries.meaning: Of a company whose total stock value is small. ---
examples: He put part of his savings in a small-cap fund.
Small-cap stocks swing more than the big names.
The index tracks about two thousand small-cap companies.
entries.contrast: A finance word: it describes the size of the company, not the price of the share.

entries.meaning: Interested only in small things, and unwilling to accept other people's ideas. ---
examples: It was a small-minded rule about who could park where.
He left town to get away from small-minded gossip.
The longer the argument went on, the more small-minded both sides sounded.

entries.meaning: Done at a limited size, not across a whole country or industry. ---
examples: They started with a small-scale pilot in two schools.
Small-scale farmers can't compete on price.
For now the project is deliberately small-scale.

entries.meaning: Working on a small, unimportant level — usually said with a shrug. ---
examples: He was a small-time dealer who got caught in a big case.
They started as a small-time operation out of a garage.
She is tired of small-time clients and the fees that come with them.

entries.meaning: Fairly small. ---
examples: It's a smallish town, maybe nine thousand people.
He ordered a smallish coffee and sat by the window.
The yard is smallish but the house is bright.
entries.contrast: The -ish softens the word: smallish means fairly small, and avoids sounding too definite.

entries.meaning: Polite and flattering in a way that feels false and unpleasant. ---
examples: The host has a smarmy way of complimenting people.
He sent a smarmy thank-you note to the whole board.
That ad is the smarmiest thing on television.

entries.meaning: Smart has 3 distinct senses.
examples: She's the smartest person in the room and she knows it.
That was a smart decision.
We put in a smart thermostat last winter.
The building runs on smart lighting that shuts itself off.
He looked smart in a navy blazer.
The restaurant asks for smart casual dress.

senses.head: Intelligent, quick to understand
examples: She's the smartest person in the room and she knows it.
That was a smart decision.

senses.head: Of a machine: controlled by a computer and able to react on its own
examples: We put in a smart thermostat last winter.
The building runs on smart lighting that shuts itself off.

senses.head: Neat and stylish in appearance
examples: He looked smart in a navy blazer.
The restaurant asks for smart casual dress.

entries.contrast: In American English the first meaning is intelligent; in Britain smart usually means well-dressed. The technology sense is not gradable — a thermostat is smart or it isn't.

entries.meaning: Smashed has 2 distinct senses.
examples: A smashed headlight lay in the middle of the road.
The package arrived with everything inside smashed.
He swept up the smashed glass before the kids came in.
They got totally smashed at the wedding.
Half the crew was smashed by ten o'clock.

senses.head: Broken into pieces by a blow or a fall
examples: A smashed headlight lay in the middle of the road.
The package arrived with everything inside smashed.
He swept up the smashed glass before the kids came in.

senses.head: Very drunk (informal)
examples: They got totally smashed at the wedding.
Half the crew was smashed by ten o'clock.

entries.meaning: Wonderful; very successful. ---
examples: The fundraiser was a smashing success.
Her first show got smashing reviews.
They threw a smashing party for his retirement.
entries.contrast: In American English smashing survives mostly in the fixed phrase a smashing success; used on its own for "great", it still sounds British.

entries.meaning: With a smile on the face. ---
examples: A smiling clerk waved us to the front of the line.
The wall was covered with smiling faces.
He gave me a smiling nod and kept walking.
entries.contrast: Before a noun it is an adjective (a smiling face); after be it is normally the verb: She was smiling at me.

entries.meaning: Suddenly and completely in love with someone, or charmed by something. ---
examples: He was completely smitten with his new neighbor.
She's smitten — she talks about him all day.
They were smitten by the little house the moment they walked in.

entries.meaning: Full of smog — dirty, hazy city air. ---
examples: It was a hot, smoggy afternoon in the valley.
The air downtown is smoggier than out by the coast.
We couldn't see the mountains through the smoggy haze.

entries.meaning: Full of smoke. ---
examples: They argued for hours in a smoke-filled back room.
Firefighters crawled down the smoke-filled hallway.
The deal was made in smoke-filled rooms long before the vote.

entries.meaning: Where smoking is not allowed. ---
examples: The whole campus has been smoke-free since 2010.
We booked a smoke-free room on the third floor.
City buses and train platforms are smoke-free.

entries.meaning: Smoked has 2 distinct senses.
examples: We had bagels with smoked salmon.
He ordered the smoked turkey sandwich.
The store sells smoked ham by the pound.
The car came with smoked windows.
She wore glasses with smoked lenses.

senses.head: Cured and flavored by hanging in smoke
examples: We had bagels with smoked salmon.
He ordered the smoked turkey sandwich.
The store sells smoked ham by the pound.

senses.head: Made dark, so that you cannot see through it clearly
examples: The car came with smoked windows.
She wore glasses with smoked lenses.

entries.meaning: Producing no smoke. ---
examples: The stove burns smokeless fuel.
Smokeless tobacco is banned in the stadium.
They switched to a smokeless fire pit.

entries.meaning: Giving off smoke. ---
examples: Firefighters stood in front of the smoking ruins.
A smoking pan filled the kitchen with a burnt smell.
The email was the smoking gun the lawyers needed.
entries.contrast: In a smoking area or the smoking section, smoking is a noun (the activity), not this adjective.

entries.meaning: Smoky has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The bar was dark and smoky.
A smoky haze hung over the whole valley.
The cheese has a rich, smoky flavor.
This whiskey is smokier than the one we tried last time.

senses.head: Full of smoke, or clouded by it
examples: The bar was dark and smoky.
A smoky haze hung over the whole valley.

senses.head: Tasting or smelling of smoke
examples: The cheese has a rich, smoky flavor.
This whiskey is smokier than the one we tried last time.

entries.contrast: American spelling is smoky, without the e.

entries.meaning: Smoldering has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Firefighters watered down the smoldering debris.
A smoldering cigarette had started the whole thing.
There was a smoldering resentment between the two brothers.
She gave him a smoldering look across the table.

senses.head: Burning slowly, with smoke but no flame
examples: Firefighters watered down the smoldering debris.
A smoldering cigarette had started the whole thing.

senses.head: Strong but held in, of a feeling
examples: There was a smoldering resentment between the two brothers.
She gave him a smoldering look across the table.

entries.contrast: American spelling smoldering; British smouldering.

entries.meaning: Smooth has 3 distinct senses.
examples: The stones by the river are worn smooth.
Beat the sauce until it's completely smooth.
She ran her hand over the smooth tabletop.
We had a smooth flight to Denver.
The move to the new system was smoother than anyone expected.
He's a smooth talker — don't sign anything today.
The salesman was a little too smooth for my taste.

senses.head: Flat and even to the touch, with no bumps or lumps
examples: The stones by the river are worn smooth.
Beat the sauce until it's completely smooth.
She ran her hand over the smooth tabletop.

senses.head: Going along without jolts or problems
examples: We had a smooth flight to Denver.
The move to the new system was smoother than anyone expected.

senses.head: Charming and confident in a way you do not quite trust, of a person
examples: He's a smooth talker — don't sign anything today.
The salesman was a little too smooth for my taste.

entries.meaning: So heavy or so constant that you feel you cannot breathe. ---
examples: The smothering heat made it hard to sleep.
She moved out to get away from her mother's smothering attention.
A smothering blanket of smoke settled over the town.

entries.meaning: Too pleased with yourself, in a way that annoys other people. ---
examples: He had a smug look on his face after the test.
Nobody likes a smug winner.
She got smugger with every point she scored.

entries.meaning: Brought into or out of a country secretly and illegally. ---
examples: Police found smuggled cigarettes in the back of the truck.
The museum returned several smuggled artifacts.
Smuggled goods are seized at the border every day.

entries.meaning: Snappy has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The movie has snappy dialogue and a short runtime.
Give me a snappier headline for the front page.
He showed up in a snappy blue suit.
That's a snappy pair of shoes.

senses.head: Quick, short and lively
examples: The movie has snappy dialogue and a short runtime.
Give me a snappier headline for the front page.

senses.head: Stylish and sharp-looking (informal)
examples: He showed up in a snappy blue suit.
That's a snappy pair of shoes.

entries.contrast: Make it snappy means "hurry up".

entries.meaning: Stylish and eye-catching, often a little flashy (informal). ---
examples: He drove up in a snazzy red convertible.
That's a snazzy jacket — is it new?
Their new website looks snazzier than ours.

entries.meaning: Done without warning, before anyone can react. ---
examples: It was a sneak attack on a sleeping base.
The studio held a sneak preview on Thursday night.
She gave us a sneak peek at the new design.
entries.contrast: sneak is also a noun and a verb; as an adjective it lives only in fixed pairs — a sneak attack, a sneak preview, a sneak peek.

entries.meaning: Felt quietly and kept to yourself. ---
examples: I have a sneaking suspicion that he already knows.
She had a sneaking admiration for her rival.
There was a sneaking feeling that the deal was too good.
entries.contrast: Almost always with suspicion, feeling or admiration: a quiet thought you do not say out loud.

entries.meaning: Acting in secret to get what you want, in a way people find dishonest. ---
examples: That was a sneaky way to get out of paying.
He's sneakier than his brother ever was.
Don't be sneaky about it — just ask her.

entries.meaning: Insulting in an indirect, sly way. ---
examples: He made a snide remark about her accent.
The review was full of snide comments.
Her tone was snide rather than funny.

entries.meaning: Looking down on people you think have less money, taste or education. ---
examples: The staff was polite but a little snobbish.
He has a snobbish attitude about wine.
Don't be snobbish about where other people shop.

entries.meaning: Acting superior to other people (informal). ---
examples: The restaurant felt snobby the minute we walked in.
Her new friends are snobbier than she is.
He's not snobby about music at all.
entries.contrast: snobby is the casual spoken word; snobbish is the one you write.

entries.meaning: Too interested in other people's private business (informal). ---
examples: Our snoopy neighbor watches every car on the street.
Don't be snoopy about other people's mail.
She got snoopier after she retired.
entries.русский: любопытный, сующий нос в чужие дела

entries.meaning: Treating other people as beneath you (informal). ---
examples: The hostess gave us a snooty look.
It's a snooty little shop on the corner.
The service got snootier the longer we waited.

entries.meaning: Young and annoyingly sure of himself (informal, insulting). ---
examples: Some snot-nosed kid told me I was parked wrong.
He was a snot-nosed rookie back then.
I'm not taking orders from a snot-nosed intern.
entries.contrast: Rude and dismissive — fine in speech between friends, never in writing about a real person.

entries.meaning: Snotty has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Don't get snotty with me.
She sent a snotty email to the whole team.
His tone got snottier with every question.
Wipe that snotty nose before we go in.
The toddler handed me a snotty tissue.

senses.head: Rude and superior (informal)
examples: Don't get snotty with me.
She sent a snotty email to the whole team.
His tone got snottier with every question.

senses.head: Covered with mucus from the nose
examples: Wipe that snotty nose before we go in.
The toddler handed me a snotty tissue.

entries.meaning: With snow on top, of a mountain. ---
examples: Snow-capped peaks rose behind the town.
We could see the snow-capped mountains from the hotel.
The postcard showed a snow-capped volcano.

entries.meaning: With snow lying all over it. ---
examples: We drove slowly down the snow-covered road.
The snow-covered fields went on for miles.
By morning every car on the block was snow-covered.

entries.meaning: Pure white. ---
examples: He had a snow-white beard.
The tablecloth was snow-white.
She wore a snow-white dress to the ceremony.
entries.form: compound — noun + adjective, "as white as snow"

entries.meaning: Unable to travel or get out because of heavy snow. ---
examples: We were snowbound at the cabin for three days.
A snowbound village waited all week for the plows.
The storm left hundreds of travelers snowbound at the airport.

entries.meaning: Snowy has 2 distinct senses.
examples: It was a cold, snowy January.
This is the snowiest winter in twenty years.
He stroked his snowy beard.
Snowy sheets hung on the line behind the house.

senses.head: With a lot of snow
examples: It was a cold, snowy January.
This is the snowiest winter in twenty years.

senses.head: White like snow
examples: He stroked his snowy beard.
Snowy sheets hung on the line behind the house.

entries.meaning: Snub-nosed has 2 distinct senses.
examples: A snub-nosed boy answered the door.
She has her father's snub-nosed face.
He carried a snub-nosed revolver.
The detective's snub-nosed .38 lay on the desk.

senses.head: With a short nose that turns up at the end
examples: A snub-nosed boy answered the door.
She has her father's snub-nosed face.

senses.head: With a very short barrel, of a gun
examples: He carried a snub-nosed revolver.
The detective's snub-nosed .38 lay on the desk.

entries.meaning: Snug has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The cabin was tiny but snug.
The kids were snug under two blankets.
The jacket is a little snug across the shoulders.
These boots feel snugger than the last pair.

senses.head: Warm, small and comfortable
examples: The cabin was tiny but snug.
The kids were snug under two blankets.

senses.head: Fitting closely, sometimes a little too closely
examples: The jacket is a little snug across the shoulders.
These boots feel snugger than the last pair.

entries.meaning: Neither good nor bad; average (informal). ---
examples: The food was so-so, but the view was great.
He got so-so grades his first semester.
How was the movie? So-so.
entries.contrast: Also used as an adverb (He plays so-so), and always written with a hyphen.

entries.meaning: Full of soap, or covered with it. ---
examples: Wash the pan in hot soapy water.
The floor was still soapy and slippery.
This water is soapier than it needs to be.

entries.meaning: Soaring has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Soaring rents have pushed families out of the city.
The airline blamed soaring fuel costs.
The church has a soaring ceiling.
She held the soaring high note at the end of the song.

senses.head: Rising fast, of prices or numbers
examples: Soaring rents have pushed families out of the city.
The airline blamed soaring fuel costs.

senses.head: Rising very high into the air
examples: The church has a soaring ceiling.
She held the soaring high note at the end of the song.

entries.meaning: Sober has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He's been sober for six years.
Someone has to stay sober and drive.
She was perfectly sober when she said it.
It was a sober assessment of the damage.
The mood in the room was sober.

senses.head: Not drunk
examples: He's been sober for six years.
Someone has to stay sober and drive.
She was perfectly sober when she said it.

senses.head: Serious and unexcited
examples: It was a sober assessment of the damage.
The mood in the room was sober.

entries.meaning: Making you suddenly serious about how bad something is. ---
examples: The accident report makes for sobering reading.
It was a sobering reminder of how fast things change.
The numbers in the study are sobering.
entries.contrast: sobering is the thing that makes you think; a person who is not drunk is sober.

entries.meaning: Enjoying the company of other people. ---
examples: She's a sociable kid who makes friends anywhere.
He's not very sociable before his first coffee.
The dogs are sociable with strangers.
entries.contrast: sociable describes a person who enjoys company; social describes society or gatherings (a social event). You cannot say "a sociable problem".

entries.meaning: Social has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The city is facing serious social problems.
She studies social change in small towns.
We met at a social event at the club.
He has a busy social life.

senses.head: Having to do with society and how people live together
examples: The city is facing serious social problems.
She studies social change in small towns.

senses.head: Having to do with spending time with other people
examples: We met at a social event at the club.
He has a busy social life.

entries.position: attributive only — except the informal He's very social (= sociable)
entries.contrast: social is about society or about gatherings; a friendly person is sociable.

entries.meaning: Based on socialism — the idea that the state or the workers should own the main industries. ---
examples: The party ran on a socialist platform.
He studies socialist movements in postwar Europe.
Socialist governments came to power across the region.
entries.contrast: Also a noun: She is a socialist.

entries.meaning: Socialized has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Critics call the plan socialized medicine.
He argued against socialized health care for an hour.
The puppy is well socialized around children.
Kids who are poorly socialized struggle in big groups.

senses.head: Run and paid for by the government instead of private companies
examples: Critics call the plan socialized medicine.
He argued against socialized health care for an hour.

senses.head: Trained to behave well with others
examples: The puppy is well socialized around children.
Kids who are poorly socialized struggle in big groups.

entries.contrast: American spelling -ized; British -ised.

entries.meaning: Belonging to society as a whole. ---
examples: The report looks at the societal costs of long commutes.
Societal attitudes toward the issue have changed fast.
These are societal problems, not personal failings.
entries.contrast: societal is formal and means "of society as a whole"; everyday English says social.

entries.meaning: Having to do with both society and culture. ---
examples: The study takes a sociocultural approach to language learning.
Sociocultural factors shape what people eat.
They mapped the sociocultural history of the neighborhood.

entries.meaning: Having to do with both money and social position. ---
examples: Test scores track socioeconomic status closely.
The two neighborhoods differ in socioeconomic background.
The researchers controlled for socioeconomic factors.

entries.meaning: Having to do with the study of society. ---
examples: She published a sociological study of small-town churches.
From a sociological point of view, the change is enormous.
He teaches sociological theory to first-year students.

entries.meaning: Behaving with no conscience and no feeling for other people. ---
examples: The novel's villain is charming and sociopathic.
Experts described the behavior as sociopathic.
He shows sociopathic traits under pressure.

entries.meaning: Teaching by asking question after question, in the manner of Socrates. ---
examples: Law schools still teach by the Socratic method.
The class was run as a Socratic dialogue.
He answered every question with another one, in true Socratic style.

entries.meaning: Soaked through with water, and heavy because of it. ---
examples: We walked the last mile in sodden shoes.
The field was sodden after three days of rain.
He pulled off his sodden coat and hung it by the door.

entries.meaning: Soft has 4 distinct senses.
examples: The mattress is too soft for my back.
Leave the butter out until it's soft.
That blanket is the softest thing she owns.
The baby has soft pink skin.
She answered in a soft voice.
The music was soft enough to talk over.
The judge is soft on first offenders.
Don't be too soft with them or nothing gets done.

senses.head: Easy to press or bend; not hard
examples: The mattress is too soft for my back.
Leave the butter out until it's soft.

senses.head: Smooth and pleasant to touch
examples: That blanket is the softest thing she owns.
The baby has soft pink skin.

senses.head: Quiet; not loud
examples: She answered in a soft voice.
The music was soft enough to talk over.

senses.head: Gentle; not strict enough
examples: The judge is soft on first offenders.
Don't be too soft with them or nothing gets done.

entries.takes: on + noun in the sense "not strict": soft on crime

entries.meaning: Boiled only a few minutes, so the yolk is still runny. ---
examples: He had a soft-boiled egg and toast.
I like my eggs soft-boiled.
The diner serves soft-boiled eggs all day.

entries.meaning: Speaking in a quiet, gentle voice. ---
examples: He's a soft-spoken man who never interrupts.
She was soft-spoken but completely firm.
Our soft-spoken coach has never yelled at anyone.

entries.meaning: Wet and limp, in a way that spoils food or ground. ---
examples: Nobody wants soggy fries.
The cereal went soggy in the milk.
The bottom of the pie was even soggier the next day.

entries.meaning: Made dirty by use. ---
examples: Put the soiled towels in the blue bin.
The nurse changed the soiled sheets.
His shirt was soiled at the collar.
entries.contrast: soiled is the polite, slightly formal word for dirty — hospitals and hotels say soiled linens, not "dirty sheets".

entries.meaning: Solar has 2 distinct senses.
examples: A solar eclipse will be visible from the coast.
There are eight planets in the solar system.
They put solar panels on the roof last spring.
The whole house runs on solar power.

senses.head: Of or from the sun
examples: A solar eclipse will be visible from the coast.
There are eight planets in the solar system.

senses.head: Using the sun's energy
examples: They put solar panels on the roof last spring.
The whole house runs on solar power.

entries.contrast: solar means "of the sun" as a scientific term; a bright day is sunny, never "solar".

entries.meaning: With every ticket already sold. ---
examples: They played to a sold-out arena.
The concert has been sold-out for weeks.
It's a sold-out crowd tonight.
entries.contrast: Hyphenated before a noun (a sold-out show), two separate words after the verb (The show sold out in an hour).

entries.meaning: Solemn has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The room went solemn when he stood up to speak.
She had a solemn look on her face all morning.
He made a solemn promise to pay it back.
The new officers took a solemn oath.

senses.head: Very serious, with no smiling
examples: The room went solemn when he stood up to speak.
She had a solemn look on her face all morning.

senses.head: Formal and binding
examples: He made a solemn promise to pay it back.
The new officers took a solemn oath.

entries.meaning: Showing careful, almost anxious concern for someone. ---
examples: The host was solicitous about our comfort all evening.
She is solicitous of her elderly father.
A solicitous waiter refilled every glass before it was empty.

entries.meaning: Solid has 4 distinct senses.
examples: The lake was frozen solid by January.
Water becomes solid at 32 degrees.
It's an old table, but it's solid.
They built a solid stone wall around the yard.
The ring is solid gold.
The door is solid wood, not veneer.
He gave a solid performance in the second half.
The case rests on solid evidence.

senses.head: Hard and keeping its shape; not liquid or gas
examples: The lake was frozen solid by January.
Water becomes solid at 32 degrees.

senses.head: Strongly built and not likely to break
examples: It's an old table, but it's solid.
They built a solid stone wall around the yard.

senses.head: Made of one material all the way through
examples: The ring is solid gold.
The door is solid wood, not veneer.

senses.head: Dependable and good, without being brilliant
examples: He gave a solid performance in the second half.
The case rests on solid evidence.

entries.contrast: three solid hours means "three hours without a break" — a fourth, time meaning.

entries.meaning: All one color, with no pattern. ---
examples: Wear a solid-colored shirt for the photo.
She prefers solid-colored dresses to prints.
The uniform has to be solid-colored.
entries.contrast: American spelling -colored; British -coloured.

entries.meaning: Built from solid electronic parts, with nothing moving inside. ---
examples: The laptop has a solid-state drive.
Solid-state amplifiers replaced the old tube ones.
It's a solid-state sensor with no moving parts.

entries.meaning: Solitary has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He took a solitary walk along the beach.
Tigers are solitary animals.
Not a solitary word was said about the money.
A solitary streetlight lit the whole block.

senses.head: Alone, or done alone
examples: He took a solitary walk along the beach.
Tigers are solitary animals.

senses.head: Only one, and no more
examples: Not a solitary word was said about the money.
A solitary streetlight lit the whole block.

entries.position: both — the "only one" sense goes before a noun
entries.contrast: solitary means alone by habit or by choice; lonely means sad because you are alone. Russian одинокий covers both.

entries.meaning: Done by one person alone. ---
examples: She released her first solo album in March.
He made a solo flight across the Atlantic.
The climb was solo, with no support team.
entries.contrast: Also an adverb (She flew solo) and a noun (a piano solo).

entries.meaning: Able to dissolve in a liquid. ---
examples: Salt is soluble in water.
The tablets come in a soluble form.
Vitamin D is fat-soluble, so take it with a meal.

entries.meaning: Able to be solved. ---
examples: The puzzle is solvable in under a minute.
These are solvable problems if we start now.
He treats every crisis as solvable.

entries.meaning: Having enough money to pay what you owe. ---
examples: The company is barely solvent.
Two good quarters kept the firm solvent.
A bank has to stay solvent to keep its license.
entries.contrast: Also a noun: a solvent is a liquid that dissolves other things.

entries.meaning: From Somalia, or having to do with Somalia and its people. ---
examples: She grew up in a Somali neighborhood in Minneapolis.
The restaurant serves Somali food.
Many of the students in the class are Somali.
entries.contrast: Also a noun — a Somali (a person) and Somali (the language). The country is Somalia.

entries.meaning: Somber has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The mood at the meeting was somber.
She read the news in a somber voice.
He wore a somber gray suit to the service.
The room is painted in somber browns.

senses.head: Sad and serious in mood
examples: The mood at the meeting was somber.
She read the news in a somber voice.

senses.head: Dark and dull in color
examples: He wore a somber gray suit to the service.
The room is painted in somber browns.

entries.contrast: American spelling somber; British sombre.

entries.meaning: Having to do with sound or the speed of sound. ---
examples: The jet made a sonic boom over the coast.
The band is known for its sonic experiments.
Engineers measured the sonic range of the hall.

entries.meaning: Deep, full and pleasant in sound. ---
examples: He has a deep, sonorous voice.
The bells were sonorous in the empty square.
She read the poem in sonorous tones.

entries.meaning: Making pain or worry easier to bear. ---
examples: Her voice on the phone was soothing.
He put on some soothing music and lay down.
The cream is soothing on a sunburn.

entries.meaning: Covered or blackened with soot. ---
examples: He wiped his sooty hands on a rag.
The wall above the stove was sooty.
The chimney got sootier every winter.

entries.meaning: Of the second year of high school or college, or second in a series. ---
examples: She's taking chemistry her sophomore year.
The band's sophomore album flopped.
He had a sophomore slump after a great rookie season.
entries.contrast: Also a noun — a sophomore is a second-year student. As an adjective it means "second in a series": a sophomore album.

entries.meaning: Making you sleepy. ---
examples: The lecture had a soporific effect on the whole class.
He read the list in a soporific monotone.
The heat in that room is soporific.

entries.meaning: Morally dirty — involving lies, greed or shabby behavior. ---
examples: The paper printed every sordid detail.
It's a sordid story of money and lies.
The whole business was more sordid than anyone expected.

entries.meaning: Sore has 2 distinct senses.
examples: I woke up with a sore throat.
My legs were sorer the day after the hike.
Her shoulder is still sore from the fall.
He's still sore about losing the bet.
Don't be a sore loser.

senses.head: Painful, especially from use or infection
examples: I woke up with a sore throat.
My legs were sorer the day after the hike.
Her shoulder is still sore from the fall.

senses.head: Annoyed and hurt about something (informal)
examples: He's still sore about losing the bet.
Don't be a sore loser.

entries.contrast: a sore point is a subject that upsets someone. Do not confuse sore (hurting) with sorry.

entries.meaning: Full of deep sadness, or showing it. ---
examples: She gave me a sorrowful look and said nothing.
The song is slow and sorrowful.
His face was sorrowful but calm.
entries.contrast: sorrowful is literary; everyday American English says sad.

entries.meaning: Wanted by many people, and therefore hard to get. ---
examples: He's the most sought-after photographer in town.
These tickets are highly sought-after.
It's a sought-after address on the north side.
entries.position: both — often after much or most
entries.form: compound — past participle of seek + after

entries.meaning: Full of deep feeling that you can hear or see. ---
examples: She sang a soulful version of the old hymn.
The dog gave him a soulful look.
His playing is soulful and unhurried.

entries.meaning: With no warmth or feeling in it. ---
examples: They tore down the old theater and put up a soulless office block.
The remake is technically perfect and completely soulless.
It's soulless work, but it pays the rent.

entries.meaning: Sound has 3 distinct senses.
examples: The inspector said the roof is sound.
The kids came back safe and sound.
That's sound advice.
His plan is sounder than mine.
She's a sound sleeper — the storm never woke her.
He fell into a sound sleep on the couch.

senses.head: In good condition; not damaged or ill
examples: The inspector said the roof is sound.
The kids came back safe and sound.

senses.head: Sensible and based on good reasoning
examples: That's sound advice.
His plan is sounder than mine.

senses.head: Deep and unbroken, of sleep
examples: She's a sound sleeper — the storm never woke her.
He fell into a sound sleep on the couch.

entries.contrast: Also a noun (a loud sound) and a verb (That sounds good). safe and sound is a fixed phrase.

entries.meaning: Deeply asleep and hard to wake. ---
examples: The baby was sound asleep by seven.
Both kids were sound asleep in the back seat.
He's sound asleep — don't wake him up.
entries.form: fixed phrase — sound here is an old adverb meaning "deeply"
entries.contrast: Only after a verb. Never "a sound asleep baby" — before a noun use a sleeping baby.

entries.meaning: Built so that sound cannot pass through. ---
examples: The studio is completely soundproof.
They put in soundproof windows facing the highway.
It's not a soundproof room, so keep your voice down.
entries.form: compound — sound + -proof, "that sound cannot get through"

entries.meaning: Soupy has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The risotto came out soupy.
Add more rice if it still looks soupy.
We drove through soupy fog all morning.
The August air was soupier than ever.

senses.head: Too thin and watery, of food
examples: The risotto came out soupy.
Add more rice if it still looks soupy.

senses.head: Thick and heavy, of fog or air
examples: We drove through soupy fog all morning.
The August air was soupier than ever.

entries.meaning: Sour has 3 distinct senses.
examples: These cherries are too sour to eat raw.
She likes sour candy.
The milk has gone sour.
There was a sour smell in the fridge.
He gave me a sour look.
Her mood got sourer as the day went on.

senses.head: Sharp in taste, like a lemon
examples: These cherries are too sour to eat raw.
She likes sour candy.

senses.head: Spoiled, of milk or cream
examples: The milk has gone sour.
There was a sour smell in the fridge.

senses.head: Unfriendly and bad-tempered
examples: He gave me a sour look.
Her mood got sourer as the day went on.

entries.contrast: go sour is also used of plans and relationships: The deal went sour.

entries.meaning: Soured has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Soured relations between the two countries dragged on for years.
He left the company and a soured friendship behind him.
A carton of soured milk sat on the counter.
You can still bake with slightly soured milk.

senses.head: Turned unfriendly or bitter, of a relationship or mood
examples: Soured relations between the two countries dragged on for years.
He left the company and a soured friendship behind him.

senses.head: Turned sour, of milk or cream
examples: A carton of soured milk sat on the counter.
You can still bake with slightly soured milk.

entries.meaning: On or facing the south side. ---
examples: Their office is on the south side of the building.
A south wind brought warmer air.
We parked by the south entrance.
entries.contrast: Also a noun (the South) and an adverb (drive south). For a region or its people use southern: southern cooking, not "south cooking".

entries.meaning: From South Africa, or having to do with it. ---
examples: He's a South African journalist based in London.
We tried a South African wine with dinner.
Two of the players are South African.
entries.contrast: Also a noun (a South African). Both words are capitalized, with no hyphen.

entries.meaning: From South America, or having to do with it. ---
examples: The bird is native to South American rainforests.
She writes about South American politics.
Most of the group is South American.
entries.contrast: Also a noun (a South American).

entries.meaning: From South Korea, or having to do with it. ---
examples: The company is South Korean.
He drives a South Korean car.
South Korean films have won major prizes.
entries.contrast: Also a noun (a South Korean).

entries.meaning: Traveling toward the south. ---
examples: The southbound lanes are closed until noon.
We took the southbound train from Penn Station.
Most of the traffic this morning is southbound.

entries.meaning: In or facing the southeast. ---
examples: The storm hit the southeast corner of the state.
A southeast wind is pushing the smoke inland.
Their farm is in southeast Kansas.
entries.contrast: Also a noun and an adverb. For a whole region the usual adjective is southeastern.

entries.meaning: In or from the southeast part of a country or region. ---
examples: She grew up in southeastern Ohio.
The plant grows across the southeastern United States.
Southeastern Europe was hit hardest by the drought.

entries.meaning: From the south, or toward the south. ---
examples: A southerly wind kept the night warm.
We took a more southerly route to avoid the snow.
The island is the most southerly point of the country.
entries.contrast: An -ly word that is an adjective, not an adverb. A southerly wind blows from the south, but a southerly course goes toward the south.

entries.meaning: Farthest to the south. ---
examples: Key West is the southernmost city in the continental United States.
They reached the southernmost tip of the island at dusk.
This is the southernmost vineyard in the state.
entries.comparison: not gradable — it is already a superlative

entries.meaning: In or facing the southwest. ---
examples: A southwest wind carried the smoke into town.
The house has a southwest exposure and gets sun all afternoon.
They drove through southwest Texas for two days.
entries.contrast: Also a noun and an adverb. For a whole region the usual adjective is southwestern.

entries.meaning: In or from the southwest part of a country or region. ---
examples: Southwestern cooking uses a lot of chiles.
The rain never reached the southwestern counties.
He moved to a small southwestern town for the dry air.

entries.meaning: Sovereign has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Ukraine is a sovereign state.
They demanded sovereign control of their own waters.
In a monarchy the king is sovereign.
Congress holds sovereign authority over the budget.

senses.head: Independent and governing itself, of a country
examples: Ukraine is a sovereign state.
They demanded sovereign control of their own waters.

senses.head: Holding the highest power
examples: In a monarchy the king is sovereign.
Congress holds sovereign authority over the budget.

entries.contrast: Also a noun — the sovereign is a king or queen.

entries.meaning: Belonging to the Soviet Union, the country that existed from 1922 to 1991. ---
examples: My grandfather grew up in a Soviet apartment block.
The museum has a large collection of Soviet posters.
Both sides signed the treaty during the Soviet era.
entries.contrast: Always capitalized. Soviet means 'of the USSR', which was more than Russia: a Soviet passport, but the Russian language.

entries.meaning: Not able to think clearly, as if your mind were somewhere else. ---
examples: I was spaced-out from the cold medicine.
He gave me a spaced-out look and said nothing.
After the night shift she felt completely spaced-out.

entries.meaning: Dreamy and not paying attention to what is going on. ---
examples: She's a little spacey before her first coffee.
He gets spacier when he hasn't slept.
He had a spacey grin and no idea where he was.
entries.contrast: Informal, and about a person's attention, not about space travel.

entries.meaning: Large inside, with plenty of room. ---
examples: The kitchen is bright and spacious.
They moved into a more spacious apartment last spring.
The hotel lobby was surprisingly spacious.

entries.meaning: Using Spanish as the main language. ---
examples: She works in a Spanish-speaking neighborhood.
The clinic needs two Spanish-speaking nurses.
Mexico is the largest Spanish-speaking country in the world.

entries.meaning: Spare has 3 distinct senses.
examples: There's a spare key under the mat.
Do you have a spare minute?
We put the guests in the spare room.
The room was spare: a bed, a chair, a lamp.
His prose is spare and fast.
The new design is more spare than the original.
He was tall and spare.
Years of running left her lean and spare.

senses.head: Extra, and kept in case you need it
examples: There's a spare key under the mat.
Do you have a spare minute?
We put the guests in the spare room.

senses.head: Plain and simple, with nothing added
examples: The room was spare: a bed, a chair, a lamp.
His prose is spare and fast.
The new design is more spare than the original.

senses.head: Thin, with no extra flesh
examples: He was tall and spare.
Years of running left her lean and spare.

entries.contrast: Before a noun spare usually means 'extra' (a spare tire); after a verb it more often means 'plain' or 'lean' (the room was spare).

entries.meaning: Using or giving only a little of something. ---
examples: She is sparing with praise.
Be sparing with the salt.
Sparing use of color makes the room feel calm.
entries.takes: with or of + noun; in + noun
entries.contrast: You will meet the adverb far more often: use it sparingly.

entries.meaning: Sparkling has 3 distinct senses.
examples: The lake was covered with sparkling ice.
She wore a sparkling silver dress.
His eyes were bright and sparkling.
Would you like still or sparkling water?
We opened a bottle of sparkling wine.
She gave a sparkling performance as Juliet.
The dinner was full of sparkling conversation.

senses.head: Shining with many small points of light
examples: The lake was covered with sparkling ice.
She wore a sparkling silver dress.
His eyes were bright and sparkling.

senses.head: With bubbles in it, said of a drink
examples: Would you like still or sparkling water?
We opened a bottle of sparkling wine.

senses.head: Lively and brilliant, said of talk or a performance
examples: She gave a sparkling performance as Juliet.
The dinner was full of sparkling conversation.

entries.meaning: Covered with small shiny points that catch the light. ---
examples: She picked out a sparkly pair of shoes.
The card is covered in sparkly stars.
His new jacket is a little too sparkly for the office.

entries.meaning: Small in number and spread thinly over a wide area. ---
examples: The audience was sparse on Monday night.
Sparse pine trees dotted the hillside.
News about the crash is even sparser today than yesterday.

entries.meaning: Very plain and simple, with no comfort at all. ---
examples: The dorm rooms are spartan but clean.
He keeps a spartan diet of rice and fish.
Her office is spartan: a desk, a chair, no pictures.
entries.form: from Sparta, the ancient Greek city known for hard living
entries.contrast: Lowercase when it means plain and hard; capital Spartan means 'from ancient Sparta'.
