entries.meaning: Having to do with space and with where things sit in it. ---
examples: Kids build spatial skills by playing with blocks.
She has excellent spatial awareness behind the wheel.
The test includes a spatial reasoning section.

entries.meaning: Operated on so that a female animal cannot have young. ---
examples: All of our cats are spayed.
The shelter adopts out only spayed females.
She was already spayed when we got her.
entries.contrast: spayed is only for females; a male animal is neutered.

entries.meaning: Special has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Today is a special day for our family.
You don't need anything special, just a pen.
That song is more special to me than any other.
He gets special treatment because of his last name.
The school has a special program for new arrivals.

senses.head: Not ordinary; better or more important than usual
examples: Today is a special day for our family.
You don't need anything special, just a pen.
That song is more special to me than any other.

senses.head: Meant for one particular purpose or group
examples: He gets special treatment because of his last name.
The school has a special program for new arrivals.

entries.takes: to + person, for the 'important to someone' sense

entries.meaning: Made or trained for one narrow job or subject. ---
examples: The surgery needs specialized equipment.
She has a specialized knowledge of tax law.
The work is more specialized than the title suggests.
entries.contrast: American spelling is specialized; British writing has specialised.

entries.meaning: Specific has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Can you be more specific about the time?
She left me specific instructions.
I need a specific date, not 'sometime in May'.
This rule is specific to New York.
The disease is specific to one breed of dog.

senses.head: Exact and clearly stated, not general
examples: Can you be more specific about the time?
She left me specific instructions.
I need a specific date, not 'sometime in May'.

senses.head: Belonging to one thing or group and to nothing else
examples: This rule is specific to New York.
The disease is specific to one breed of dog.

entries.takes: to + noun, for the 'belonging to one thing only' sense

entries.meaning: Named or stated exactly, usually in writing. ---
examples: Return the form by the specified date.
Use only the specified replacement parts.
Payment is due within the specified period.
entries.contrast: specified names the thing that was stated; specific describes how exact you are being.

entries.meaning: Looking correct or reasonable at first, but actually false. ---
examples: That's a specious argument.
The ad makes a specious claim about weight loss.
His reasoning sounds good, but it is specious.

entries.meaning: Covered with small spots of another color. ---
examples: The hen lays small brown speckled eggs.
His beard is speckled with gray.
The countertop is speckled black and white.

entries.meaning: Speculative has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The report is speculative at this point.
That's a speculative explanation, nothing more.
Her second theory is even more speculative than the first.
He made a speculative bet on oil.
Speculative buying pushed housing prices up.

senses.head: Based on guessing rather than on facts
examples: The report is speculative at this point.
That's a speculative explanation, nothing more.
Her second theory is even more speculative than the first.

senses.head: Done in the hope of a profit, with a real risk of losing the money
examples: He made a speculative bet on oil.
Speculative buying pushed housing prices up.

entries.meaning: So surprised, angry or moved that you cannot say anything. ---
examples: Her gift left me speechless.
He stood there speechless with rage.
I was speechless when they called my name.
entries.position: both — nearly always after a verb

entries.meaning: Happening or moving fast. ---
examples: We wish you a speedy recovery.
Their reply was speedier than I expected.
He's a speedy little dog for his size.

entries.meaning: So interesting that you cannot look away or stop listening. ---
examples: The last twenty minutes of the movie are spellbinding.
She told a spellbinding story about her escape.
His voice on the radio was spellbinding.
entries.contrast: spellbinding is the thing that holds you; spellbound is how you feel.

entries.meaning: So interested that you cannot move or look away, as if under a spell. ---
examples: The children sat spellbound through the whole story.
The audience was spellbound.
He held us spellbound for an hour.
entries.contrast: The listener is spellbound; the story is spellbinding.

entries.meaning: Spending money carelessly and far too fast. ---
examples: His spendthrift habits ruined the business.
The paper attacked the mayor's spendthrift budget.
She married a charming spendthrift musician.
entries.contrast: Also a noun: he's a spendthrift. The opposite quality is thrifty, not spendthrifty.

entries.meaning: Spent has 2 distinct senses.
examples: A pile of spent shells lay in the grass.
Spent fuel is stored on site.
By the last mile I was spent.
The team looked spent after two overtimes.

senses.head: Already used up, with nothing left in it
examples: A pile of spent shells lay in the grass.
Spent fuel is stored on site.

senses.head: Completely out of energy
examples: By the last mile I was spent.
The team looked spent after two overtimes.

entries.contrast: Also the past form of spend: we spent the whole day there.

entries.meaning: Shaped like a ball. ---
examples: The seeds are small and spherical.
The earth is not perfectly spherical.
They hung a spherical paper lamp over the table.

entries.meaning: Perfectly clean and tidy. ---
examples: The kitchen was spick-and-span when we arrived.
She keeps the shop spick-and-span.
Everything was spick-and-span for the inspection.
entries.contrast: Also written spic-and-span; both spellings are met in American writing.

entries.meaning: Spicy has 2 distinct senses.
examples: This curry is spicier than the last one.
I ordered the spicy chicken.
She doesn't eat spicy food.
The book has a few spicy chapters.
He left out the spicy details.

senses.head: Having a strong hot taste from pepper or other spices
examples: This curry is spicier than the last one.
I ordered the spicy chicken.
She doesn't eat spicy food.

senses.head: A little shocking, about sex or scandal
examples: The book has a few spicy chapters.
He left out the spicy details.

entries.meaning: Neat and stylish, in a cheerful, informal way. ---
examples: You look spiffy in that jacket.
They gave the lobby a spiffy new look.
His shoes were even spiffier than mine.

entries.meaning: Spiked has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The dog wore a spiked collar.
Spiked shoes grip the ice.
Someone brought a bowl of spiked punch.
She thinks her drink was spiked.

senses.head: Having sharp points sticking out of it
examples: The dog wore a spiked collar.
Spiked shoes grip the ice.

senses.head: With alcohol or a drug secretly added
examples: Someone brought a bowl of spiked punch.
She thinks her drink was spiked.

entries.meaning: Covered with sharp points, or standing up in stiff points. ---
examples: The plant has long spiky leaves.
He had spiky black hair.
Her hair was even spikier in high school.

entries.meaning: Having to do with the backbone. ---
examples: She had spinal surgery in May.
The accident damaged his spinal cord.
The doctor ordered a spinal X-ray.

entries.meaning: Long, thin and weak-looking. ---
examples: The tomato plant had spindly stems.
A spindly teenager answered the door.
The chair's legs look even spindlier than they are.

entries.meaning: Spineless has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The committee was spineless about the whole thing.
He's too spineless to say no.
Critics called the statement spineless.
Jellyfish are spineless animals.
They planted a spineless variety of cactus.

senses.head: Too weak to stand up for yourself or for other people
examples: The committee was spineless about the whole thing.
He's too spineless to say no.
Critics called the statement spineless.

senses.head: Having no backbone, or no sharp spines
examples: Jellyfish are spineless animals.
They planted a spineless variety of cactus.

entries.meaning: Winding in a curve around a center, going up or outward. ---
examples: We took the spiral staircase to the roof.
She writes in a spiral notebook.
The shell has a tight spiral pattern.
entries.contrast: Also a noun (a spiral of smoke) and a verb (prices spiraled).

entries.meaning: Rising fast and getting out of control. ---
examples: Spiraling rents pushed families out of the city.
They blamed spiraling costs for the delay.
The country faces a spiraling debt problem.
entries.contrast: American spelling has one l: spiraling; British writing doubles it.

entries.meaning: Full of energy and determination. ---
examples: They put up a spirited defense.
It was a spirited debate that ran past midnight.
Her playing is more spirited than technically perfect.
entries.contrast: Very common in compounds: high-spirited, low-spirited, public-spirited.

entries.meaning: Spiritual has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She went on a spiritual retreat.
The book asks spiritual questions.
He became more spiritual after his illness.
The monks are the village's spiritual leaders.
She turned to her spiritual adviser.

senses.head: Having to do with the soul and the inner life rather than the body or money
examples: She went on a spiritual retreat.
The book asks spiritual questions.
He became more spiritual after his illness.

senses.head: Connected with religion and its teaching
examples: The monks are the village's spiritual leaders.
She turned to her spiritual adviser.

entries.meaning: Wanting to hurt someone on purpose, out of bad feeling. ---
examples: That was a spiteful thing to say.
She gets spiteful when she loses.
He wrote a spiteful review of his old boss's book.

entries.meaning: Big, bright and meant to be noticed. ---
examples: The company made a splashy announcement.
She wore a splashy red coat.
This year's opening was even splashier than last year's.

entries.meaning: Very good, or beautiful and impressive to look at. ---
examples: We had a splendid time in Chicago.
The view from the top is splendid.
She wore a splendid green dress.

entries.meaning: Split has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The court reached a split decision.
The town is split over the new school.
She trimmed her split ends.
The bag was split down the side.

senses.head: Divided into parts, or into two sides that disagree
examples: The court reached a split decision.
The town is split over the new school.

senses.head: Broken open along a line
examples: She trimmed her split ends.
The bag was split down the side.

entries.takes: over or on + noun, for the 'divided in opinion' sense
entries.contrast: Also a verb whose forms never change: split, split, split.

entries.meaning: Very bad, said of a headache that feels as if your head were breaking open. ---
examples: I woke up with a splitting headache.
She had a splitting headache all afternoon.
The noise gave him a splitting headache.
entries.position: attributive only — almost always with headache

entries.meaning: Spoiled has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He's a spoiled kid who never hears no.
Their youngest is the most spoiled of the three.
The milk was spoiled.
Throw out any spoiled meat.

senses.head: Given everything and allowed to behave badly
examples: He's a spoiled kid who never hears no.
Their youngest is the most spoiled of the three.

senses.head: No longer good to eat
examples: The milk was spoiled.
Throw out any spoiled meat.

entries.contrast: American English uses spoiled for both meanings; spoilt is British.

entries.meaning: Said out loud, not written down. ---
examples: Her spoken English is better than her writing.
The exam has a spoken section.
We had a spoken agreement, nothing on paper.
entries.contrast: Also the past participle of speak, and the second half of soft-spoken, well-spoken.

entries.meaning: Soft and full of air, springing back when you press it. ---
examples: The ground was spongy after the rain.
She baked a light, spongy cake.
The old mattress got spongier every year.

entries.meaning: Done suddenly, out of feeling and without planning. ---
examples: We took a spontaneous trip to the coast.
The crowd broke into spontaneous applause.
She's more spontaneous than her sister.

entries.meaning: Strange and a little frightening. ---
examples: The old house looks spooky at night.
That's a spooky coincidence.
The basement is even spookier with the lights off.

entries.meaning: Happening now and then, with no regular pattern. ---
examples: There was sporadic gunfire through the night.
Her attendance has been sporadic all semester.
We get sporadic emails from him.

entries.meaning: Sporting has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He buys his gear at a sporting goods store.
The town has a long sporting tradition.
You have a sporting chance of winning.
Letting him go first was a sporting gesture.

senses.head: Having to do with sports
examples: He buys his gear at a sporting goods store.
The town has a long sporting tradition.

senses.head: Fair, giving the other side a real chance
examples: You have a sporting chance of winning.
Letting him go first was a sporting gesture.

entries.meaning: Behaving fairly and with respect toward the other side in a game. ---
examples: Shaking hands after the loss was sportsmanlike.
He made a sportsmanlike apology to the referee.
Her response was gracious and sportsmanlike.

entries.meaning: Sporty has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She drives a sporty little hatchback.
The new model is sportier than the old one.
He's the sporty one in the family.
She was never very sporty.

senses.head: Looking fast and stylish, the way sports cars and sports clothes do
examples: She drives a sporty little hatchback.
The new model is sportier than the old one.

senses.head: Good at sports, or fond of playing them
examples: He's the sporty one in the family.
She was never very sporty.

entries.meaning: Covered with round marks of another color. ---
examples: A spotted dog ran across the yard.
She wore a black and white spotted scarf.
The eggs are pale blue and spotted.
entries.contrast: Also the past of spot: I spotted her in the crowd.

entries.meaning: Good in some parts and bad in others; not steady. ---
examples: The cell service out here is spotty.
He has a spotty work record.
Coverage gets spottier once you leave town.
entries.contrast: In American English spotty means uneven; in British English it usually means 'covered in pimples'.

entries.meaning: Having to do with a husband or a wife. ---
examples: She receives spousal support.
The plan offers spousal benefits.
The form asks for spousal consent.

entries.meaning: Spreading out over a large area without a neat shape. ---
examples: They live on a sprawling ranch outside Austin.
Phoenix is a sprawling city.
The novel is a sprawling family story.

entries.meaning: Lively and quick on your feet, often said of an older person. ---
examples: Her grandmother is still sprightly at ninety.
He walked down the hall with a sprightly step.
She seemed sprightlier after the trip.

entries.meaning: Fitted with a spring, so that it shuts or pops open by itself. ---
examples: The box has a spring-loaded lid.
The gate is spring-loaded and closes behind you.
Use a spring-loaded clamp to hold the boards.

entries.meaning: Warm and fresh, the way early spring feels. ---
examples: We had a springlike afternoon in February.
The weather turned springlike over the weekend.
There was a springlike smell in the air.

entries.meaning: Going back into shape right after you press or step on it. ---
examples: The new track feels springy underfoot.
She has a springy walk.
This mattress is springier than the old one.

entries.meaning: Still active and quick, especially at an older age. ---
examples: He's spry for eighty-five.
A spry old man sold us the tickets.
She's spryer than people half her age.
entries.contrast: The comparative forms are also spelled sprier, spriest.

entries.meaning: Stubborn has 2 distinct senses.
examples: My grandfather is the most stubborn man I know.
Don't be so stubborn — just let me help you.
She's stubborn about doing everything herself.
There's a stubborn stain on the carpet.
She has a stubborn cough that won't go away.

senses.head: Refusing to change your mind, even when you should
examples: My grandfather is the most stubborn man I know.
Don't be so stubborn — just let me help you.
She's stubborn about doing everything herself.

senses.head: Hard to get rid of or deal with, of a thing
examples: There's a stubborn stain on the carpet.
She has a stubborn cough that won't go away.

entries.meaning: Short and thick. ---
examples: He has short, stubby fingers.
The dog has a stubby little tail.
This pencil is even stubbier than the last one.

entries.meaning: Stuck has 3 distinct senses.
examples: The window is stuck — I can't get it open.
We were stuck in traffic for an hour.
I'm stuck on question four.
If you get stuck, ask the TA.
I got stuck with the whole bill.
We're stuck with this couch until we can afford a new one.

senses.head: Held fast and unable to move
examples: The window is stuck — I can't get it open.
We were stuck in traffic for an hour.

senses.head: Unable to go on because you don't know what to do next
examples: I'm stuck on question four.
If you get stuck, ask the TA.

senses.head: Forced to keep something or someone you don't want
examples: I got stuck with the whole bill.
We're stuck with this couch until we can afford a new one.

entries.position: both — usually after a verb: the window is stuck
entries.takes: in + a place (stuck in traffic); on + a problem; with + something you can't get rid of
entries.preposition patterns: stuck in · stuck on · stuck with

entries.meaning: Acting as if you are better than other people. ---
examples: The other kids thought she was stuck-up.
He's not stuck-up, he's just shy.
Nobody is more stuck-up than that whole crowd.
entries.contrast: Informal, and always about a person who acts superior. Nothing to do with stuck meaning 'unable to move'.

entries.meaning: Studded has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He wore a studded leather jacket.
She had on a studded belt and heavy boots.
The night sky was studded with stars.
The cast is studded with names you'll recognize.

senses.head: Having small metal pieces or jewels set into the surface
examples: He wore a studded leather jacket.
She had on a studded belt and heavy boots.

senses.head: Dotted all over with something
examples: The night sky was studded with stars.
The cast is studded with names you'll recognize.

entries.meaning: Done on purpose and carefully worked out, while meant to look effortless. ---
examples: He answered with studied calm.
Her studied indifference fooled nobody.
There was a studied casualness about the whole performance.
entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: a studied calm
entries.contrast: As an adjective it does not mean 'that has been studied'. It means done on purpose while trying to look natural: studied indifference.

entries.meaning: Spending a lot of time studying and enjoying it. ---
examples: She was a quiet, studious kid.
He's more studious than his brother ever was.
The studious ones sat in the front row.

entries.meaning: Stuffed has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The kids sleep with their stuffed animals.
We had stuffed peppers for dinner.
No more for me — I'm stuffed.
Everyone was stuffed by the time the pie came out.

senses.head: Filled with something, especially soft filling or food
examples: The kids sleep with their stuffed animals.
We had stuffed peppers for dinner.

senses.head: So full of food that you can't eat any more
examples: No more for me — I'm stuffed.
Everyone was stuffed by the time the pie came out.

entries.contrast: Stuffed up is a different thing: it means your nose is blocked by a cold.

entries.meaning: Stuffy has 3 distinct senses.
examples: It's stuffy in here — can we open a window?
The bedroom gets stuffier as the night goes on.
It's a stuffy old club where you still need a tie.
His parents are nice, just a little stuffy.
I have a stuffy nose and a sore throat.
My nose gets stuffy every spring.

senses.head: Warm and airless, with no fresh air
examples: It's stuffy in here — can we open a window?
The bedroom gets stuffier as the night goes on.

senses.head: Formal, old-fashioned and no fun
examples: It's a stuffy old club where you still need a tie.
His parents are nice, just a little stuffy.

senses.head: Blocked, of your nose
examples: I have a stuffy nose and a sore throat.
My nose gets stuffy every spring.

entries.meaning: So shocked that you can't react. ---
examples: We were stunned by the news.
There was a stunned silence in the room.
I was stunned that nobody said anything.
entries.position: both — mostly after a verb; before a noun in a stunned silence
entries.contrast: Stunned is how the person feels; stunning is what causes it. I was stunned, but the news was stunning.

entries.meaning: Stunning has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She looked stunning in that dress.
The view from the top is stunning.
It's the most stunning building in the city.
The team pulled off a stunning upset.
It was a stunning reversal for the company.

senses.head: Extremely beautiful or impressive
examples: She looked stunning in that dress.
The view from the top is stunning.
It's the most stunning building in the city.

senses.head: So surprising that it shocks people
examples: The team pulled off a stunning upset.
It was a stunning reversal for the company.

entries.contrast: The pair to watch: stunning describes the thing (a stunning view), stunned describes the person (I was stunned).

entries.meaning: Kept from growing or developing fully. ---
examples: The trees along the ridge are stunted by the wind.
Poor nutrition leads to stunted growth.
His emotional development was stunted by those years.
entries.form: -ed from stunt, to hold growth back
entries.contrast: Nothing to do with the noun stunt in a movie stunt.

entries.meaning: So shocked, tired or bored that you can barely think. ---
examples: We sat there stupefied by the heat.
He stared at the screen with a stupefied look.
The audience was simply stupefied.

entries.meaning: Amazingly big or amazingly good. ---
examples: They did a stupendous amount of work in one week.
The final number was stupendous — the whole theater stood up.
That's the most stupendous thing I've ever seen.

entries.meaning: Sturdy has 2 distinct senses.
examples: We need a sturdy table for the printer.
These boots are sturdier than the ones I had.
He was a short, sturdy man with big hands.
The pony is small but sturdy.

senses.head: Strongly built and not easily broken
examples: We need a sturdy table for the printer.
These boots are sturdier than the ones I had.

senses.head: Strong and solid-looking, of a person or animal
examples: He was a short, sturdy man with big hands.
The pony is small but sturdy.

entries.meaning: Fashionable and good-looking. ---
examples: She always looks stylish, even in jeans.
It's a small but very stylish hotel.
His apartment is the most stylish place I've been in.

entries.meaning: Having to do with the style of a piece of writing, music or art. ---
examples: It's a stylistic choice, not a grammar rule.
The two albums have stylistic differences but the same band.
The edits were purely stylistic.
entries.contrast: Stylistic is about style in writing or art; stylish is about looking good. A stylistic choice is not the same as a stylish one.

entries.meaning: Drawn or done in an artificial style instead of a realistic one. ---
examples: The logo is a stylized bird.
The fight scenes are highly stylized.
It's a stylized version of a 1950s diner.
entries.contrast: American spelling stylized; British stylised.

entries.meaning: Smooth, confident and polite, usually a man. ---
examples: He's a suave guy in an expensive suit.
The host was suave and a little too smooth.
He was the most suave person at the party.
entries.contrast: Often a little negative: suave suggests charm you don't quite trust. Said SWAHV, not 'soo-AHV'.

entries.meaning: Of the part of Africa south of the Sahara desert. ---
examples: Most of the program's work is in sub-Saharan Africa.
Sub-Saharan countries were hit hardest by the drought.
She studies sub-Saharan trade routes.
entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: sub-Saharan Africa

entries.meaning: Of the cold region just south of the Arctic. ---
examples: They spent a winter at a subarctic research station.
Subarctic forests cover much of Canada.
The town has a subarctic climate with short summers.
entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: a subarctic climate

entries.meaning: Smaller than an atom, or happening inside one. ---
examples: Protons and electrons are subatomic particles.
The lab does subatomic physics.
At the subatomic level the rules are different.
entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: subatomic particles

entries.meaning: Happening in your mind without you knowing it. ---
examples: It was a subconscious decision — I didn't plan it.
She has a subconscious fear of open water.
Subconscious bias shows up in who gets called back.
entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: a subconscious fear
entries.contrast: Also a noun: your subconscious. The near-synonym unconscious is the one doctors use for someone who has passed out.

entries.meaning: Subdued has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Everyone was subdued after the meeting.
The crowd was strangely subdued for a playoff game.
The restaurant has subdued lighting.
She painted the walls in subdued grays.

senses.head: Quieter and less cheerful than usual
examples: Everyone was subdued after the meeting.
The crowd was strangely subdued for a playoff game.

senses.head: Soft and not bright, of light or color
examples: The restaurant has subdued lighting.
She painted the walls in subdued grays.

entries.meaning: Below what any human being should have to live with, or treated as less than human. ---
examples: The families lived in subhuman conditions.
The camp's subhuman conditions shocked the inspectors.
The propaganda painted them as subhuman.
entries.position: both — before a noun (subhuman conditions) or after a verb
entries.contrast: An ugly word. Calling people subhuman is the language of propaganda; subhuman conditions is the safer, ordinary use.

entries.meaning: Likely to be affected by something, or depending on it. ---
examples: All prices are subject to change without notice.
The plan is subject to the board's approval.
This area is subject to flooding in the spring.
entries.position: predicative only — after a verb, always with to: subject to change
entries.contrast: The adjective is stressed on the first syllable like the noun, SUHB-jikt; the verb subject is suhb-JEKT. As an adjective it never stands alone — it always has to.

entries.meaning: Based on personal feelings and opinions rather than facts. ---
examples: Taste in music is completely subjective.
That's a subjective judgment, not a fact.
Grading essays is more subjective than grading math.
entries.contrast: Subjective is based on one person's feelings; objective is based on facts anyone can check.

entries.meaning: Of the verb form used for wishes, demands and unreal situations. ---
examples: English has a subjunctive mood, but it's easy to miss.
Subjunctive forms show up after insist, demand and suggest.
The teacher marked it wrong because the subjunctive form was missing.
entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: the subjunctive mood
entries.contrast: Also a noun: use the subjunctive. In American English you meet it in I insist that he be there and If I were you.

entries.meaning: So beautiful or great that it fills you with wonder. ---
examples: The view from the ridge was sublime.
Her performance was nothing short of sublime.
The pie was sublime — I had two pieces.
entries.contrast: Also a noun in from the sublime to the ridiculous. Said suh-BLYM, not like subliminal.

entries.meaning: Affecting your mind below the level where you notice it. ---
examples: The ad was accused of using subliminal messages.
There's a subliminal push to buy more than you need.
The effect is subliminal — you don't notice it happening.

entries.meaning: Under the surface of the water. ---
examples: Half the town was submerged after the storm.
Submerged rocks make the channel dangerous.
The car sat submerged in six feet of water.

entries.meaning: Always doing what other people want, without arguing. ---
examples: He was raised to be quiet and submissive.
The dog rolled over in a submissive pose.
Her tone got more submissive the longer the boss talked.

entries.meaning: Subordinate has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Everything else is subordinate to safety.
She holds a subordinate position in the department.
Subordinate clauses start with words like because and although.
Underline the subordinate clause in each sentence.

senses.head: Lower in rank or less important than something else
examples: Everything else is subordinate to safety.
She holds a subordinate position in the department.

senses.head: In grammar, of a clause that depends on a main clause
examples: Subordinate clauses start with words like because and although.
Underline the subordinate clause in each sentence.

entries.contrast: The adjective and the noun end in a schwa, suh-BOR-duh-nuht; the verb ends -nate, suh-BOR-duh-nayt.

entries.meaning: Coming after something else in time. ---
examples: The subsequent investigation found nothing.
In subsequent years the town grew fast.
Each subsequent payment is smaller than the last.
entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: subsequent years
entries.takes: to + noun, in formal writing: subsequent to the hearing
entries.contrast: Formal. Subsequent just means later; consequent means caused by it.

entries.meaning: Too willing to obey, or kept in a lower position. ---
examples: He hated the subservient tone his coworkers used with the boss.
The board became subservient to the CEO.
She refuses to be subservient to anyone.

entries.meaning: Less important than the main thing, and connected to it. ---
examples: Money was a subsidiary concern at that point.
She played a subsidiary role in the negotiations.
These questions are subsidiary to the main one.
entries.contrast: Also a common noun: a subsidiary of the company.

entries.meaning: Paid for in part by a government or an employer, so it costs less. ---
examples: They live in subsidized housing.
The bus passes are subsidized by the city.
Subsidized school lunches keep a lot of kids fed.
entries.contrast: American spelling subsidized; British subsidised.

entries.meaning: Below the quality that is required or expected. ---
examples: The building went up with substandard materials.
Tenants complained about substandard heating.
The work was substandard and had to be redone.

entries.meaning: Substantial has 2 distinct senses.
examples: They made a substantial donation to the school.
There's been substantial progress since March.
We had a substantial breakfast before the hike.
The desk is old but substantial.

senses.head: Large in amount or important enough to matter
examples: They made a substantial donation to the school.
There's been substantial progress since March.

senses.head: Solidly built, or big and filling
examples: We had a substantial breakfast before the hike.
The desk is old but substantial.

entries.contrast: Substantial is about size or solidity; substantive is about real content. A substantial meal fills you up; a substantive discussion gets somewhere.

entries.meaning: Dealing with the real content of something, not the surface. ---
examples: The draft needs substantive changes, not just edits.
For the first time they had a substantive discussion.
Nothing substantive came out of the meeting.
entries.contrast: Not the same as substantial: substantive changes change the meaning, substantial changes are simply big.

entries.meaning: Taking the place of the usual person or thing. ---
examples: We had a substitute teacher all week.
The coach put in a substitute goalie in the third period.
The district keeps a list of substitute drivers.
entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: a substitute teacher
entries.contrast: Also a noun (find a substitute) and a verb (substitute butter for oil). As an adjective it only goes before a noun — you cannot say the teacher was substitute.

entries.meaning: Under the ground. ---
examples: The city has a whole subterranean network of tunnels.
Subterranean rivers run under the limestone.
They found a subterranean chamber beneath the church.
entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: a subterranean tunnel

entries.meaning: Of the warm regions just outside the tropics. ---
examples: South Florida has a subtropical climate.
Subtropical plants won't survive a hard freeze.
The storm formed in subtropical waters.
entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: a subtropical climate

entries.meaning: Suburban has 2 distinct senses.
examples: They moved to a suburban school district.
Suburban traffic is worst around three o'clock.
The whole movie makes fun of suburban life.
This street feels more suburban than the rest of the city.

senses.head: In or of the suburbs, the residential areas outside a city
examples: They moved to a suburban school district.
Suburban traffic is worst around three o'clock.

senses.head: Typical of the suburbs — comfortable, ordinary and a little dull
examples: The whole movie makes fun of suburban life.
This street feels more suburban than the rest of the city.

entries.contrast: Urban is the city itself, suburban the ring of towns around it, rural the countryside.

entries.meaning: Quietly working against a government, a system or accepted ideas. ---
examples: The book was banned as subversive.
Her comedy is quietly subversive.
They were charged with subversive activity.
entries.contrast: Also a noun for a person: the government called them subversives.

entries.meaning: Coming after, one after another. ---
examples: Each succeeding year the festival got bigger.
Succeeding generations told the story differently.
The rule was kept by every succeeding administration.
entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: succeeding generations
entries.form: -ing from succeed in its older sense, to follow
entries.contrast: Here succeeding means following, not doing well. Each succeeding year means each year after it.

entries.meaning: Following one after the other without a break. ---
examples: It rained for five successive days.
She won three successive elections.
Each successive draft got shorter.
entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: three successive wins
entries.contrast: Successive means one after another; successful means it worked. Three successive wins is three in a row.

entries.meaning: Saying a lot in very few words. ---
examples: Her answer was succinct and clear.
Keep the summary succinct — one page at most.
The second draft is more succinct than the first.

entries.meaning: Succulent has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The lamb was succulent and fell off the bone.
We ate succulent peaches all through August.
Cactus and aloe are succulent plants.
Succulent leaves hold water through the dry season.

senses.head: Juicy and delicious, of meat or fruit
examples: The lamb was succulent and fell off the bone.
We ate succulent peaches all through August.

senses.head: Thick and fleshy, of a plant that stores water
examples: Cactus and aloe are succulent plants.
Succulent leaves hold water through the dry season.

entries.contrast: Also a noun for plants like aloe and jade: a shelf of succulents.

entries.meaning: Of or from Sudan, or its people. ---
examples: The Sudanese students meet on Fridays.
Her father is Sudanese.
Sudanese coffee is served with ginger.
entries.contrast: Like all -ese words it adds no -s for people: two Sudanese students. For one person say a Sudanese man, not a Sudanese.

entries.meaning: Happening quickly and without warning. ---
examples: There was a sudden drop in temperature.
A sudden noise woke everyone up.
His death was sudden — nobody had time to say goodbye.
entries.contrast: The adverb is suddenly, never sudden. All of a sudden is a fixed phrase meaning suddenly.

entries.meaning: As much as is needed. ---
examples: There wasn't sufficient evidence to charge anyone.
One cup of rice is sufficient for two people.
The money was sufficient to cover the repairs.
entries.contrast: More formal than enough, and it goes before the noun: sufficient evidence, but enough evidence.

entries.meaning: Suffocating has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The bus was suffocating by noon.
A suffocating heat hung over the city.
She found the relationship suffocating.
It was a suffocating little town to grow up in.

senses.head: So hot and airless that it is hard to breathe
examples: The bus was suffocating by noon.
A suffocating heat hung over the city.

senses.head: So controlling that you feel trapped
examples: She found the relationship suffocating.
It was a suffocating little town to grow up in.

entries.meaning: Of the mystical tradition within Islam. ---
examples: She teaches Sufi poetry in translation.
The Sufi orders spread across North Africa.
We heard Sufi music at the festival.
entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: Sufi poetry
entries.contrast: Also a noun for a person: a Sufi. The tradition itself is Sufism, the mystical side of Islam.

entries.meaning: Sugar-coated has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Sugar-coated cereal is basically dessert.
The pills are sugar-coated so kids will take them.
He gave us the sugar-coated version of the story.
Her report was sugar-coated, but the numbers were bad.

senses.head: Covered with a layer of sugar
examples: Sugar-coated cereal is basically dessert.
The pills are sugar-coated so kids will take them.

senses.head: Made to sound nicer than it really is
examples: He gave us the sugar-coated version of the story.
Her report was sugar-coated, but the numbers were bad.

entries.meaning: Made without sugar. ---
examples: She chews sugarless gum all day.
They sell a sugarless version of the syrup.
Sugarless candy usually uses sorbitol.
entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: sugarless gum
entries.contrast: Sugar-free is the more common label in American stores; sugarless is mostly used for gum and candy.

entries.meaning: Sugary has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The kids drink way too many sugary sodas.
The sauce was thin and sugary.
She answered in a sugary voice that fooled nobody.
He gave me a sugary smile and walked off.

senses.head: Containing a lot of sugar, or too sweet
examples: The kids drink way too many sugary sodas.
The sauce was thin and sugary.

senses.head: Too sweet in the way someone speaks or smiles
examples: She answered in a sugary voice that fooled nobody.
He gave me a sugary smile and walked off.

entries.meaning: Suggestive has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The symptoms are suggestive of the flu.
The room had a smell suggestive of old books.
The lyrics are pretty suggestive.
He made a suggestive comment and the table went quiet.

senses.head: Making you think of something; hinting at it
examples: The symptoms are suggestive of the flu.
The room had a smell suggestive of old books.

senses.head: Hinting at sex
examples: The lyrics are pretty suggestive.
He made a suggestive comment and the table went quiet.

entries.contrast: Watch out for the second meaning: a suggestive remark is usually about sex, not about making a suggestion.

entries.meaning: Suicidal has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He called the hotline because he was feeling suicidal.
Suicidal thoughts are a reason to get help right away.
Raising prices now would be suicidal.
It was a suicidal charge across open ground.

senses.head: Wanting to kill yourself
examples: He called the hotline because he was feeling suicidal.
Suicidal thoughts are a reason to get help right away.

senses.head: So dangerous or foolish that it could destroy you
examples: Raising prices now would be suicidal.
It was a suicidal charge across open ground.

entries.meaning: Right for a particular job, person or situation. ---
examples: She's well suited to this kind of work.
The house isn't suited for a family of six.
Of the three, he's the best suited to run the meeting.
entries.position: predicative only — after a verb, with to or for: well suited to the job
entries.comparison: not gradable — but almost always with well, better or ideally: better suited to the job
entries.contrast: Suited needs well, better or ideally in front of it; plain He is suited sounds wrong. Suitable is the word that goes before a noun: a suitable candidate.

entries.meaning: Silently angry and showing it, the way a child does. ---
examples: He's been sulky ever since we said no.
She gave me a sulky look and went to her room.
The longer we waited, the sulkier he got.

entries.meaning: Sullen has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The boy sat sullen and quiet through dinner.
She answered with a sullen shrug.
A sullen gray sky hung over the lake.
The morning was cold and sullen.

senses.head: Quiet and bad-tempered, refusing to talk
examples: The boy sat sullen and quiet through dinner.
She answered with a sullen shrug.

senses.head: Dark and gloomy, of the sky or weather
examples: A sullen gray sky hung over the lake.
The morning was cold and sullen.

entries.contrast: Sullen is grown-up and heavy; sulky is childish. Neither one is solemn, which is serious without the anger.

entries.meaning: Sultry has 2 distinct senses.
examples: It was a sultry August afternoon.
August in Houston is sultrier than anything I grew up with.
She has a sultry voice.
He gave her a sultry look across the bar.

senses.head: Hot and humid, of the weather
examples: It was a sultry August afternoon.
August in Houston is sultrier than anything I grew up with.

senses.head: Attractive in a slow, sexual way
examples: She has a sultry voice.
He gave her a sultry look across the bar.

entries.meaning: Of the ancient people of southern Mesopotamia, or their language. ---
examples: The museum has a room of Sumerian tablets.
Sumerian is the oldest written language we can still read.
They spent the semester on Sumerian myths.
entries.contrast: Also a noun for the people and the language. Not Sumatran, which is about the island of Sumatra.

entries.meaning: Graduating with the highest level of honors. ---
examples: The program takes mostly summa cum laude graduates.
She put her summa cum laude honors right at the top of her résumé.
He was the only summa cum laude student in his class that year.
entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: a summa cum laude graduate
entries.contrast: Latin, 'with highest praise'. It is used even more often as an adverb after graduate: She graduated summa cum laude. The three levels, lowest first, are cum laude, magna cum laude, summa cum laude.

entries.meaning: Done quickly and without the usual procedure. ---
examples: The judge granted summary judgment for the defense.
He was fired in a summary dismissal with no hearing.
The report described summary executions in the border towns.
entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: summary judgment
entries.contrast: Far more common as a noun (write a summary). The adjective is legal or official and means done fast, skipping the usual steps: summary judgment, summary dismissal.

entries.meaning: Like summer, or right for summer. ---
examples: She wore a light, summery dress.
It's unusually summery for April.
The menu turns summery in June — lots of tomatoes and corn.
entries.contrast: Said exactly like summary, but it means 'like summer': a summery dress, summery weather.

entries.meaning: Expensive and grand, in a way that shows. ---
examples: They served a sumptuous dinner.
The hotel lobby is sumptuous — marble everywhere.
It was the most sumptuous meal I've had in years.

entries.meaning: Getting a lot of bright sunshine. ---
examples: We ate lunch on a sun-drenched patio.
The brochure promised sun-drenched beaches.
It's a sun-drenched apartment with windows on three sides.
entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: a sun-drenched patio
entries.contrast: Travel-brochure English. It almost never comes after a verb.

entries.meaning: Dried in the sun instead of by machine. ---
examples: Add sun-dried tomatoes to the pasta.
They sell sun-dried apricots by the pound.
Sun-dried bricks are still used in the region.
entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: sun-dried tomatoes

entries.meaning: Red and sore from too much sun. ---
examples: My shoulders are sunburned.
A sunburned tourist came in asking for aloe.
We got back from the lake sunburned and happy.
entries.comparison: not gradable — degree comes from badly or a little: badly sunburned
entries.contrast: American English says sunburned; sunburnt is mostly British. Tanned is the brown you want, sunburned is the red you don't.

entries.meaning: Of several different kinds, not worth listing one by one. ---
examples: The drawer is full of pens, cords and sundry junk.
She handles billing, scheduling and sundry other tasks.
Various and sundry relatives showed up for dinner.
entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: sundry items
entries.contrast: Formal or joking, and usually in the phrases various and sundry or all and sundry (everybody). The noun sundries means small odds and ends.

entries.meaning: Sunken has 3 distinct senses.
examples: Divers found the sunken ship in 300 feet of water.
They mapped the sunken village under the reservoir.
He had sunken cheeks and dark circles under his eyes.
Her sunken eyes made her look exhausted.
The house has a sunken living room.
There's a sunken garden behind the church.

senses.head: Lying under the water after sinking
examples: Divers found the sunken ship in 300 feet of water.
They mapped the sunken village under the reservoir.

senses.head: Hollow, of eyes or cheeks
examples: He had sunken cheeks and dark circles under his eyes.
Her sunken eyes made her look exhausted.

senses.head: Built lower than the floor or ground around it
examples: The house has a sunken living room.
There's a sunken garden behind the church.

entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: a sunken ship
entries.form: the old participle of sink; the modern one is sunk
entries.contrast: Sunken only goes before a noun. After a verb you need sunk: a sunken ship, but the ship has sunk.

entries.meaning: Lit by the sun. ---
examples: We sat in a sunlit corner of the café.
The sunlit kitchen is the best room in the house.
Dust floated in the sunlit air.
entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: a sunlit room

entries.meaning: Sunny has 2 distinct senses.
examples: It'll be sunny and warm all weekend.
They have a sunny apartment on the top floor.
Saturday was sunnier than Sunday.
She has a sunny personality.

A supercharged engine eats gas.

entries.meaning: Acting as if other people are beneath you. ---

senses.head: Only on the surface, of a wound or damage

senses.head: Caring only about looks and appearances, of a person

He's not superficial — he just likes nice clothes.

entries.meaning: Having to do with managing other workers. ---

entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: a supervisory role

entries.meaning: Supple has 2 distinct senses.

The leather gets more supple with use.
Yoga keeps her supple.

senses.head: Bending easily without cracking, of leather or cloth

The leather gets more supple with use.

senses.head: Able to bend and move easily, of a body
examples: Yoga keeps her supple.
Dancers stay supple into their fifties.

entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: supplemental income

senses.head: Backing something up — a claim, or a structure

Don't cut into a supporting wall.

entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: a supporting role

entries.meaning: Giving help, encouragement and sympathy. ---

entries.contrast: Not supporting: a supportive friend helps you, a supporting actor has the second-biggest part.

entries.meaning: Said to be so, but probably not true. ---

entries.meaning: Suppressed has 2 distinct senses.

senses.head: Held back so it doesn't show, of a feeling or a sound

There was a suppressed laugh at the back of the room.

senses.head: Kept from being published or made known

Suppressed evidence can get a case thrown out.

He was the supreme commander of the allied forces.
In this house the cat reigns supreme.

entries.meaning: Sure-footed has 2 distinct senses.

senses.head: Able to walk or climb without slipping

senses.head: Confident and unlikely to make a mistake

senses.head: Rising quickly and by a lot
examples: Surging rents pushed families out of the city.
The company blamed surging costs for the layoffs.

senses.head: Moving forward in a powerful wave
examples: The surging crowd carried us toward the gate.
Surging water tore the dock loose.

entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: surging prices

entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: a surreptitious glance

senses.head: Made by a chemical process instead of coming from nature
examples: The jacket is filled with a synthetic material.
Synthetic rubber holds up better in the cold.
Most of the vitamins on that shelf are synthetic.

senses.head: Not genuine — made to look or sound real
examples: The dialogue felt synthetic.
There was something synthetic about his enthusiasm.

entries.position: both — a synthetic fabric, The fibers are synthetic
entries.comparison: not gradable — but more synthetic is possible about a sound or a feeling

entries.meaning: Of or from Syria, its people or its culture. ---
examples: We ate at a Syrian restaurant on Fifth Street.
She studies Syrian history.
My co-worker is Syrian.
entries.position: both — Syrian food, Her husband is Syrian
entries.contrast: Always capitalized, and the same word names the people: a Syrian family, He's Syrian, two Syrians.

entries.meaning: Done carefully, in an organized, step-by-step way. ---
examples: They made a systematic search of the building.
We need a more systematic way to track orders.
The report describes systematic abuse over many years.
entries.position: both — mostly before a noun: a systematic search
entries.contrast: Systematic means done step by step, on a plan; systemic means built into the whole system: a systematic search but systemic corruption.

entries.meaning: Systemic has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The audit found systemic problems, not one bad manager.
They call it a systemic failure of oversight.
The infection became systemic.
Systemic drugs travel through the bloodstream.

senses.head: Affecting a whole organization or society, not just one part of it
examples: The audit found systemic problems, not one bad manager.
They call it a systemic failure of oversight.

senses.head: Affecting the entire body, in medicine
examples: The infection became systemic.
Systemic drugs travel through the bloodstream.

entries.position: both — mostly before a noun: systemic failure
entries.contrast: Don't mix it up with systematic, which means methodical. Systemic means running through the whole system: systemic racism, a systemic infection.
